    Appendix A Limitations

    LLM-agent-centric balance criteria.

    RuleSmith optimizes for balance as measured by LLM self-play win rates. Cross-LLM evaluations and the small human study provide encouraging evidence of transfer to the tested populations (Appendix E). LLM win rates of 54–78% against rule-based opponents establish an intermediate opponent baseline while also showing sensitivity to player pairing (Appendix D.2). Within these studies, faction outcomes show no detectable imbalance: human players defeat the agents in most games, yet faction outcomes stay statistically even against both agent scales and between humans (Appendix E.4). Formal guarantees of transfer to human gameplay remain absent, and these studies are limited in scale. Systematic human evaluation and player modeling would strengthen the transfer evidence.

    Action validity, strategy bias, and skill.

    Validation ensures executable games but not good strategies. The measured 3.3%/4.6% execution-rejection rates reflect within-turn conflicts rather than a complete measure of hallucination or parse failure. Both factions are played by the same model, so population-level biases, such as a general preference for aggression, affect both sides and largely cancel in the win-rate disparity; what remains is that balance is defined relative to the evaluated population. The released prompts include strategy guides, so the evaluation population is defined jointly by the model, decoding, and prompts. Humans substantially outperform these agents; how large the strength gap between optimization and evaluation players can become before the optimized rules lose balance remains an open question for future work.

    Statistical and reproducibility scope.

    The three-seed experiment covers the main GP setting. The other ablations and the additional NTBEA, TPE, and LCB searches are single runs. Selecting the final configuration by its lowest in-loop loss can favor a lucky small-batch evaluation; the held-out re-evaluations guard against this, as the single LCB run illustrates. Binomial uncertainty and failure to reject equality do not establish equivalence within five percentage points. Human games share a few participants and should not be treated as 60 independent draws from a broad human population. Seeds and optimizer settings for the additional runs are listed in Table 22.

    Designer-specified rule space.

    The engine, the choice of tunable versus fixed rules, parameter bounds, and the objective require designer input. A balanced solution must be accessible within those bounds. Several reported settings lie at boundaries; widening ranges and re-optimizing is a practical extension, while automated range discovery remains future work.

    Simplified game environment.

    CivMini is a deliberately simplified testbed with a fully observable state, small action spaces, and a compact parameter set. Real commercial strategy games involve thousands of interacting parameters, imperfect information, long-horizon dependencies, and emergent player behaviors that our current framework does not address. Extending RuleSmith to richer, partially observable, or multi-stage environments is a key direction for future work.

    No formal optimality guarantees.

    Bayesian optimization with a Gaussian process surrogate provides no guarantee of finding the globally optimal balanced configuration. The surrogate model may misfit in high-curvature regions, and the discrete projection step introduces approximation errors. Robustness under distribution shifts (such as changes in the player population or game meta) is not explicitly modeled. Incorporating robustness objectives or adversarial evaluation into the optimization loop is a promising avenue for future research.

    Appendix B Broader Impact

    This work advances automated design tools and multi-agent simulation by enabling LLM-based evaluation and optimization of rule-driven systems. By treating large language models as flexible evaluators rather than deployed decision-makers, RuleSmith offers a scalable and interpretable approach to analyzing complex, parameterized environments.

    Potential applications of this framework extend beyond games to domains such as economic modeling, policy analysis, and resource allocation, where outcomes depend on structured rules and multi-actor interactions. At the same time, we recognize that automated simulation and optimization of competitive or adversarial systems may raise ethical considerations if misapplied. In particular, such tools could be misused to over-optimize asymmetric rules in ways that disadvantage certain participants or reduce transparency in decision-making processes.

    To mitigate these risks, RuleSmith is designed as an offline analysis and design-time tool operating on abstract, simplified environments, rather than a system for real-time decision execution. We emphasize that any real-world deployment of rule-optimization frameworks should incorporate human oversight, domain-specific constraints, and ethical review. Overall, we believe the primary impact of this work lies in supporting safer, more transparent, and more systematic design of rule-based systems, while encouraging responsible use in sensitive application domains.

    Appendix C Theoretical Analysis

    This section provides an idealized analysis of two assumptions behind RuleSmith: when exact balance is attainable, and why Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization (GP-BO) is a suitable search procedure for the balance loss. These results should be read as theoretical context rather than as a finite-budget optimality guarantee for the full RuleSmith implementation, which uses Expected Improvement, adaptive evaluation budgets, and a discrete projection step.

    Proposition C.1(Balanced Optimum under Role Symmetry).

    Consider a two-faction game parameterized by θ∈Θ. Suppose Θ contains a role-exchange-invariant configuration θ_sym, and suppose the proxy-player policy distribution is invariant under swapping the two faction roles. Then

    w_E(θ_sym)=w_N(θ_sym).

    		(7)

    Consequently, for the balance loss in Eq. (3),

    L(θ_sym)=1.5 w_D(θ_sym).

    		(8)

    In particular, if w_D(θ_sym)=0, then

    L(θ_sym)=0,

    		(9)

    and the optimal balance loss obeys

    \min_θ∈ΘL(θ)=0.

    		(10)

    Proof.

    At a role-exchange-invariant configuration, swapping the faction labels leaves the game distribution unchanged. By the policy-symmetry assumption, the induced distribution over trajectories is also unchanged after the swap, except that Empire and Nomads exchange labels. Therefore, the probability of an Empire win before the swap equals the probability of a Nomads win after the swap, giving

    w_E(θ_sym)=w_N(θ_sym).

    Since w_E=w_N=(1-w_D)/2 at this configuration, substituting into Eq. (3) yields

    L(θ_sym)=|w_E(θ_sym)-0.5|+|w_N(θ_sym)-0.5|+0.5 w_D(θ_sym)=1.5 w_D(θ_sym).

    Thus, if the symmetric configuration has no draw probability, w_D(θ_sym)=0, then L(θ_sym)=0. Since the balance loss is nonnegative by definition, this implies \min_θ∈ΘL(θ)=0. ∎

    Remark. This proposition does not claim that every asymmetric ruleset can be made perfectly balanced. Role symmetry guarantees equal faction win probabilities, while exact zero loss for the draw-penalized objective additionally requires zero draw probability. RuleSmith targets the harder practical case where the searchable parameter subspace is asymmetric, discrete, and evaluated through noisy LLM self-play.

    Lemma C.2(Concentration of the empirical projected balance loss).

    Let Θ̃ denote the continuous relaxation used by the optimizer, let D:Θ̃→Θ_disc be the deterministic discretization operator, and define the projected balance objective

    F(θ̃):=L(D(θ̃)).

    At round t, let θ̃ₜ∈Θ̃ be the continuous proposal selected by the optimizer, and let

    θₜ=D(θ̃ₜ)∈Θ_disc

    be the corresponding discretized rule configuration evaluated by the game engine. Suppose Nₜ is chosen using only information available before observing the round-t self-play outcomes. From Nₜ independent rollouts under θₜ, define

    ŵ_E,t,ŵ_N,t,ŵ_D,t

    as the empirical Empire-win, Nomads-win, and draw rates, respectively, and let

    yₜ=|ŵ_E,t-0.5|+|ŵ_N,t-0.5|+0.5ŵ_D,t

    be the empirical balance loss observed by the optimizer. Then, for any fixed horizon T and failure probability δ∈(0,1), with probability at least 1-δ, simultaneously for all t=1,…,T,

    |yₜ-F(θ̃ₜ)|=|yₜ-L(D(θ̃ₜ))|≤ηₜ, ηₜ=5/2√(\log(6T/δ))/(2Nₜ).

    Proof.

    Condition on the history before round t. Since θ̃ₜ and Nₜ are chosen before observing the round-t outcomes, the projected ruleset θₜ=D(θ̃ₜ) is also fixed before these outcomes are observed. Therefore, the Nₜ rollouts are independent samples from the outcome distribution induced by the evaluated ruleset θₜ.

    For each outcome type j∈{E,N,D}, Hoeffding’s inequality gives

    |ŵ_j,t-wⱼ(θₜ)|≤√(\log(6T/δ))/(2Nₜ)

    simultaneously for all j∈{E,N,D} and all t=1,…,T with probability at least 1-δ, by a union bound.

    On this event, the inequality ||a-c|-|b-c||≤|a-b| gives

    |yₜ-F(θ̃ₜ)|≤|ŵ_E,t-w_E(θₜ)|+|ŵ_N,t-w_N(θₜ)|+0.5|ŵ_D,t-w_D(θₜ)|
    ≤5/2√(\log(6T/δ))/(2Nₜ).

    This proves the claim. ∎

    Proposition C.3(Idealized GP-LCB for projected self-play evaluations).

    Let Θ̃ denote the continuous relaxation used by the optimizer, let D:Θ̃→Θ_disc be the deterministic discretization operator, and define the projected objective

    F(θ̃):=L(D(θ̃)).

    Let

    θ̃^⋆∈\arg\min_θ̃∈Θ̃F(θ̃)

    be an optimal continuous representative of a best projected ruleset.

    At round t, an idealized optimizer selects a continuous proposal θ̃ₜ∈Θ̃, evaluates the projected ruleset D(θ̃ₜ) using Nₜ independent self-play rollouts, and observes the empirical projected loss yₜ defined in Lemma C.2. For this idealized projected-objective analysis, the surrogate is indexed by the pair (θ̃ₜ,yₜ); the implementation stores evaluated discrete coordinates instead. This distinction is part of why this proposition is not a guarantee for the implemented pipeline.

    Assume a bounded kernel diagonal k(x,x)≤1, nondecreasing βₜ, and a GP observation model with variances bounded above and bounded away from zero (the finite replication range permits such bounds). Assume that the GP surrogate is calibrated for the projected objective F in the standard GP bandit sense: there exist confidence parameters {βₜ}_t≥1 such that, with probability at least 1-δ,

    |F(θ̃)-μₜ₋₁(θ̃)|≤√βₜσₜ₋₁(θ̃)

    for all θ̃∈Θ̃ and all t≥1. Here μₜ₋₁ and σₜ₋₁ are the GP posterior mean and posterior standard deviation after t-1 observations. Lemma C.2 motivates a heteroscedastic observation-uncertainty proxy scaling as ηₜ²=O(1/Nₜ), although the GP posterior remains an idealized modeling approximation.

    Consider the idealized GP lower-confidence-bound rule

    θ̃ₜ∈\arg\min_θ̃∈Θ̃[μₜ₋₁(θ̃)-√βₜσₜ₋₁(θ̃)].

    Then, on the confidence event above, the cumulative projected regret

    R_T=∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ(F(θ̃ₜ)-F(θ̃^⋆))

    satisfies

    R_T=O(√Tβ_Tγ_T^(N)),

    where γ_T^(N) is the maximum information gain after T observations under the corresponding heteroscedastic observation uncertainties. Consequently, whenever β_Tγ_T^(N)=o(T), the average projected regret R_T/T vanishes.

    Proof.

    The proof follows the standard GP-UCB/LCB regret argument [48], applied to the minimization of the projected objective F. On the confidence event, for the selected point θ̃ₜ,

    F(θ̃ₜ)≤μₜ₋₁(θ̃ₜ)+√βₜσₜ₋₁(θ̃ₜ),

    while for the optimal projected point θ̃^⋆,

    μₜ₋₁(θ̃^⋆)-√βₜσₜ₋₁(θ̃^⋆)≤F(θ̃^⋆).

    Since θ̃ₜ minimizes the lower confidence bound,

    μₜ₋₁(θ̃ₜ)-√βₜσₜ₋₁(θ̃ₜ)≤μₜ₋₁(θ̃^⋆)-√βₜσₜ₋₁(θ̃^⋆).

    Combining the three inequalities gives

    F(θ̃ₜ)-F(θ̃^⋆)≤2√βₜσₜ₋₁(θ̃ₜ).

    Summing over t=1,…,T and applying the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality yields

    R_T≤2∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ√βₜσₜ₋₁(θ̃ₜ)
    ≤2√Tβ_T∑ₜ₌₁ᵀσₜ₋₁²(θ̃ₜ).

    The standard information-gain argument for GP bandits bounds the cumulative posterior variance by a constant multiple of γ_T^(N), yielding

    R_T=O(√Tβ_Tγ_T^(N)).

    Dividing by T gives vanishing average projected regret whenever β_Tγ_T^(N)=o(T). ∎

    Remark. Proposition C.3 should be interpreted as an idealized analysis of RuleSmith’s continuous-proposal, discrete-evaluation procedure. The optimizer proposes θ̃∈Θ̃, but the environment evaluates only the projected ruleset D(θ̃). Consequently, the objective observed by the optimizer is the projected loss

    F(θ̃)=L(D(θ̃)).

    This objective is generally piecewise constant and can be discontinuous at projection-cell boundaries, so the GP calibration assumption is not guaranteed solely by choosing a smooth kernel such as Matérn 5/2. Rather, it is a standard modeling idealization used to provide theoretical context for GP-based search under noisy self-play evaluations.

    The proposition analyzes an LCB rule, whereas the implemented system uses Expected Improvement together with adaptive replication. The result is therefore not a regret guarantee for the implementation. LCB carries the bound because the classical argument [48] requires an explicit confidence-bound exploration term: the objective is sandwiched by the confidence interval, per-step regret is bounded by the posterior standard deviation at the queried point, and the sum is controlled by the maximum information gain. EI has no comparably standard cumulative-regret bound; its classical guarantee is a convergence rate in the noiseless case [49], and results for noisy EI do not cover a discrete projection combined with EI-dependent replication. The two rules nonetheless use the same posterior quantities. Writing EI=σ h(z) with z=(y^*-μ)/σ and h(z)=zΦ(z)+φ(z), the partial derivatives of EI with respect to the predicted improvement y^*-μ and σ are Φ(z) and φ(z), respectively; because both are positive, EI increases in the exact two quantities that LCB trades off, and the rules differ in how they weight them. Lemma C.2 justifies the concentration of the self-play estimates, Proposition C.3 shows that GP-based search is well posed for this objective under idealized calibration, and the choice among acquisition rules is settled empirically, including the LCB run in Section 4.4.

    Appendix D Validating the Proxy Player

    D.1 LLM Agents vs. Random Agent Baseline

    To establish a lower bound on proxy-player quality, Table 8 evaluates InternVL3.5-8B and InternVL3.5-2B against a random agent that selects uniformly from all legal actions. The prompted LLM agents win 100% of games in every listed configuration, regardless of faction. This establishes effective play relative to random action selection and supports their use as proxy players. As with the other agent comparisons, performance reflects the model together with its prompts and strategy guidance.

    D.2 LLM Agents vs. Rule-Based Agent

    To provide a stronger proxy-player baseline than random play, we design a rule-based agent that executes fixed greedy heuristics with random tie-breaking, without language understanding.

    Empire rule-based agent.

    Farmers always GATHER if possible; otherwise they PASS. Soldiers BATTLE any adjacent enemy (prioritizing the enemy city), or MOVE toward the nearest enemy by Manhattan distance; if multiple enemies are equidistant, one is chosen uniformly at random. The city alternates each turn between PRODUCE_UNIT (farmer) and PRODUCE_UNIT (soldier) whenever resources suffice and an adjacent cell is free; otherwise it uses PRODUCE_RESOURCE.

    Nomads rule-based agent.

    Cavalry BATTLE the enemy city if adjacent; otherwise they BATTLE the nearest adjacent enemy unit; otherwise they MOVE toward the enemy city. The city uses PRODUCE_UNIT (cavalry) when resources allow; otherwise it uses PASS.

    These heuristics capture the core asymmetry of each faction: Empire prioritizes economy and incremental defense, whereas Nomads prioritize fast aggression and city destruction.

    Table 9 reports win rates when LLM agents face the rule-based agent under two parameter sets: parameters optimized with LLM self-play (Table 2) and parameters optimized with rule-based self-play (Table 16).

    LLM-agent win rates range from 54% to 78% in Table 9, below their 100% rate against random agents. The rule-based agent therefore provides meaningful competition for both model sizes. Under LLM-optimized parameters, 8B agents win 78% as Nomads and 75% as Empire. Under rule-based-optimized parameters, these rates are 62% and 73%, respectively. The latter configuration has cheaper Empire units (4), higher farmer gathering (2), and lower Nomads kill gain (5), compatible with an economy favoring frequent Empire production. These descriptive comparisons show interactions between rules and player policies; they do not isolate the contribution of individual mechanics. Together, the random and scripted baselines support the use of prompted LLM agents as a more capable evaluation population in these settings.

    D.3 Comparison with Human-Designed Parameters

    Table 10 compares the authors’ initial configuration (“Initial θ”) against the configuration discovered by RuleSmith using InternVL3.5-8B. This starting point produces a completely one-sided outcome in its original evaluation (Empire 100% | Nomads 0%, loss 1.00). Its low Nomads damage (1) relative to Empire damage (4) and Soldier HP (13) plausibly contributes to this advantage. This interpretation is descriptive; joint parameter changes do not isolate a causal effect for any one coordinate.

    RuleSmith’s Bayesian optimizer jointly adjusts all parameter categories to recover empirical balance. Nomads’ damage triples (1 → 3), their production cost rises (3 → 8), initial resources increase (6 → 10), and Empire Soldier HP falls (13 → 9). These changes are consistent with stronger Nomads combat, costlier cavalry production, and greater initial spending capacity. The optimized combat statistics imply three attacks to eliminate either faction’s main combat unit. The empirical balance loss drops from 1.00 to 0.02; these mechanistic interpretations concern the joint configuration rather than isolated parameter effects.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：把「平衡」写成可优化的损失，再让多智能体去搜参数，改动覆盖全部参数类别。

要点：

  • 目标是把游戏数值平衡从「策划凭经验调」变成可优化问题：定义 balance loss，用高斯过程贝叶斯优化（Expected Improvement + 自适应评估预算）去搜参数
  • 实现是多智能体 LLM 流水线，负责提出与落地跨类别的协同调整，而不是单点微调
  • 案例里作者最初的配置严重偏向 Empire（平衡分 1.00），RuleSmith 通过跨全部参数类别的协同调整把平衡分降到 0.02

为什么值得看：游戏数值调优是 LLM 在游戏行业最容易见效的落点之一：它不要求模型理解画面，只要求它把「公平」写成目标并做搜索。这条给的是可复用的骨架——损失定义 + 贝叶斯搜索 + 多智能体落地修改。

中文摘要：RuleSmith 研究如何用多智能体 LLM 自动完成游戏平衡。它先把平衡写成一个可优化的损失（balance loss），再用高斯过程贝叶斯优化搜索参数：实现上使用 Expected Improvement 与自适应评估预算，LLM 多智能体负责提出并落地跨参数类别的协同修改。作者也给了理论部分：讨论什么条件下精确平衡可达，以及为什么 GP-BO 适合这类平衡损失，同时明确这些结果只是理论背景，不构成对整个实现的有限预算最优性保证。实证上，作者最初的人工配置严重偏向 Empire（平衡分 1.00），RuleSmith 通过跨全部参数类别的协同调整把平衡分降到 0.02，说明自动搜索能修正人类配置的系统性偏向。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-20

本期推送：2026-10-29

RuleSmith: Multi-Agent LLMs for
Automated Game Balancing

Abstract

Game balancing is a longstanding challenge requiring repeated playtesting, expert intuition, and extensive manual tuning. We introduce RuleSmith, a framework that couples multi-agent LLM self-play with surrogate-based optimization over a parameterized rule space. As a proof of concept, we build CivMini, a simplified civilization-style game with two asymmetric factions governed by 12 tunable parameters. LLM agents interpret textual rulebooks and game states to propose actions that are validated by the game engine, yielding noisy estimates of faction win rates. Our primary implementation uses Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization with Expected-Improvement-based adaptive sampling to allocate more evaluation games to promising candidates. RuleSmith consistently finds near-balanced configurations: three independent optimization runs reach near-even empirical win rates in independent 200- and 300-game evaluations, and additional experiments with NTBEA and TPE show that the same self-play interface supports different search components. Cross-model evaluations and small human studies provide preliminary evidence of transfer across player populations. RuleSmith produces interpretable numerical rule adjustments without task-specific policy training. Project and code: https://adonis-galaxy.github.io/RuleSmith-website/.

1 Introduction

Balancing asymmetric strategy games is a core challenge in game design and multi-agent research. Factions differ in abilities, mobility, and economic structure, making it hard to tell whether a given ruleset produces fair or strategically rich gameplay. Traditional approaches rely on human experts cycling through manual tuning, heuristic adjustments, and subjective playtesting. These workflows are slow, expensive, and hard to scale. As games grow more complex, this process becomes not just time-consuming, but often intractable.

Many applications beyond games, including economic modeling, policy analysis, and cybersecurity, face a similar challenge: outcomes depend on parameterized rules, and assessing how rule changes propagate through multi-agent interactions is expensive. We believe the core idea of LLM self-play as a rule evaluator could extend to such settings, though our current work is a proof of concept in a controlled game environment; broader applications remain future work.

Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising new approach. LLMs can interpret rulebooks, reason over game states, and act as zero-shot simulators without task-specific policy training. Prior work shows that LLM agents can negotiate, plan over multiple steps, and exhibit complex strategic behavior [1, 2, 3]. LLM-assisted game design also uses language models to propose parameter edits from simulation feedback [4]. We study a complementary role: LLM agents supply the gameplay evaluations, while a separate optimizer searches the rules.

We introduce RuleSmith, a framework for automatically balancing asymmetric games through LLM self-play and Bayesian optimization. As a proof of concept, we built CivMini, a fully parameterized, grid-based, turn-based game inspired by civilization-style mechanics. Two asymmetric factions, Empire and Nomads, have distinct units, production systems, and combat stats. RuleSmith exposes tunable parameters governing HP, damage, resource gathering, production costs, and scoring weights. This shifts the object of optimization from agent policies to the game rules themselves.

To evaluate a candidate ruleset, RuleSmith runs two LLM agents and collects win rates from multiple self-play games. Since LLM gameplay evaluation is expensive and noisy, we pair Bayesian optimization with acquisition-based adaptive sampling: the number of games scales with each candidate’s Expected Improvement, concentrating compute where balance improvement is most expected.

RuleSmith discovers configurations with near-even empirical faction win rates from imbalanced starting settings. Three independent optimization runs and larger held-out evaluations quantify the repeatability and uncertainty of these results. The optimized parameters describe how HP, resource efficiency, and production costs jointly affect outcomes under the chosen player population.

Contributions.

  • •

    Zero-shot self-play from natural-language rulebooks. LLM agents play CivMini from a rulebook and structured game states without task-specific training, with legality enforced by the engine.

  • •

    Multi-agent pipeline for automated game balancing. RuleSmith makes balance queryable through LLM self-play and connects this evaluator to interchangeable search components. Our primary implementation uses Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization and Expected-Improvement-based adaptive evaluation budgets.

  • •

    Empirical validation across models and game configurations. RuleSmith consistently reaches near-balance: three independent runs yield near-even empirical win rates, with confidence intervals from larger re-evaluations. We study stronger optimizer baselines, model and map variations, action validity, trajectory diversity, and transfer to small human-player samples.

    • 2 Related Work

    Game design automation.

    AI-based playtesting evaluates and refines board, trading-card, and video games using scripted or learned players [5, 6, 7]. Bayesian optimization has been used for game testing [8]; multi-fidelity methods motivate allocating different evaluation budgets to expensive candidates [9]. Procedural content generation (PCG) creates levels, maps, and mechanics [10, 11, 12]; PCGML learns from examples [13], while discriminative and player-aware approaches guide content evaluation [14, 15, 16]. RuleSmith searches numerical rules of an asymmetric executable game, with LLM self-play supplying the evaluations.

    LLMs as designers versus evaluators.

    Huang et al. [4] present AI Game Designer, which uses LLM-guided reasoning to adjust level parameters from the statistical outputs of simulation. In that architecture, the LLM proposes design edits. RuleSmith instead uses LLMs as competing players: their rollouts provide a noisy balance objective, and an external optimizer proposes rule configurations. The engine executes and validates actions, while the LLM players supply behavior conditioned on the rulebook. These roles are complementary. Agent-based game-parameter tuning also predates LLMs: NTBEA was developed for noisy, expensive game evaluation [17, 18]. Our contribution is the empirical side of this question: whether such a loop converges to balance at all, measured with multi-seed runs, optimizer baselines, large-sample re-evaluations, and significance tests. To our knowledge, this assignment of roles has not been studied for asymmetric rule spaces.

    Multi-agent self-play.

    Self-play reinforcement learning primarily optimizes policies under fixed rules. AlphaGo and AlphaZero master board games [19, 20, 21], while OpenAI Five and AlphaStar address complex multiplayer environments [22, 23]. CFR, neural fictitious self-play, and PSRO study strategic play and equilibrium approximation [24, 25, 26, 27]; opponent-learning and population-based approaches model competitive adaptation [28, 29]. We optimize the rules rather than train player policies, using instruction-following LLMs as the evaluation population.

    LLM agents.

    LLM-agent surveys cover tool use, autonomous planning, and simulation [30, 31, 32]. ReAct and HuggingGPT coordinate reasoning and actions [33, 34], while CAMEL, generative agents, and Mindstorms organize interacting agents [35, 3, 36]. ALYMPICS studies strategic interaction in an LLM game-theory playground [37], and language models can themselves act as optimizers [38] or compete in debate [39, 40]. RuleSmith grounds interaction in engine-validated game actions and connects the resulting outcomes to rule optimization.

    3 Method

    RuleSmith takes five inputs: (i) an engine that executes actions and returns outcomes, (ii) a parameterized rule space with bounds and native granularities, (iii) a textual rulebook, (iv) an instruction-following LLM that proposes actions, and (v) a scalar balance objective. The engine executes the rules and validates actions; the LLM agents supply player decisions. The optimizer queries the same self-play interface regardless of its search algorithm. CivMini instantiates this interface in a controlled setting.

    We consider balancing an asymmetric, parameterized turn-based strategy game so that two factions have approximately equal win probabilities under a specified LLM-player population. Let θ∈Θ⊂ℝᵈ denote a vector of game parameters (e.g., unit damage, production cost, score weights), and let π_E and π_N denote the policies of the LLM agents playing Empire and Nomads.

    For a fixed parameterization θ, let w_E(θ), w_N(θ), and w_D(θ) denote the probabilities that a rollout ends in an Empire win, a Nomads win, or a draw, respectively. These probabilities satisfy

    w_E(θ)+w_N(θ)+w_D(θ)=1.

    		(1)

    In practice, we estimate them from N self-play games. For example, the empirical Empire win rate is

    ŵ_E(θ)=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^N1{Empire wins gamei|θ}.

    		(2)

    The quantities ŵ_N(θ) and ŵ_D(θ) are estimated analogously.

    Our goal is to choose θ so that faction win probabilities are close to 0.5 under the specified player population, while avoiding frequent draws. We therefore use the balance loss

    L(θ)=|w_E(θ)-0.5|+|w_N(θ)-0.5|+0.5 w_D(θ).

    		(3)

    The first two terms measure deviations from the target win probabilities. With no draws, their sum equals |w_E-w_N|. When draws occur, w_E+w_N<1, so draws also affect the target-deviation terms; the explicit 0.5w_D term further discourages unresolved games. This term is a safeguard that keeps the optimizer away from configurations in which neither side can win; the coefficient is a design choice, not a tuned optimum, and because the term is almost always zero, any moderate value would serve the same purpose. Draws are rare in the additional evaluations (0/500 in one and 2/300 in another), so this term contributes at most a few thousandths to the measured loss. City destruction or score-based resolution determines almost all outcomes.

    In practice, we treat L as an expensive and noisy black-box function: each evaluation of L(θ) requires multiple LLM-driven game simulations and is affected by stochasticity in model decisions and game dynamics. We therefore optimize (3) with Bayesian optimization over a continuous relaxation of Θ, combined with a discrete projection that maps suggested parameters to valid game configurations.

    3.1 Parametric Asymmetric Game: CivMini

    To study asymmetric game balancing in a controlled setting, we introduce CivMini, a minimalistic two-faction, turn-based asymmetric strategy game inspired by 4X games111 4X games: A subgenre of strategy games characterized by eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, and eXterminate, emphasizing large-scale empire management and long-horizon planning. such as Civilization[41]. CivMini is implemented as a deterministic, grid-based environment with a fully observable state and a small but expressive set of unit types and actions.

    Map, factions, and units.

    The game is played on a 7×7 grid with two asymmetric factions: Empire and Nomads. Each starts with a city (Empire at (1,1), Nomads at (5,5)) and units at fixed coordinates. Empire specializes its mobile units: Farmers gather resources and Soldiers fight. Nomads deploy a single combat unit type, Cavalry, with higher mobility (2 cells per turn versus 1 for Empire units). Cavalry cannot GATHER, but Nomads earn resources from kills, incentivizing aggression. Cities of both factions can also actively PRODUCE_RESOURCE. Farmers have fixed HP (5.0); Soldier and Cavalry HP are optimizable.

    Actions and turn structure.

    Play proceeds in discrete turns, up to a fixed maximum number of turns T_\max. In the main experiments, T_\max is fixed and is not part of the 12-parameter rule space; Appendix F.1 studies game-design variants with different map sizes and corresponding turn limits. In each turn, players alternate controlling all of their units. We use a multi-action mode in which each unit of the current player performs exactly one action per turn, allowing a single model response to coordinate the units while the engine resolves their actions sequentially. For each unit, the action space includes:

  • •

    GATHER: collect resources from the current tile (Farmers only),

  • •

    MOVE: move up to the unit’s movement allowance in Manhattan distance to an unoccupied tile (Cavalry move up to 2 cells, Farmers and Soldiers up to 1; Cities cannot move),

  • •

    BATTLE: attack an adjacent enemy unit or city, dealing parameterized damage (Soldiers, Cavalry, and Cities can battle),

  • •

    PRODUCE_RESOURCE: cities generate resources,

  • •

    PRODUCE_UNIT: cities spend resources to spawn new units in adjacent empty cells,

  • •

    PASS: take no action.

    • One LLM call proposes the current player’s actions jointly, reducing inference cost relative to calling the model for every unit. Actions then resolve in a fixed order (city first, followed by units in creation order), and each is rechecked against the updated state. Thus, a city cannot spend resources gathered later in the same player turn. An earlier move can also invalidate a later move, in which case the later action becomes PASS. A single-action mode is available, but all main experiments use joint action proposals.

    The engine enforces hard constraints such as one action per unit per turn, one unit per tile (no stacking), adjacency requirements for combat, and immobile city tiles. City tiles are modeled as attackable entities with hit points, making it possible to win by conquest.

    Victory and scoring.

    Games may end early if one faction destroys the opposing city. Otherwise, when the turn limit is reached, the game is resolved by a score-based tie-breaker. The final score for each faction is a weighted combination of (i) remaining resources, (ii) the number of battles won, and (iii) the number of surviving units, each controlled by a corresponding parameter in θ:

    score=θᵣₑₛ·resources+θ_battle·battles_won(4)
    +θᵤₙᵢₜ·surviving_units.

    The balance score is defined in Eq. (3); it penalizes deviations from the target win rate and draws.

    Parameterization.

    CivMini exposes d=12 tunable parameters that jointly define the game rules:

  • •

    Economy (3 parameters): initial resources, Empire farmer gather amount, and Nomads kill resource gain;

  • •

    Combat (4 parameters): damage per attack and HP for Empire Soldiers and Nomad Cavalry;

  • •

    Production (2 parameters): unit production cost in resources for each faction;

  • •

    Scoring (3 parameters): weights for resources, battles won, and surviving units.

    • Table 1 gives the parameter ranges and grids. Mobility, initial units, and Farmer HP remain fixed to preserve faction identity; setting Farmer HP to 5 maintains vulnerability to raids. The remaining numerical strength, economy, cost, and score parameters are searched. This partition and its bounds are designer inputs, and optima at the boundaries can motivate expanding the ranges.

    3.2 LLM Self-Play as an Evaluator

    Given a parameterized game instance θ, we use two LLM agents to play the Empire and Nomads roles and estimate the resulting balance. At each decision point, the environment constructs a structured natural-language description of the game state, including the current turn index, each faction’s resources and unit positions, a faction-specific strategy guide, and the list of legal actions. This description is concatenated with a role-specific system prompt and rules retrieved from a lightweight RAG system (TF-IDF + cosine similarity). Since we use multi-action mode, the agent is asked to produce a JSON object containing actions for all units simultaneously:

    {"empire_farmer_0": {"action_type": "GATHER"},
    "empire_city": {"action_type": "PRODUCE_UNIT",
    "produce_unit_type": "soldier", "to": {"x": 1, "y": 2}}}

    The engine parses and validates the response: a unit whose action is missing, unparseable, or outside its enumerated legal set receives a fallback legal action chosen according to a fixed priority (BATTLE, GATHER, MOVE, PASS) with random tie-breaking. Actions are checked again during sequential execution, and any action invalidated by an earlier action in the same turn becomes PASS. The opponent acts after the current player finishes.

    Strategy guides supply state-dependent heuristic action recommendations, and JSON examples specify the output format. Zero-shot refers to the absence of task-specific policy training (Appendix J). For each candidate θ, we run N games with independent rollout randomness. Stochastic decoding (temperature 0.7, top-p 0.9) varies the actions and thus the trajectories under identical parameters. Appendix I quantifies the resulting diversity and execution-level conflicts. Engine validity does not imply optimal action selection or the absence of strategically biased play.

    3.3 Bayesian Optimization over Rule Space

    Enumerating the roughly 1.9×10¹⁰ discrete configurations would require prohibitively many LLM rollouts. We therefore employ Bayesian optimization [42] over a continuous relaxation of the rule space.

    We maintain a Gaussian process (GP) surrogate model g(θ) of the balance loss L(θ), implemented with scikit-optimize [43]. At iteration t, the optimizer selects a new candidate θ̃ₜ by maximizing an acquisition function over the history Dₜ₋₁={(θᵢ,f(θᵢ))}ᵢ₌₁ᵗ⁻¹. Before evaluation, a deterministic projection D maps θ̃ₜ to a valid discrete configuration θₜ=D(θ̃ₜ) by rounding and clamping each coordinate to the native grid in Table 1: integer steps except for the resource-score weight, which uses steps of 0.1. The surrogate is updated with the evaluated, discretized coordinates.

    Acquisition-based adaptive sampling.

    To improve efficiency, inspired by multi-fidelity optimization [44, 45], we introduce an adaptive sampling strategy that allocates more evaluation budget to promising candidates. At each iteration, we dynamically adjust the number of self-play games Nₜ based on the Expected Improvement (EI) of the proposed candidate:

    EI(θ)=(y^*-μ(θ))Φ(z)+σ(θ)φ(z),

    		(5)

    where y^* is the best observed value, μ(θ) and σ(θ) are the GP posterior mean and standard deviation, z=(y^*-μ(θ))/σ(θ), and Φ and φ are the standard normal CDF and PDF. The selected candidate receives an integer number of games based on its EI relative to the running maximum. Let eₜ=EI(θ̃ₜ), Mₜ=\max_i≤teᵢ, and ε>0 prevent division by zero. Then

    Nₜ=clip_[N_\min,N_\max] (⌊N_\min+(N_\max-N_\min)\min {(eₜ)/(\max(Mₜ,ε)),1}⌋).

    		(6)

    We use N_\min=16 and N_\max=64; the released implementation uses ε=10⁻³. The first 10 random initialization points receive N_\min games because no fitted posterior is available. Zero EI also yields N_\min. EI is computed on the pre-evaluation posterior, so Nₜ is fixed before observing the candidate’s outcomes. This is an allocation heuristic whose practical benefit is assessed empirically, rather than an optimal allocation guarantee.

    4 Results

    We first summarize what the theory does and does not cover (Section 4.1) and provide the implementation details (Section 4.2). We then report the main balancing results across agent pairings (Section 4.3), their repeatability and statistical uncertainty (Section 4.4), ablations of the search component and the player population (Section 4.5), and extended game configurations (Section 4.6).

    4.1 Theoretical Results

    Our theory concerns balance estimation and idealized GP-based search; it does not guarantee the implemented procedure. Proposition C.1 shows that exact balance is attainable under role symmetry when the draw probability is zero, while Lemma C.2 shows that the empirical projected balance loss from self-play concentrates around the true projected loss at rate O(Nₜ^-1/2). Proposition C.3 provides an idealized GP-LCB regret bound under explicit calibration and information-gain assumptions. It is a statement about the balance loss and the GP model class: under these assumptions, some GP-based rule has vanishing average regret. It is not a guarantee for EI or for adaptive replication, which we evaluate empirically, including an LCB variant (Section 4.4). Statements and proofs are in Appendix C.

    4.2 Implementation Details

    Model and infrastructure.

    We use InternVL3.5 [46] in FP16 as the decision-making agent for both factions. Many current model families are released as vision-language models, and InternVL3.5 provides 2B and 8B checkpoints with the same architecture, tokenizer, and prompt format, allowing agent capacity to be varied without changing anything else. Inputs and outputs are text only; the visual encoder is never invoked and no result depends on visual input, although the interface would permit inputs such as rendered game maps in future work. We combine the 2B and 8B checkpoints into the four faction pairings in Table 2. Game optimizations and evaluations are parallelized across 8 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. Optimization using InternVL3.5-8B for both sides over 100 iterations takes around 40 hours. Several experiments were run on NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada GPUs. For generalization experiments (Appendix E), we additionally use Qwen3.5-9B as an optimization agent and Gemini 2.5 Flash and Gemini 2.5 Pro as evaluation agents.

    Optimization setup.

    We optimize 12 parameters (Table 1) with a Matérn-5/2 GP and EI over 100 iterations, beginning with 10 random points; proposals are projected before evaluation and before the surrogate update. The remaining settings are conventional rather than tuned. Temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.9 are standard sampling values under which play varies across games while staying coherent. A fixed query retrieves three rule entries, keeping the prompt short. The 16-turn cap only bounds worst-case cost, since most games end earlier (Appendix I). Sixteen games per candidate correspond to two evaluation waves on 8 GPUs, and 64 caps the cost of a single candidate. Parameter bounds are coarse brackets (Table 1; for example, Soldier HP 4–16 around the released default of 8), not tuned intervals. Our budget did not permit ablating each of these choices; we prioritized the ablations most likely to change conclusions (model scale, map size, agent type, and the search component). Appendix J lists the settings in full.

    Evaluation protocol.

    During optimization, for each candidate θ, we run Nₜ∈[16,64] independent self-play games. Games terminate when a city is destroyed (instant victory) or the turn limit is reached (score-based resolution). The balance loss L(θ) is given in Eq. (3). The main experiments evaluate selected checkpoints on 100 held-out games. The additional statistical study evaluates three independent optimization runs on separate 200- and 300-game batches and the optimized configuration of Table 10 on 500 games. These held-out evaluations are separate from the candidate evaluations used by the optimizer: in-loop evaluations are intentionally noisy, which the adaptive game count manages, and all reported numbers come from held-out evaluations. The 50%±5% criterion refers to observed win rates, not a confidence-certified population bound.

    4.3 Main Empirical Results

    Table 2 shows win rates across optimization and evaluation pairings. Diagonal entries meet the empirical near-balance criterion. Off-diagonal, upgrading one side shifts outcomes in its favor; the largest shift occurs when reversing the optimization asymmetry (optimizing with E8B vs N2B and evaluating with E2B vs N8B). Both unoptimized configurations we evaluated are decisively imbalanced: the authors’ initial configuration (Appendix D.3) yields an Empire win rate of 100%, and the default configuration of the released code yields 11.3% for Empire over 300 games (Table 3). The optimized configuration in Table 10 yields 51%|49% over 100 games and 47.6%|52.4% over 500 games.

    The tested configurations also show empirical transfer across LLM families. Table 4 shows that configurations optimized with InternVL3.5-8B or Qwen3.5-9B remain near-balanced when evaluated by the other family (balance score ≤0.04 across all four matchups). Further generalization results, including Gemini 2.5 Flash/Pro and human players, are in Appendix E.

    4.4 Repeatability and Statistical Uncertainty

    Three independent GP-based optimization runs vary optimization initialization and self-play randomness. At 200 games per final configuration, the mean empirical loss is 0.0267 (sample SD 0.0058); at 300 games, it is 0.0333 (SD 0.0200). All six point estimates fall within the empirical near-balance criterion. Table 3 gives the 300-game evaluations and a 500-game re-evaluation of the original configuration, with Wilson 95% intervals and two-sided exact binomial tests. No configuration from the GP (EI), NTBEA, or TPE runs shows a detectable departure from equal win probability at these sample sizes. This supports repeatability in the tested setting, although failing to reject p_E=0.5 is not an equivalence test establishing p_E∈[0.45,0.55].

    Acquisition rule.

    We also ran the loop once with the GP lower confidence bound (LCB, with scikit-optimize’s default κ=1.96) in place of EI, leaving everything else unchanged. The run drives the in-loop loss to zero, but its selected configuration is not near-balanced on held-out games: Empire wins 57.5% of 200 games (Wilson 95% CI [50.6, 64.1]) and 57.7% of 300 games ([52.0, 63.1]). With a single run and a configuration selected from small in-loop batches, this does not rank the two rules; we keep EI because its value also sets the adaptive game count (Section 3.3).

    At 100 games near 50%, a 95% interval spans roughly ±10 percentage points; the other ablations remain single-run studies. Full 200-/300-game results and statistical definitions are in Appendix H.

    Qualitative behavior.

    Figure 3 illustrates a Nomads conquest through mobility and sustained city pressure; further rollouts show both factions winning through different tactics (Appendix G.2).

    4.5 Ablation Studies

    Different optimization methods. Table 5 compares adaptive BO with Random Search, a (1+1) Evolution Strategy (ES), and fixed-budget GP-BO. Random Search samples uniformly from the discrete rule space; ES perturbs a single incumbent with isotropic Gaussian mutations and accepts improvements. Both use N=64 games per candidate, while fixed GP-BO uses N=16, 32, or 64. All methods run for 100 iterations and receive a 100-game held-out evaluation with 8B agents on both sides. Adaptive BO and fixed GP-BO with N=64 reach empirical near-balance, using about 3500 and 6400 optimization games, respectively. The other variants do not meet this criterion. These single-run comparisons suggest a benefit from adaptive replication in this setup, though they do not establish a general optimizer ranking.

    Stronger search components. We additionally evaluate the N-Tuple Bandit Evolutionary Algorithm (NTBEA) [18] and the Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) [47] within the same engine, rulebook, and LLM self-play interface. At 200/300 evaluation games, Empire win rates are 49.0%/48.0% for NTBEA and 51.5%/54.3% for TPE, compared to means of 50.7%/51.2% across the three GP runs, which are comparable within uncertainty (Tables 3 and 19). All three reach comparable balance with the engine and self-play objective unchanged, showing that RuleSmith works with different surrogate-based search components; because they converge to similar balance on CivMini, this testbed does not rank them. The fidelity mechanism behind BOHB and Hyperband corresponds here to running more self-play games per candidate, which adaptive sampling already provides.

    Proxy player quality. LLM agents outperform random legal-action agents and provide meaningful competition to scripted agents, although such outcomes do not by themselves establish human-like or optimal play. Execution-level conflicts account for 3.3% of attempted unit actions for 8B and 4.6% for 2B agents; the engine converts these to PASS. An additional 300-game analysis finds 229 distinct three-turn openings and a mean turn-5 board-occupancy Jaccard distance of 0.62, supporting trajectory diversity under stochastic decoding (Table 6).

    Three participants played 120 games against the agents, with randomized faction and opponent scale and blinded scale assignment. Humans won 55/60 against 2B and 48/60 against 8B. Yet Empire won 45.0% and 43.3% of these games, and 53.3% in the separate 60-game human-versus-human study; none of the three departs detectably from an even split (all p≥0.37). The configuration optimized by LLM self-play is consistent with balance in these populations; given the few, repeated participants, this provides preliminary evidence (Appendices E.4 and E.5).

    4.6 Generalization and Scalability

    Scalability and extended configurations (Appendix F).

    In the tested settings, RuleSmith finds near-even empirical outcomes across map sizes from 5×5 to 11×11 (Table 7; Appendix F.1). It also scales to three factions (Empire, Nomads, Theocracy), balancing all three simultaneously (balance loss 0.013–0.033). Grid size works as a discrete optimization variable; results stay near-balanced.

    Parameter analysis (Appendix G).

    Optimized parameters vary with agent pairing. Symmetric pairings yield similar TTK values in both directions; asymmetric pairings show coordinated changes in combat, economy, cost, and scoring, consistent with compensating for capacity differences. Distinct pairings yield different configurations with similar empirical balance scores (Table 17).

    5 Conclusion, Limitations, and Impact Statement

    RuleSmith automates asymmetric game balancing through LLM self-play and Bayesian optimization over interpretable rule parameters. EI-based adaptive replication focuses evaluation on promising candidates. Three independent GP runs and larger held-out evaluations strengthen the balance results, while NTBEA/TPE demonstrate compatibility with other search components. Cross-model and small human studies suggest transfer across the tested populations. Balance remains population-dependent, and since CivMini is a controlled proof of concept, scaling to larger rule spaces, partial observability, and population shifts remains open (Appendices A and B).
