    Appendix A Limitations

    LLM-agent-centric balance criteria.

    RuleSmith optimizes for balance as measured by LLM self-play win rates. Cross-LLM evaluations and the small human study provide encouraging evidence of transfer to the tested populations (Appendix E). LLM win rates of 54–78% against rule-based opponents establish an intermediate opponent baseline while also showing sensitivity to player pairing (Appendix D.2). Within these studies, faction outcomes show no detectable imbalance: human players defeat the agents in most games, yet faction outcomes stay statistically even against both agent scales and between humans (Appendix E.4). Formal guarantees of transfer to human gameplay remain absent, and these studies are limited in scale. Systematic human evaluation and player modeling would strengthen the transfer evidence.

    Action validity, strategy bias, and skill.

    Validation ensures executable games but not good strategies. The measured 3.3%/4.6% execution-rejection rates reflect within-turn conflicts rather than a complete measure of hallucination or parse failure. Both factions are played by the same model, so population-level biases, such as a general preference for aggression, affect both sides and largely cancel in the win-rate disparity; what remains is that balance is defined relative to the evaluated population. The released prompts include strategy guides, so the evaluation population is defined jointly by the model, decoding, and prompts. Humans substantially outperform these agents; how large the strength gap between optimization and evaluation players can become before the optimized rules lose balance remains an open question for future work.

    Statistical and reproducibility scope.

    The three-seed experiment covers the main GP setting. The other ablations and the additional NTBEA, TPE, and LCB searches are single runs. Selecting the final configuration by its lowest in-loop loss can favor a lucky small-batch evaluation; the held-out re-evaluations guard against this, as the single LCB run illustrates. Binomial uncertainty and failure to reject equality do not establish equivalence within five percentage points. Human games share a few participants and should not be treated as 60 independent draws from a broad human population. Seeds and optimizer settings for the additional runs are listed in Table 22.

    Designer-specified rule space.

    The engine, the choice of tunable versus fixed rules, parameter bounds, and the objective require designer input. A balanced solution must be accessible within those bounds. Several reported settings lie at boundaries; widening ranges and re-optimizing is a practical extension, while automated range discovery remains future work.

    Simplified game environment.

    CivMini is a deliberately simplified testbed with a fully observable state, small action spaces, and a compact parameter set. Real commercial strategy games involve thousands of interacting parameters, imperfect information, long-horizon dependencies, and emergent player behaviors that our current framework does not address. Extending RuleSmith to richer, partially observable, or multi-stage environments is a key direction for future work.

    No formal optimality guarantees.

    Bayesian optimization with a Gaussian process surrogate provides no guarantee of finding the globally optimal balanced configuration. The surrogate model may misfit in high-curvature regions, and the discrete projection step introduces approximation errors. Robustness under distribution shifts (such as changes in the player population or game meta) is not explicitly modeled. Incorporating robustness objectives or adversarial evaluation into the optimization loop is a promising avenue for future research.

    Appendix B Broader Impact

    This work advances automated design tools and multi-agent simulation by enabling LLM-based evaluation and optimization of rule-driven systems. By treating large language models as flexible evaluators rather than deployed decision-makers, RuleSmith offers a scalable and interpretable approach to analyzing complex, parameterized environments.

    Potential applications of this framework extend beyond games to domains such as economic modeling, policy analysis, and resource allocation, where outcomes depend on structured rules and multi-actor interactions. At the same time, we recognize that automated simulation and optimization of competitive or adversarial systems may raise ethical considerations if misapplied. In particular, such tools could be misused to over-optimize asymmetric rules in ways that disadvantage certain participants or reduce transparency in decision-making processes.

    To mitigate these risks, RuleSmith is designed as an offline analysis and design-time tool operating on abstract, simplified environments, rather than a system for real-time decision execution. We emphasize that any real-world deployment of rule-optimization frameworks should incorporate human oversight, domain-specific constraints, and ethical review. Overall, we believe the primary impact of this work lies in supporting safer, more transparent, and more systematic design of rule-based systems, while encouraging responsible use in sensitive application domains.

    Appendix C Theoretical Analysis

    This section provides an idealized analysis of two assumptions behind RuleSmith: when exact balance is attainable, and why Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization (GP-BO) is a suitable search procedure for the balance loss. These results should be read as theoretical context rather than as a finite-budget optimality guarantee for the full RuleSmith implementation, which uses Expected Improvement, adaptive evaluation budgets, and a discrete projection step.

    Proposition C.1(Balanced Optimum under Role Symmetry).

    Consider a two-faction game parameterized by θ∈Θ. Suppose Θ contains a role-exchange-invariant configuration θ_sym, and suppose the proxy-player policy distribution is invariant under swapping the two faction roles. Then

    w_E(θ_sym)=w_N(θ_sym).

    		(7)

    Consequently, for the balance loss in Eq. (3),

    L(θ_sym)=1.5 w_D(θ_sym).

    		(8)

    In particular, if w_D(θ_sym)=0, then

    L(θ_sym)=0,

    		(9)

    and the optimal balance loss obeys

    \min_θ∈ΘL(θ)=0.

    		(10)

    Proof.

    At a role-exchange-invariant configuration, swapping the faction labels leaves the game distribution unchanged. By the policy-symmetry assumption, the induced distribution over trajectories is also unchanged after the swap, except that Empire and Nomads exchange labels. Therefore, the probability of an Empire win before the swap equals the probability of a Nomads win after the swap, giving

    w_E(θ_sym)=w_N(θ_sym).

    Since w_E=w_N=(1-w_D)/2 at this configuration, substituting into Eq. (3) yields

    L(θ_sym)=|w_E(θ_sym)-0.5|+|w_N(θ_sym)-0.5|+0.5 w_D(θ_sym)=1.5 w_D(θ_sym).

    Thus, if the symmetric configuration has no draw probability, w_D(θ_sym)=0, then L(θ_sym)=0. Since the balance loss is nonnegative by definition, this implies \min_θ∈ΘL(θ)=0. ∎

    Remark. This proposition does not claim that every asymmetric ruleset can be made perfectly balanced. Role symmetry guarantees equal faction win probabilities, while exact zero loss for the draw-penalized objective additionally requires zero draw probability. RuleSmith targets the harder practical case where the searchable parameter subspace is asymmetric, discrete, and evaluated through noisy LLM self-play.

    Lemma C.2(Concentration of the empirical projected balance loss).

    Let Θ̃ denote the continuous relaxation used by the optimizer, let D:Θ̃→Θ_disc be the deterministic discretization operator, and define the projected balance objective

    F(θ̃):=L(D(θ̃)).

    At round t, let θ̃ₜ∈Θ̃ be the continuous proposal selected by the optimizer, and let

    θₜ=D(θ̃ₜ)∈Θ_disc

    be the corresponding discretized rule configuration evaluated by the game engine. Suppose Nₜ is chosen using only information available before observing the round-t self-play outcomes. From Nₜ independent rollouts under θₜ, define

    ŵ_E,t,ŵ_N,t,ŵ_D,t

    as the empirical Empire-win, Nomads-win, and draw rates, respectively, and let

    yₜ=|ŵ_E,t-0.5|+|ŵ_N,t-0.5|+0.5ŵ_D,t

    be the empirical balance loss observed by the optimizer. Then, for any fixed horizon T and failure probability δ∈(0,1), with probability at least 1-δ, simultaneously for all t=1,…,T,

    |yₜ-F(θ̃ₜ)|=|yₜ-L(D(θ̃ₜ))|≤ηₜ, ηₜ=5/2√(\log(6T/δ))/(2Nₜ).

    Proof.

    Condition on the history before round t. Since θ̃ₜ and Nₜ are chosen before observing the round-t outcomes, the projected ruleset θₜ=D(θ̃ₜ) is also fixed before these outcomes are observed. Therefore, the Nₜ rollouts are independent samples from the outcome distribution induced by the evaluated ruleset θₜ.

    For each outcome type j∈{E,N,D}, Hoeffding’s inequality gives

    |ŵ_j,t-wⱼ(θₜ)|≤√(\log(6T/δ))/(2Nₜ)

    simultaneously for all j∈{E,N,D} and all t=1,…,T with probability at least 1-δ, by a union bound.

    On this event, the inequality ||a-c|-|b-c||≤|a-b| gives

    |yₜ-F(θ̃ₜ)|≤|ŵ_E,t-w_E(θₜ)|+|ŵ_N,t-w_N(θₜ)|+0.5|ŵ_D,t-w_D(θₜ)|
    ≤5/2√(\log(6T/δ))/(2Nₜ).

    This proves the claim. ∎

    Proposition C.3(Idealized GP-LCB for projected self-play evaluations).

    Let Θ̃ denote the continuous relaxation used by the optimizer, let D:Θ̃→Θ_disc be the deterministic discretization operator, and define the projected objective

    F(θ̃):=L(D(θ̃)).

    Let

    θ̃^⋆∈\arg\min_θ̃∈Θ̃F(θ̃)

    be an optimal continuous representative of a best projected ruleset.

    At round t, an idealized optimizer selects a continuous proposal θ̃ₜ∈Θ̃, evaluates the projected ruleset D(θ̃ₜ) using Nₜ independent self-play rollouts, and observes the empirical projected loss yₜ defined in Lemma C.2. For this idealized projected-objective analysis, the surrogate is indexed by the pair (θ̃ₜ,yₜ); the implementation stores evaluated discrete coordinates instead. This distinction is part of why this proposition is not a guarantee for the implemented pipeline.

    Assume a bounded kernel diagonal k(x,x)≤1, nondecreasing βₜ, and a GP observation model with variances bounded above and bounded away from zero (the finite replication range permits such bounds). Assume that the GP surrogate is calibrated for the projected objective F in the standard GP bandit sense: there exist confidence parameters {βₜ}_t≥1 such that, with probability at least 1-δ,

    |F(θ̃)-μₜ₋₁(θ̃)|≤√βₜσₜ₋₁(θ̃)

    for all θ̃∈Θ̃ and all t≥1. Here μₜ₋₁ and σₜ₋₁ are the GP posterior mean and posterior standard deviation after t-1 observations. Lemma C.2 motivates a heteroscedastic observation-uncertainty proxy scaling as ηₜ²=O(1/Nₜ), although the GP posterior remains an idealized modeling approximation.

    Consider the idealized GP lower-confidence-bound rule

    θ̃ₜ∈\arg\min_θ̃∈Θ̃[μₜ₋₁(θ̃)-√βₜσₜ₋₁(θ̃)].

    Then, on the confidence event above, the cumulative projected regret

    R_T=∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ(F(θ̃ₜ)-F(θ̃^⋆))

    satisfies

    R_T=O(√Tβ_Tγ_T^(N)),

    where γ_T^(N) is the maximum information gain after T observations under the corresponding heteroscedastic observation uncertainties. Consequently, whenever β_Tγ_T^(N)=o(T), the average projected regret R_T/T vanishes.

    Proof.

    The proof follows the standard GP-UCB/LCB regret argument [48], applied to the minimization of the projected objective F. On the confidence event, for the selected point θ̃ₜ,

    F(θ̃ₜ)≤μₜ₋₁(θ̃ₜ)+√βₜσₜ₋₁(θ̃ₜ),

    while for the optimal projected point θ̃^⋆,

    μₜ₋₁(θ̃^⋆)-√βₜσₜ₋₁(θ̃^⋆)≤F(θ̃^⋆).

    Since θ̃ₜ minimizes the lower confidence bound,

    μₜ₋₁(θ̃ₜ)-√βₜσₜ₋₁(θ̃ₜ)≤μₜ₋₁(θ̃^⋆)-√βₜσₜ₋₁(θ̃^⋆).

    Combining the three inequalities gives

    F(θ̃ₜ)-F(θ̃^⋆)≤2√βₜσₜ₋₁(θ̃ₜ).

    Summing over t=1,…,T and applying the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality yields

    R_T≤2∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ√βₜσₜ₋₁(θ̃ₜ)
    ≤2√Tβ_T∑ₜ₌₁ᵀσₜ₋₁²(θ̃ₜ).

    The standard information-gain argument for GP bandits bounds the cumulative posterior variance by a constant multiple of γ_T^(N), yielding

    R_T=O(√Tβ_Tγ_T^(N)).

    Dividing by T gives vanishing average projected regret whenever β_Tγ_T^(N)=o(T). ∎

    Remark. Proposition C.3 should be interpreted as an idealized analysis of RuleSmith’s continuous-proposal, discrete-evaluation procedure. The optimizer proposes θ̃∈Θ̃, but the environment evaluates only the projected ruleset D(θ̃). Consequently, the objective observed by the optimizer is the projected loss

    F(θ̃)=L(D(θ̃)).

    This objective is generally piecewise constant and can be discontinuous at projection-cell boundaries, so the GP calibration assumption is not guaranteed solely by choosing a smooth kernel such as Matérn 5/2. Rather, it is a standard modeling idealization used to provide theoretical context for GP-based search under noisy self-play evaluations.

    The proposition analyzes an LCB rule, whereas the implemented system uses Expected Improvement together with adaptive replication. The result is therefore not a regret guarantee for the implementation. LCB carries the bound because the classical argument [48] requires an explicit confidence-bound exploration term: the objective is sandwiched by the confidence interval, per-step regret is bounded by the posterior standard deviation at the queried point, and the sum is controlled by the maximum information gain. EI has no comparably standard cumulative-regret bound; its classical guarantee is a convergence rate in the noiseless case [49], and results for noisy EI do not cover a discrete projection combined with EI-dependent replication. The two rules nonetheless use the same posterior quantities. Writing EI=σ h(z) with z=(y^*-μ)/σ and h(z)=zΦ(z)+φ(z), the partial derivatives of EI with respect to the predicted improvement y^*-μ and σ are Φ(z) and φ(z), respectively; because both are positive, EI increases in the exact two quantities that LCB trades off, and the rules differ in how they weight them. Lemma C.2 justifies the concentration of the self-play estimates, Proposition C.3 shows that GP-based search is well posed for this objective under idealized calibration, and the choice among acquisition rules is settled empirically, including the LCB run in Section 4.4.

    Appendix D Validating the Proxy Player

    D.1 LLM Agents vs. Random Agent Baseline

    To establish a lower bound on proxy-player quality, Table 8 evaluates InternVL3.5-8B and InternVL3.5-2B against a random agent that selects uniformly from all legal actions. The prompted LLM agents win 100% of games in every listed configuration, regardless of faction. This establishes effective play relative to random action selection and supports their use as proxy players. As with the other agent comparisons, performance reflects the model together with its prompts and strategy guidance.

    D.2 LLM Agents vs. Rule-Based Agent

    To provide a stronger proxy-player baseline than random play, we design a rule-based agent that executes fixed greedy heuristics with random tie-breaking, without language understanding.

    Empire rule-based agent.

    Farmers always GATHER if possible; otherwise they PASS. Soldiers BATTLE any adjacent enemy (prioritizing the enemy city), or MOVE toward the nearest enemy by Manhattan distance; if multiple enemies are equidistant, one is chosen uniformly at random. The city alternates each turn between PRODUCE_UNIT (farmer) and PRODUCE_UNIT (soldier) whenever resources suffice and an adjacent cell is free; otherwise it uses PRODUCE_RESOURCE.

    Nomads rule-based agent.

    Cavalry BATTLE the enemy city if adjacent; otherwise they BATTLE the nearest adjacent enemy unit; otherwise they MOVE toward the enemy city. The city uses PRODUCE_UNIT (cavalry) when resources allow; otherwise it uses PASS.

    These heuristics capture the core asymmetry of each faction: Empire prioritizes economy and incremental defense, whereas Nomads prioritize fast aggression and city destruction.

    Table 9 reports win rates when LLM agents face the rule-based agent under two parameter sets: parameters optimized with LLM self-play (Table 2) and parameters optimized with rule-based self-play (Table 16).

    LLM-agent win rates range from 54% to 78% in Table 9, below their 100% rate against random agents. The rule-based agent therefore provides meaningful competition for both model sizes. Under LLM-optimized parameters, 8B agents win 78% as Nomads and 75% as Empire. Under rule-based-optimized parameters, these rates are 62% and 73%, respectively. The latter configuration has cheaper Empire units (4), higher farmer gathering (2), and lower Nomads kill gain (5), compatible with an economy favoring frequent Empire production. These descriptive comparisons show interactions between rules and player policies; they do not isolate the contribution of individual mechanics. Together, the random and scripted baselines support the use of prompted LLM agents as a more capable evaluation population in these settings.

    D.3 Comparison with Human-Designed Parameters

    Table 10 compares the authors’ initial configuration (“Initial θ”) against the configuration discovered by RuleSmith using InternVL3.5-8B. This starting point produces a completely one-sided outcome in its original evaluation (Empire 100% | Nomads 0%, loss 1.00). Its low Nomads damage (1) relative to Empire damage (4) and Soldier HP (13) plausibly contributes to this advantage. This interpretation is descriptive; joint parameter changes do not isolate a causal effect for any one coordinate.

    RuleSmith’s Bayesian optimizer jointly adjusts all parameter categories to recover empirical balance. Nomads’ damage triples (1 → 3), their production cost rises (3 → 8), initial resources increase (6 → 10), and Empire Soldier HP falls (13 → 9). These changes are consistent with stronger Nomads combat, costlier cavalry production, and greater initial spending capacity. The optimized combat statistics imply three attacks to eliminate either faction’s main combat unit. The empirical balance loss drops from 1.00 to 0.02; these mechanistic interpretations concern the joint configuration rather than isolated parameter effects.

item.title: 把控制序列当上下文喂进去：World-in-Context 用累积的动作条件做交互世界模型，导航分 81.2、视角切换成功率 90.6% ｜ World-in-Context: Interactive Video World Modeling with In-Context Conditioning
item.description:
一句话：只给端点位移会丢掉中间动力学；把整段控制序列累积进 RoPE 才补得回来。

要点：

  • 核心是 in-context 条件化：把「整段控制序列」而不是端点位移累积进位置编码（IT-RoPE），消融显示完整版明显优于只用端点（80.5/86.6），说明中间动力学信息不可省
  • 因果版 WiC-Causal 在 WBench 上达到平均导航分 81.2、Fpp↔Tpp 成功率 90.6%，相比双向版本（81.5 / 93.8%）只掉一点点，却保住了更好的相对优势
  • ICC 注入方式在所有数据规模上都优于加性注入，尤其在视角切换场景；跨规模实验显示有数据效率优势

为什么值得看：「给端点还是给轨迹」是世界模型接手柄时最先撞上的工程选择。这条用消融把答案钉死：必须累积中间控制量；同时给出因果化之后掉多少分的具体数字，方便评估能不能上实时交互。

中文摘要：World-in-Context 研究如何让交互式视频世界模型吃准用户控制。它发现常见的「只给起点到终点的位移」会丢掉中间动力学，于是把整段控制序列累积进位置编码（IT-RoPE）；消融显示完整版本明显优于只用端点的变体。在注入方式上，它提出的 ICC 在所有数据规模上都优于加性注入，视角切换场景尤其明显，并表现出数据效率优势。因果版本 WiC-Causal 在 WBench 上取得平均导航分 81.2、Fpp↔Tpp 成功率 90.6%，相比双向版本（81.5 / 93.8%）仅有微小退化，同时相对现有 5B 基线仍有明显领先。作者还通过跨规模实验讨论了这套条件化在不同模型规模下的可迁移性。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-23

本期推送：2026-10-29

World-in-Context: Interactive Video World Modeling with In-Context Conditioning

Abstract

Interactive video world models require coordinated control over viewing perspectives, character actions, and camera motion. Existing methods typically leave view modes implicit in text captions, conflate action with camera motion, and inject controls through fragmented architectural pathways that capture interdependencies only indirectly. In this work, we present World-in-Context, an interactive world modeling framework powered by In-Context Conditioning (ICC). Rather than relying on specialized conditioning pathways, World-in-Context unifies view, action, and camera controls into explicit tokens contextualized directly within a shared self-attention space. Our formulation reveals that (i) explicit view tokens disentangle conflicting dynamics and unlock emergent view switching from single-view data, while (ii) action and camera inputs play complementary roles in governing local responsiveness and global stability. To preserve temporal continuity across execution intervals, we further introduce Interaction-Transport RoPE (IT-RoPE), parameterizing temporal attention with accumulated control transitions. On WBench, World-in-Context-5B achieves navigation performance on par with 22B EchoWM (81.5vs.81.6) and attains a 93.8% perspective-switching success rate, substantially outperforming existing 5B baselines (18.8%). Controlled analyses further demonstrate compounding advantages of World-in-Context under richer conditioning mixtures, favorable data efficiency, and natural applicability to causal rollouts.

1 Introduction

Video generation has rapidly advanced from passive video generation [41, 10, 22] toward interactive world models [40, 9, 38, 45], empowering users to actively steer dynamic visual environments. In this paradigm, the model acts as an interactive simulator where users provide control inputs to navigate and explore the environment, while the model dynamically predicts the evolving visual observations in response. At its core, effectively simulating such an interactive world hinges on two fundamental dimensions [28, 43]: ➀ how the world is viewed across distinct perspectives, and ➁ how user inputs concurrently govern character dynamics and camera viewports. Together, these dimensions define how an agent actively perceives and intervenes in an unfolding generative world.

Despite recent progress [40, 55, 59, 39, 15], current interactive pipelines often overlook the systematic formulation of these two essential dimensions: ❶ view-mode ambiguity: first- (Fpp) and third-person (Tpp) perspectives increasingly appear in interactive data, yet view mode is often specified only implicitly through text captions [9, 38, 39, 55], while free-camera (Free) roaming is frequently conflated with Fpp control despite their different motion semantics; and ❷ action-camera entanglement: most pipelines rely primarily on continuous camera trajectories alone for control [31, 39, 55, 13], overlooking the distinct role of discrete actions, especially in third-person interaction where character and camera motion form separate degrees of freedom.

A naive remedy would be simply attaching auxiliary condition channels for each missing signal. However, existing paradigms [40, 9, 19, 56, 33, 45] typically accommodate interactive controls through separate modules (e.g., AdaLN modulation), which tends to isolate different control signals and leaves their cross-dependencies to be captured only indirectly, as shown in Figure2 (Left). As interaction becomes richer and more compositional, coordinating these modular branches grows increasingly intricate, especially when the interpretation of one signal inherently depends on concurrent inputs and the active viewport.

In this work, we propose World-in-Context, which unifies multi-dimensional interaction through an In-Context Conditioning (ICC) paradigm. Rather than routing controls into isolated architectural branches, World-in-Context casts diverse interactive signals into token sequences and prepends them directly into the shared self-attention space alongside visual latents. Within this unified interface, we revisit the aforementioned limitations along two fronts: ♣ Explicit view-mode modeling: Rather than leaving perspectives implicit in text captions [9, 40, 38, 59], we explicitly incorporate discrete view tokens (Free, Fpp, and Tpp) into the context. Joint training across these regimes distinguishes their motion semantics, while enabling in-video view switching to emerge naturally. ♠ Joint action-camera modeling: We jointly incorporate discrete actions and continuous camera trajectories into the context. Crucially, beyond their necessary separation in Tpp interaction, we further study the less-examined Fpp and Free regimes, where camera trajectories often stand in for both forms of control [31, 15, 39]. Our analysis reveals complementary roles: action governs local command fidelity, whereas camera anchors global trajectory stability.

Built upon ICC, World-in-Context natively captures cross-condition dependencies within a unified attention space. While in-context tokens specify what controls are present at individual frames, naive token conditioning can still leave the dynamic evolution between distant moments to be modeled implicitly. To this end, we further introduce IT-RoPE (Interaction-Transport RoPE), a lightweight positional encoding that incorporates pairwise control transitions directly into temporal attention. By jointly modeling control conditions and their temporal evolution, World-in-Context supports coherent interaction across viewing regimes and makes effective use of interactive supervision, with increasing benefits as controls become richer. More broadly, it reframes multi-condition interaction as context modeling, offering a unified interface for interactive world modeling.

To summarize, this work contributes threefold:

  • ➢

    We introduce In-Context Conditioning (ICC) for interactive world modeling and present World-in-Context, which represents view, action, and camera controls as tokens within a shared attention space, providing a unified interface for diverse interaction signals.

  • ➢

    We investigate the often-overlooked roles of viewing regimes and joint action-camera control, revealing distinct view-dependent dynamics, emergent view switching, and complementary action-camera roles in command fidelity and trajectory stability.

  • ➢

    Extensive experiments on WBench demonstrate that World-in-Context-5B matches the 22B EchoWM in navigation (81.5vs.81.6) and substantially outperforms existing 5B baselines in perspective switching (93.8%vs.18.8%). Controlled studies further confirm compounding gains of World-in-Context under richer controls, favorable sample efficiency, and causal applicability.

    • 2 Related Work

    Interactive Video World Models.

    Interactive world models extend video generation toward closed-loop interaction, where future observations evolve according to user-steered conditions [32, 6, 3, 36, 45]. Following recent formulations [28, 43], existing models mainly navigate two core dimensions: (i) How the world is viewed. Interactive environments span Free, Fpp, and Tpp regimes. Prior works [9, 38, 39, 55] typically subsume them into a shared camera formulation, leaving perspective implicit in text captions and often conflating Free roaming with Fpp motion. We instead explicitly condition on discrete view modes, distinguishing their physical motion semantics and naturally enabling dynamic view switching. (ii) How user inputs affect its evolution. Existing systems rely almost exclusively on continuous camera trajectories for navigation [31, 59, 39, 9, 55, 13] for all view modes, which inevitably entangles character and camera dynamics in Tpp. To incorporate richer signals, recent approaches either formulate a unified action interface across different regimes [19], or inject actions and camera poses through distinct architectural pathways [36]. Differing from these paradigms, we explicitly maintain view modes and represent character actuation alongside camera motion as jointly contextualized controls within the same attention space, effectively treating them as coexisting yet independent degrees of freedom.

    In-Context Conditioning.

    In-context learning, originally developed for language models [7], has increasingly been explored in visual generation. Prompt Diffusion [44] first enables diffusion models to infer visual tasks from contextual examples, followed by works that exploit shared attention contexts for task-agnostic or unified image generation [16, 17, 50, 37, 46]. This paradigm has recently extended to video through spatial or temporal in-context generation [8, 21], unified multimodal conditioning with full attention [20, 12], and reference videos as semantic prompts [2]. IC-World [47] further explores in-context generation for shared world modeling, focusing on consistency across multiple observations of the same world. In this work, we extend in-context conditioning to interactive video world modeling.

    3 Preliminary: Problem Formulation

    Let x∈ℝ^T×H×W×3 denote a video clip of T frames, and y the initial contextual specification (e.g., a text prompt or a starting frame). In interactive video world modeling, the model generates future visual observations conditioned on temporally aligned user interaction sequences u={uₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ, parameterizing the conditional distribution:

    p_θ(x|y,u).

    		(1)

    Modern video diffusion and flow-matching backbones typically instantiate this conditional process within a latent space. Specifically, let z_τ denote the latent video representations at diffusion timestep τ∈[0,1]. Existing models typically inject interactive conditions u via modular, condition-specific pathways:

    v̂_τ=F_θ(z_τ,f_cond(u);y,τ),

    		(2)

    where f_cond(·) commonly instantiates modulation for camera trajectories [9, 18], additive token injection for discrete actions [19, 5], cross-attention for text-form controls [30], or geometry-aware positional attention and warping for camera control [55, 39, 53]. While effective for isolated signals, such architectural separation isolates diverse controls into disparate parameter spaces, hindering the model from capturing cross-condition dependencies directly. In this work, instead of introducing dedicated condition branches, we reframe multi-modal interactive conditioning as a unified in-context sequence modeling problem:

    v̂_τ=F_θ([c\mathbin∥z_τ];y,τ),

    		(3)

    where diverse controls are recast as unified condition tokens c and natively contextualized with visual latents within the shared attention manifold.

    4 World-in-Context

    4.1 Overview

    To avoid the scalability bottleneck of fragmented side channels (e.g., AdaLN or separate cross-attention layers), World-in-Context casts diverse interactive signals directly into sequence tokens within a unified attention space, as shown in Figure2 (Right). The world modeling space is organized around two complementary pillars: (i) how the world is viewed across perspectives, and (ii) how user inputs steer dynamics through concurrent character action and camera viewport movement.

    Unified In-Context Conditioning.

    Instead of introducing specialized parameter pathways for each control modality, all interactive signals are projected into a unified sequence of condition tokens c∈ℝ^L_c×D, matching the backbone hidden dimension D:

    c=[cᵛⁱᵉʷ ; cᵃᶜᵗⁱᵒⁿ ; cᶜᵃᵐᵉʳᵃ],

    		(4)

    where [ · ; · ] denotes concatenation along the sequence dimension. These condition tokens are prepended directly to the visual latents z_τ at diffusion timestep τ∈[0,1]. The flow-matching generative backbone then predicts the velocity field v̂_τ over this shared sequence:

    v̂_τ=F_θ([c ; z_τ] ; y,τ).

    		(5)

    Ingesting all controls into the shared self-attention allows cross-condition dependencies to be captured natively without ad-hoc modules, reframing interactive expansion into an in-context modeling problem.

    Decomposing Interactive Context.

    The condition sequence c of World-in-Context explicitly decouples the interactive degrees of freedom:

  • ❏

    View Mode (cᵛⁱᵉʷ): Disentangles Free, Fpp, and Tpp regimes via learned categorical tokens, mitigating view ambiguity and naturally supporting dynamic switching.

  • ❏

    Action (cᵃᶜᵗⁱᵒⁿ): Encodes hybrid keyboard-action inputs to govern local character actuation, providing responsive command dynamics.

  • ❏

    Camera (cᶜᵃᵐᵉʳᵃ): Embeds relative 6-DoF camera poses and Plücker coordinates to ensure continuous trajectory tracking and viewpoint stability.

    • To complement in-context conditioning, we further incorporates geometric transport into the temporal attention mechanism to preserve continuous physical transitions across frames. The subsequent sections elaborate on the explicit view-mode formulation (§4.2), examine joint action-camera decoupling (§4.3), and introduce IT-RoPE for parameterized temporal attention (§4.4).

    4.2 Explicit View-Mode Modeling

    Most existing models [40, 31, 38, 56, 9] convey viewing regimes either through implicit text descriptions y or directly via camera poses. However, identical geometric trajectories inherently entail different motion semantics across regimes, for example, distinguishing unconstrained Free navigation from embodied Fpp motion. Leaving such distinctions to implicit text conditioning makes it ambiguous to resolve regime-dependent motion characteristics from identical geometric inputs.

    We therefore restrict y strictly to world-state specifications and introduce explicit, time-aligned view tokens cᵛⁱᵉʷ={cₜᵛⁱᵉʷ}ₜ₌₀^T_z-1 into the shared context:

    cₜᵛⁱᵉʷ=e_view(vₜ)+e_type(view),\penalty \penalty vₜ∈{\textscFree,\textscFpp,\textscTpp}.

    		(6)

    By attending directly to visual latents, cₜᵛⁱᵉʷ acts as a contextual switch that modulates the shared attention space toward regime-appropriate physical motion fields.

    To validate the efficacy of explicit view conditioning, we compare our formulation against a baseline that specifies view modes through text alone (“w/o view modeling") Figure4 evaluates trajectory oscillations under Fpp and Free conditioning across 100 scenes, while Figure3 presents qualitative transitions alongside quantitative evaluations on the WBench Fpp↔Tpp suite. Detailed setups are provided in SectionB.2; key observations are summarized:

    Obs.❶ Explicit view modeling distinguishes regime-dependent motion dynamics. As shown in Figure4, text-based conditioning yields closely overlapping oscillation profiles for Fpp and Free, conflating their respective physical semantics. In contrast, explicit view modeling encourages a distinct separation: Fpp exhibits pronounced periodic oscillations characteristic of embodied locomotion, while Free preserves smoother camera trajectories. This indicates that explicit view tokens effectively mitigate motion ambiguity across viewing regimes.

    Obs.❷ In-video view switching emerges naturally from explicit view tokens. Because view tokens act as modular contextual switches within the shared attention space, training exclusively on single-view clips already gives rise to perspective transitions simply by varying the view token sequence during rollout, as shown in Figure3. On the WBench Fpp↔Tpp set, our base model without switching supervision achieves a 37.5% success rate, substantially outperforming the text-based baseline (6.25%). Incorporating a minimal set of 500 transition sequences further consolidates this emergent behavior to 93.8%, demonstrating that explicit view conditioning establishes a receptive interface that is readily steerable and sample-efficient to tune.

    4.3 Joint Action-Camera Modeling

    While existing interactive models typically rely on camera trajectories as the primary control signal [9, 49, 38] for all view modes, character actuation and camera viewpoint constitute separate degrees of freedom, particularly in Tpp. Rather than mapping them to a single control interface [19] or routing them into disparate conditioning branches [36], we model character actions and camera trajectories as coexisting, decoupled conditions, contextualizing both directly within the shared transformer sequence.

    Given an action sequence and a camera trajectory, World-in-Context encodes both modalities into time-aligned context tokens. For action conditioning, each input aₜ is decomposed into semantic subslots S={move,turn,Δtrans,Δrot} separating discrete key states from continuous motion increments. The corresponding action tokens are given by:

    \beginsplitc_t,p,sᵃᶜᵗⁱᵒⁿ=&LayerNorm(hₛ(aₜ)+rₛ(aₜ)+eₜ(t) &+eₚ(p)+eₛ(s))+e_type(act),\endsplit

    		(7)

    where s∈S, p∈ℙ_act indexes the within-step tokens, hₛ denotes a slot-specific encoder (e.g., MLP), and rₛ is a zero-initialized residual branch for continuous magnitude cues.

    For camera conditioning, World-in-Context converts each normalized relative pose Êₜ into a tokenized Plücker ray field, following [11, 20]. For a sampled ray (u,v) with camera center ôₜ and unit direction d_t,u,v, its Plücker coordinate is denoted by π_t,u,v=[ôₜ×d_t,u,v;d_t,u,v]. The corresponding camera token is encoded as:

    \beginsplitc_t,u,vᶜᵃᵐᵉʳᵃ=&LayerNorm(φ_ray(π_t,u,v)+ &φₚₒₛₑ(vec(Êₜ))+φ_Δ(ξₜ))+e_type(cam),\endsplit

    		(8)

    where ξₜ∈ℝ⁶ denotes the local rigid-body increment, and the three projections encode ray geometry, global relative pose, and local camera motion, respectively.

    Beyond their essential decoupling in Tpp, we further investigate the less-examined Fpp and Free regimes, where camera paths alone are typically assumed to suffice. Figure5 compares action-only, camera-only, and joint training under our setting on the WBench Navigation set (excluding Tpp scenes). Our key observations are:

    Obs.❸ Action and camera signals play complementary roles. As shown in Figure5, action-only conditioning yields higher translation and rotation accuracy (+6.5 and +3.9 points over camera-only), but can introduce visual artifacts. Conversely, camera-only conditioning improves geometric (+2.1) and photometric (+1.9) consistency, though often at the cost of insufficient travel displacement. Joint training naturally harmonizes these properties, achieving the highest rotation accuracy (90.6) and geometric consistency (90.8) while maintaining strong translation fidelity (89.3). In effect, action commands govern local responsiveness, whereas camera trajectories anchor global stability.

    4.4 Interaction-Transport Geometric Encoding

    While in-context tokens expose control inputs to the shared attention space, standard 3D-RoPE encodes only relative spatiotemporal coordinates, leaving the intervening control progression between distant frames implicit. To this end, World-in-Context further introduces Interaction-Transport RoPE (IT-RoPE), which complements spatiotemporal positional encoding by parameterizing temporal attention with control-induced transport operators accumulated along the execution sequence.

    Ordered Interval Transport.

    While input-dependent transforms [52] and geometric encoding [23] demonstrate the promise of data-driven attention biases, our interactive setting differs in that cross-temporal transitions are governed by temporally ordered user inputs. We thus maintain dual, order-preserving transport paths for character action and camera motion b∈{a,c}. Specifically, each control input induces a step transformation Uₜᵇ, which accumulates along continuous valid segments to define the relative transport across interval (i,j]:

    T_i→jᵇ=∏ₖ₌ᵢ₊₁ʲUₖᵇ, i

    		(9)

    where T_j→iᵇ=(T_i→jᵇ)^⊤, and T_i→jᵇT_j→kᵇ=T_i→kᵇ. This non-commutative composition natively preserves control order, allowing the model to distinguish trajectories that share identical endpoints but differ in execution sequences.

    View-Gated Centered Attention.

    To incorporate these accumulated transitions into cross-frame reasoning, we augment temporal attention with a centered, transport-corrected score:

    sᵢⱼ=sᵢⱼᵇᵃˢᵉ+∑_b∈{a,c}(λᵇ)/(√r)mᵢⱼᵇgᵢᵇgⱼᵇ·(qᵢᵇ)^⊤(T_tᵢ→tⱼᵇ-I)kⱼᵇ,

    		(10)

    where sᵢⱼᵇᵃˢᵉ=(q̄ᵢ^⊤k̄ⱼ)/(√d) denotes standard spatiotemporal attention with 3D-RoPE, qᵢᵇ,kⱼᵇ∈ℝʳ are control-specific sub-channels, and λᵇ is a learnable scale initialized to zero. The gate gᵢᵇ∈(0,1) dynamically modulates control influence across viewing regimes and token types, while mᵢⱼᵇ∈{0,1} restricts the correction to contiguous valid segments. Crucially, subtracting I centers the correction, ensuring it vanishes for static intervals or tᵢ=tⱼ, while zero-initializing λᵇ preserves native backbone behavior at the start of training. Further details of transport accumulation and attention computation are provided in SectionA.3.

    4.5 Training of World-in-Context

    Training Data.

    We train World-in-Context on a compact set of 100K video clips covering Free, Fpp, and Tpp viewing regimes, accompanied by temporally aligned view, action, and camera annotations when available. While joint training across these single-regime clips naturally facilitates view-mode transitions (as analyzed in Section4.2), we additionally incorporate a small fraction of cross-view switching clips (500 sequences) with dynamic view schedules to reinforce transition stability.

    Training Protocol.

    Following the conditional flow-matching objective, World-in-Context undergoes bidirectional finetuning where video and control tokens jointly interact in the shared attention manifold. This bidirectional setup serves as our default configuration to benchmark the core in-context conditioning paradigm. In Section6, we further investigate World-in-Context under broader operational settings, including causal rollout with in-context history and expanded game-control signals.

    5 Experiments

    5.1 Experimental Settings

    Baselines.

    World-in-Context is built upon the widely adopted Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [41] backbone. For direct comparisons, our primary baselines comprise models sharing this foundation: YUME 1.5 [30], ABot-World [19], DreamX-World [39], and Zing-0.5 [5]. We also include larger models as reference: EchoWM [55], LingBot-World v2 [9], Alaya-EVOKE [38], and HY-World 1.5 [18]. Since training data scales are rarely disclosed across works, we also implement public architectures and conduct controlled comparisons under our identical data for analyses.

    Evaluations.

    We evaluate World-in-Context on the widely adopted WBench [54]. Alongside the standard Navigation split for trajectory tracking, we further adopt its Perspective Switching - Fpp↔Tpp suite to systematically assess dynamic view transitions. Our framework natively supports both action-only and camera-only inference; we default to action-only control for Free and Fpp, while utilizing joint action and camera signals for character and viewpoint in Tpp. More details are in AppendixB.

    5.2 Main Results

    Quantitative Results.

    Table1 summarizes performance on WBench. Among 5B models, World-in-Context achieves the highest Navigation average (81.5), performing on par with Zing-0.5 (81.0) while improving the Interaction score from 84.2 to 86.0 via unified in-context conditioning. Its navigation capability also rivals larger models like 22B EchoWM (81.6). Crucially, World-in-Context reaches a 93.8% success rate on Fpp↔Tpp, significantly outperforming the best 5B baseline (18.8%) and confirming its capacity for dynamic viewpoint transitions within a single unified model.

    Qualitative Results.

    Figure6 further compares our World-in-Context with Zing-0.5. While both generate plausible environments, Zing-0.5 tends to incur exaggerated motion scale, whereas ours maintains more measured, balanced trajectories aligned with its higher Interaction score. Furthermore, World-in-Context smoothly executes Fpp↔Tpp switches where the baseline fails to transition. Extended rollouts across diverse scene layouts and artistic styles under Free, Fpp, and Tpp modes are detailed in Figures7, 8 and 9. Notably, Figure10 also demonstrates coherent multi-stage switching (e.g., Tpp→Fpp→Tpp) while preserving consistent scene structure throughout.

    5.3 Analysis of In-Context Conditioning

    To further examine how conditioning strategies scale with input complexity, we compare ICC with additive injection [19] and AdaLN modulation [40] under progressively richer inputs with our same data: view (V), action (A), and camera (C). We give the following observations:

    Obs.❹ ICC’s advantage scales with conditioning richness. As shown in Figure11, with camera control alone, ICC performs on par with alternative strategies (76.3vs.76.3-77.0). Its gains emerge under joint action-camera inputs (+0.6 in Navigation, +1.1 in Interaction) and expand further when adding explicit view tokens (+1.0 and +1.4, reaching 81.2 and 86.8). These widening margins indicate that a shared attention space coordinates diverse controls more effectively than separate injection pathways as interaction becomes compositional.

    5.4 Analysis of IT-RoPE

    To evaluate how trajectory-aware attention affects temporal consistency, we ablate IT-RoPE here against standard 3D-RoPE, single-branch variants, and an endpoint-only alternative under the fixed V+A+C setup, as shown in Figure12.

    Obs.❺ Tracking intervening control evolution improves interactive attention. Compared to 3D-RoPE, full IT-RoPE enhances both Navigation (80.5→81.2) and Interaction (86.2→86.8). While action transport sharpens command responsiveness and camera transport stabilizes spatial tracking, their combination delivers the most balanced performance. Moreover, full IT-RoPE clearly outperforms the endpoint-only variant (80.5/86.6), confirming that accumulating the intervening control sequence provides critical dynamics missed by endpoint offsets alone.

    5.5 Analysis of Data Efficiency

    Our default interaction-training set comprises a modest 100K navigation clips and 500 switching sequences. Since training-data scales are not consistently disclosed by existing methods, we assess data efficiency through controlled comparisons in Figure13: 50K+250, 100K+500, and 125K+750. We summarize our observations as follows:

    Obs.❻ ICC demonstrates data efficiency across scaling regimes. ICC consistently outperforms additive injection across all data regimes, especially in perspective switching. With only 50K+250 clips, ICC achieves a 75.0% switching rate, already surpassing additive injection trained on twice the data (71.9% at 100K+500). At 100K+500, ICC exceeds the largest-budget additive baseline (125K+750) in both Navigation (81.5vs.80.3) and Switch (93.8%vs.78.1%), showing that shared in-context tokens make substantially more efficient use of interactive supervision.

    6 Applicability of World-in-Context

    6.1 Causal Modeling with In-Context History

    To examine the architectural extensibility of in-context conditioning beyond bidirectional generation, World-in-Context is naturally adapted to streaming causal rollouts. Following common causal training paradigms in interactive generation [60], the model is trained autoregressively to predict future frame latents conditioned on historical context. Rather than relying on external KV cache retrieval mechanisms, WiC-Causal directly incorporates historical latents into the shared self-attention sequence. Specifically, the condition sequence c in Eq. (4) is augmented with historical latent tokens:

    c_causal=[cᵛⁱᵉʷ ; cᵃᶜᵗⁱᵒⁿ ; cᶜᵃᵐᵉʳᵃ ; cˢⁱⁿᵏ ; cʳᵉᶜᵉⁿᵗ],

    		(11)

    where cˢⁱⁿᵏ preserves initial context tokens as global semantic anchors, and cʳᵉᶜᵉⁿᵗ maintains a sliding window of recent visual tokens to enforce continuity.

    As shown in Table2, WiC-Causal exhibits competitive interactive performance, attaining an average Navigation score of 81.2 and a 90.6%Fpp↔Tpp success rate on WBench. Compared to the bidirectional counterpart (81.5 and 93.8%), causal modeling incurs negligible degradation while retaining a better performance margin over existing 5B baselines. Furthermore, qualitative rollouts in Figure15 demonstrate that WiC-Causal preserves long-horizon spatial coherence across diverse viewing regimes. Notably, in loop-closure and viewpoint reappearance scenarios (e.g., returning to previously explored landscapes or room corners), WiC-Causal consistently reproduces previously observed visual landmarks and layouts.

    6.2 Scaling to Rich Game Controls

    To further demonstrate the extensibility and token-level composability beyond canonical navigation commands, we extend World-in-Context to accommodate richer, high-frequency gameplay actions. Experiments are conducted on Counter-Strike 2 gameplay sequences from EWM [29]. To assess sample efficiency and generalizability, WiC-Game is trained on a compact subset of a single map (i.e., Dust II), and tested on unseen layouts as well as real-world scenarios. Specifically, the condition sequence is augmented with discrete game-control tokens:

    [c^fire ; cᵈᵘᶜᵏ ; cʷᵃˡᵏ],

    		(12)

    corresponding to firing (weapon dynamics and muzzle flashes), crouching (viewport descent), and slow walking (motion attenuation), respectively.

    As illustrated in Figure14, WiC-Game demonstrates sensitive, decoupled control execution across three complementary regimes: (i) In-domain: new control trajectories within the training map (Dust II) exhibit instant actuation responses; (ii) Out-of-distribution: when applied to unseen game maps (e.g., Mirage, Nuke), the model preserves scene consistency while faithfully following concurrent actions; (iii) Real-world transfer: using synthetic starting images, the learned actuation dynamics generalize naturally to realistic visual environments.

    7 Conclusion and Positioning

    Conclusion.

    In this work, we present World-in-Context, a video world modeling framework based on In-Context Conditioning (ICC) that unifies view mode, character action, and camera trajectory as tokens within a shared attention space. We systematically investigate core interactive dimensions, revealing that explicit view tokens disentangle conflicting motion dynamics while enabling emergent in-video switching, and that action and camera signals complement each other in local responsiveness and global stability. Augmented with IT-RoPE to encode accumulated control progression in temporal attention, World-in-Context achieves competitive navigation on WBench (81.5) matching the 22B EchoWM, while establishing strong perspective-switching capability (93.8%). Controlled analyses further demonstrate compounding advantages under richer conditioning, favorable sample efficiency, and natural applicability to causal rollouts, highlighting shared context modeling as a scalable interface for interactive world simulation.

    Positioning of This Report.

    This work focuses primarily on the algorithmic formulation of interactive conditioning, rather than training an all-encompassing system artifact, with World-in-Context serving as a concrete instantiation of this design. The overall capacity of an interactive world model naturally depends on data quality, model size, and training scale. We use a modest interaction-training set of 100K navigation clips and 500 switching sequences. Since comparable training-data statistics are not consistently disclosed by existing methods, we omit cross-method data-scale comparisons from the main table. Instead, we prioritize controlled comparisons that isolate the architectural advantages of shared context modeling and control-aware temporal attention, including their effectiveness across training-data budgets. Specifically, this work centers around three foundational control modalities, i.e., view mode, character action, and camera motion, as they directly address the core dimensions governing interactive navigation: how the environment is viewed across perspectives and how user inputs steer character actuation alongside viewport evolution. These algorithmic findings complement concurrent advances in scaling, presenting an extensible interface for coordinating diverse interactive controls.
