However, realistic insertion requires the object to be seamlessly lit by the scene and, conversely, to cast physically plausible shadows onto it. Existing approaches either harmonize appearance in image space, sacrificing multi-view consistency, or approximate scene illumination with an environment map at the insertion point, which cannot represent near-field area lights such as windows and lamps that dominate indoor lighting. To address this, we present GraftRay, a unified method for physically consistent insertion of mesh objects into indoor scenes represented by either 2D or 3D Gaussians. We recover scene materials and surface normals with diffusion-based priors, and explicitly model spatially-extended emitters, solving their radiance in closed form. A hybrid renderer then jointly path-traces the scene Gaussians and inserted meshes, producing view-consistent shading, interreflections, and soft shadows. On FIPT, GraftRay sets a new state of the art, outperforming recent baselines such as ComGS and EAG-PT in rendering fidelity and shadow accuracy, while maintaining highly competitive rendering efficiency.

1 Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [21] and its 2D counterpart [15] enable high-quality, real-time rendering of reconstructed scenes. However, inserting a virtual object into such scenes remains challenging. Beyond matching its appearance to the background, the inserted object must respond to the scene’s illumination, cast geometrically consistent shadows, and contribute indirect light to surrounding surfaces. Achieving these effects requires explicit light transport while preserving the visual fidelity of the original reconstruction.

Existing approaches address this problem from three main directions. Environment-map-based methods estimate local illumination from HDR environment maps [2, 26, 16]. Although effective for approximating incident illumination, environment maps do not explicitly represent the spatial positions of local emitters or their interactions with scene geometry, limiting their ability to reproduce spatially varying illumination and geometrically consistent shadows. Inverse-rendering methods jointly recover scene materials and illumination [28, 8, 13, 47, 29, 37, 3]. While physically grounded, these methods introduce additional unknowns beyond those strictly required for object insertion. Moreover, low-dynamic-range (LDR) observations weaken the photometric constraints needed to distinguish emissive sources from highly reflective surfaces. Finally, image-space harmonization methods use generative models to refine the appearance of composited objects [36, 42, 38, 24]. Despite producing visually plausible results, they do not explicitly model scene-level light transport and therefore cannot guarantee consistent relighting when the object or illumination changes.

We propose GraftRay, a unified framework for physically consistent object insertion into 2D and 3D Gaussian scenes (Fig.1). Because our pipeline extracts material priors directly from rendered views rather than relying on original capture data, it uniquely supports physically-based insertion even for synthetically generated Gaussian scenes where original training images are unavailable. We first render multi-view images from the Gaussian scene and estimate material properties, including albedo, roughness, metallicity, and normals, using robust 2D estimators such as RGB-X or diffusion-based models. These predictions are then unprojected onto individual 2D/3D Gaussians to provide scene-level material attributes, bypassing the complex joint optimization of traditional inverse rendering. Building on these attributes, we extend an OptiX-accelerated path tracer to support Gaussian primitives with stochastic transparency [9] and 3σ axis-aligned bounding boxes, traced jointly with inserted meshes. The extended path tracer incorporates a Mitsuba-style path integration scheme [17], analytic area emitters, multiple importance sampling (MIS), and explicit shadow rays to enable light transport directly on Gaussian scenes. We further recover scene illumination from LDR observations by treating saturated pixels as lower-bound constraints and using unsaturated surfaces to constrain emitter intensities. Since light transport is linear in emitter intensities with fixed geometry and materials, we precompute unit-radiance basis images and formulate light estimation as a nonnegative least-squares (NNLS) problem. Finally, we use differential rendering [7] to introduce the inserted object’s shadows and indirect illumination while preserving the original background reconstruction.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    From LDR images alone, we unproject multi-view 2D material and normal predictions onto individual 2D/3D Gaussians, providing scene-level material attributes for physically based insertion without joint inverse rendering.

  • •

    We extend an OptiX path tracer to trace stochastic-transparency Gaussians jointly with meshes, computing illumination, shadows, and indirect light between Gaussian scenes and mesh objects, while differential rendering preserves the reconstruction.

  • •

    We formulate light-intensity estimation using censored observations and path-traced radiance bases, exploiting unsaturated illumination cues to distinguish true emitters from bright reflectors and efficiently estimate nonnegative emitter intensities.

    • 2 Related Work

    Lighting estimation for object insertion.

    Classical object insertion relies on differential rendering [7], which combines a captured scene with an estimate of its illumination; Karsch et al.[20] extended this paradigm to single photographs. Subsequent methods estimate illumination from images using learned HDR environment maps [11], spatially varying lighting [12, 25], or lighting volumes [39]. Diffusion-based approaches further improve illumination estimation and adaptation: DiffusionLight [35] synthesizes environment-map observations through a rendered chrome ball, while DiPIR [26] uses a diffusion model as a critic for lighting optimization. GaSLight [2] lifts ordinary images into HDR Gaussian splats, LightHarmony3D [16] predicts environment maps for hybrid Gaussian–mesh rendering, and LuxRemix [27] decomposes indoor illumination into editable components. Unlike approaches that primarily estimate environment maps or distribute emissive radiance across scene representations, GraftRay explicitly parameterizes local area emitters and uses them in path-traced light transport, allowing their spatial extent and scene occlusion to affect illumination and shadows.

    Compositing and harmonization in 3D.

    Recent methods use generative priors to improve the visual consistency of inserted objects in reconstructed scenes. MV-CoLight [36] generates multi-view-consistent lighting and shadows, while Violante et al.[42] harmonize composite images with diffusion models and consolidate the results into 3DGS. D3DR [38] similarly uses diffusion priors for zero-shot 3DGS harmonization. Other approaches explore alternative scene representations and insertion strategies: ComGS [10] composes objects using surface octahedral probes, and FreeInsert [24] inserts text-specified objects without requiring explicit spatial priors. Related 2D methods include image harmonization [6], diffusion-based object relighting [19], token-space relighting from sparse views [5], and geometry-guided video insertion with GO-Renderer [14]. GaussianEditor [4] explores direct editing of 3DGS scenes. These methods primarily target perceptual consistency or generative scene editing, whereas GraftRay explicitly models light transport to produce view-consistent shadows and indirect illumination for inserted objects.

    Inverse rendering on Gaussian splats.

    Neural inverse rendering initially developed around radiance fields [31], factorizing geometry, reflectance, and illumination [48, 18] with ray tracing for indoor scenes [49]. For Gaussians, GS-IR [28] and GS-ID [8] recover per-Gaussian BRDFs under environment maps or spherical Gaussians. GI-GS [3] and IRGS [13] incorporate global illumination, with IRGS employing differentiable 2D Gaussian ray tracing. NeILF++ [47] couples incident and outgoing light fields, while IRIS [29] addresses indoor LDR reconstruction by estimating camera responses. Intrinsic diffusion priors [46, 23] and factorized inverse path tracing [43] offer alternative material decomposition strategies. Among these, AEGIR [37] is closely related, jointly optimizing area emitters, materials, and geometry via a differentiable deferred renderer. Similarly, EAG-PT [44] reconstructs emission-aware 2DGS with albedo only for path-traced editing. Unlike these joint factorizations, GraftRay targets object insertion with a constrained optimization: we initialize scene materials from priors and optimize emitter radiances while keeping geometry and materials fixed, reducing coupled unknowns and enabling explicit handling of saturated LDR observations.

    Ray tracing Gaussian primitives.

    Recent methods have extended ray tracing to Gaussian and particle-based representations. 3DGRT [32] traces particle scenes using ray-tracing hardware, bounding individual primitives and evaluating their responses along rays. EVER [30] supports exact ellipsoid rendering for view synthesis, while GHPT [1] combines rasterization and path tracing for real-time relightable Gaussian splats. Building on these efforts, we extend an OptiX-accelerated path tracer to support light transport directly on Gaussian scenes. Our approach shares the peak-response intersection strategy with 3DGRT but targets physical illumination rather than view synthesis. Stochastic hit acceptance [40] accounts for Gaussian transparency during ray traversal, enabling Monte Carlo light-transport estimation with analytic area emitters, multiple importance sampling, and next-event estimation.

    3 Method

    Given a reconstructed Gaussian Splatting scene and user-marked light regions, our method estimates scene illumination and inserts objects with consistent direct and indirect lighting. As illustrated in Fig.2, we first estimate per-Gaussian materials and normals from multi-view intrinsic-image predictions. We then initialize analytic area-light candidates from the marked regions and estimate their radiances using a Gaussian-aware path tracer and unit-radiance basis renders. Finally, differential compositing transfers the lighting changes induced by the inserted objects to the original 3DGS rendering while preserving its view-dependent appearance.

    3.1 Material and Normal Estimation

    A Gaussian Splatting scene consists of N anisotropic Gaussians with means μᵢ, rotations Rᵢ, scales Sᵢ=diag(sᵢ), opacities oᵢ, and view-dependent colours [21]. Physically based light transport additionally requires a surface normal nᵢ and BRDF parameters, including albedo aᵢ, roughness ρᵢ, and metallic mᵢ, which are not explicitly provided by the reconstruction. We estimate these attributes by rendering the scene from V virtual views and applying the intrinsic-image diffusion model RGB↔X [46] with S random seeds to each view. The predicted material and normal maps are then back-projected onto the Gaussians.

    Visibility.

    To avoid assigning a pixel’s prediction to occluded Gaussians, we determine the visible surface depth from accumulated transmittance along each camera ray. Specifically, we define the surface depth z as the depth at which the transmittance first falls below \tfrac12, corresponding to the median depth of the accumulated opacity. A Gaussian at camera-space depth r is accepted only if

    (|r-z|)/(z)<τ_z,

    where τ_z is a depth tolerance. This test rejects Gaussians that lie in front of or behind the visible surface.

    Aggregation.

    For each Gaussian, we first average predictions from all accepting views separately for each random seed, and then take the per-channel median across seeds. This aggregation reduces stochastic variation in the diffusion predictions and disagreements across views. Predicted normals are transformed to world space before aggregation and renormalized afterwards. We keep the resulting materials and normals fixed during illumination estimation, thereby avoiding joint optimization of lighting and material parameters.

    This per-Gaussian back-projection turns predictions that are plausible per image but mutually inconsistent into a single scene-level estimate. A 2D estimator may assign the same surface a different albedo or roughness in different views or seeds; since each Gaussian is visible in many views, the average over its accepting views acts as a multi-view consensus that suppresses view-specific errors, and the median over seeds removes outlying samples. Storing the result on the Gaussians also makes materials available wherever a path arrives, including surfaces outside the current view.

    3.2 Emitter Initialization

    Each emitter is manually specified by the user through a 2D mask, while its geometry and radiance are estimated automatically. The user marks light-emitting regions, such as windows, lamps, and ceiling panels, using SAM [22] in one or a few views. We back-project the masked pixels onto the Gaussians using the visibility test in Sec.3.1, obtaining a 3D point set for each emitter. Each emitter is represented as an analytic, one-sided rectangle Eⱼ, parameterized by its centre, in-plane axes, half-extents, and normal. We fit a plane to each point set using RANSAC weighted towards bright Gaussians, then refine the plane using PCA on the inliers. This weighting favours bright surfaces when estimating the emitter geometry. For wall-mounted emitters, we align the in-plane axes with the horizontal and vertical directions; otherwise, we use the PCA axes. The emitter’s extent is determined from the Gaussians associated with the fitted plane, and its normal is oriented towards the room. The resulting emitter candidates are subsequently refined during radiance estimation in Sec.3.5, allowing candidates with little contribution to the observed illumination to be suppressed.

    3.3 Path Tracing on Gaussian Scenes

    Gaussians as custom primitives.

    We represent each Gaussian by an axis-aligned bounding box enclosing its 3σ ellipsoid. For a ray x(t)=o+td, we transform the ray into the Gaussian’s local frame:

    p=Sᵢ⁻¹Rᵢ^⊤(o-μᵢ), q=Sᵢ⁻¹Rᵢ^⊤d.

    		(1)

    The Gaussian response along the ray reaches its maximum at

    tᵢ^⋆=-(p·q)/(∥q∥²), mᵢ²=∥p∥²-((p·q)²)/(∥q∥²),

    		(2)

    where mᵢ² is the squared Mahalanobis distance at the closest point on the ray line. The intersection program reports tᵢ^⋆ when mᵢ²<9 and assigns the effective opacity

    αᵢ=oᵢ\exp(-1/2mᵢ²).

    		(3)

    The reported intersection must also lie within the valid ray interval.

    Stochastic transparency.

    Alpha compositing requires intersections to be processed in depth order, whereas hardware ray traversal visits primitives in an arbitrary order. Following stochastic transparency [9], the any-hit program accepts an intersection with Gaussian i with probability αᵢ. OptiX then returns the nearest accepted intersection. Consequently, the probability that Gaussian i is the first accepted primitive is

    wᵢ=\Pr(K=i)=αᵢ∏_j∈Fᵢ(1-αⱼ),

    		(4)

    where Fᵢ denotes the primitives in front of i. This probability equals the corresponding alpha-compositing weight. Thus, shading the returned primitive provides a single-sample estimate of its contribution to the composited radiance. The complete estimator must also account for any background contribution when the ray misses all accepted primitives. Compared with collecting and sorting all intersections along a ray, this requires no per-ray intersection buffer: each path segment is a single hardware traversal, and the inserted meshes are traced in the same acceleration structure. The random acceptance is averaged out by the samples per pixel like the other Monte Carlo dimensions.

    Shadow rays.

    Shadow rays use a separate ray type that evaluates transmittance deterministically rather than sampling stochastic intersections. Its any-hit program accumulates transmittance by multiplying it by (1-αᵢ) and terminates when the value falls below 5×10⁻³. This continuous transmittance estimate supports smooth soft shadows at the sample counts used for basis rendering.

    3.4 Light Transport

    For each pixel, we average radiance estimates over jittered camera rays sampled across the pixel footprint. Along each ray, the outgoing radiance is composited according to

    L_ray=∑ᵢwᵢLₒ(xᵢ,v),

    		(5)

    where wᵢ is defined in Eq.4 and Lₒ is evaluated using the rendering equation with a Cook–Torrance BRDF and GGX microfacet model. Emitters are represented as analytic rectangles rather than Gaussians. We estimate direct illumination using next-event estimation on the rectangles and combine it with BSDF sampling through multiple importance sampling with the power heuristic  [41, 34]. Indirect illumination is estimated by continuing paths along BSDF-sampled directions, with Russian roulette used for path termination. Our integrator follows Mitsuba’s path integrator [17], replacing mesh intersections with the Gaussian primitives described above.

    3.5 Emitter Radiance Estimation

    Basis renders.

    With geometry, materials, and emitter placement fixed, the remaining unknowns are the non-negative emitter radiances L=(L₁,…,L_J)^⊤≥0. Since emitted radiance enters the rendering equation linearly and the scene transport is linear in the emitter radiances, the linear image can be expressed as

    I(L)=∑ⱼ₌₁^JLⱼBⱼ,

    		(6)

    where Bⱼ is the path-traced image obtained with emitter Eⱼ at unit radiance and all other emitters disabled. Each basis image includes the direct and indirect transport originating from that emitter. To prevent the reconstructed appearance of an emitter from being counted alongside its analytic representation, we remove the bright Gaussians within a thin slab around Eⱼ when rendering its own basis. In all other basis renders, these Gaussians remain in the scene and act as reconstructed surfaces. This treatment lets each basis represent a distinct emitter hypothesis.

    Clipped and unclipped observations.

    For each fitting view, let y denote the observed image and let τ=0.98 be the clipping threshold. Since a saturated colour channel provides only a lower bound on the underlying sensor response, we distinguish unclipped and clipped observations per channel:

    U_c={p:y_p,c<τ}, ℂ_c={p:y_p,c≥τ}.

    Objective.

    Let g denote the sRGB encoding function or the fitted EMoR response, and let B_p,c∈ℝ^J collect the unit-radiance basis values at pixel p and colour channel c. We estimate the emitter radiances independently per channel by solving

    \min_L_c≥0∑_p∈U_c[g(B_p,c^⊤L_c)-y_p,c]²(7)
    +∑_p∈ℂ_c[τ-g(B_p,c^⊤L_c)]₊²,

    where [x]₊=\max(x,0). Unclipped observations are matched directly, whereas clipped observations impose a one-sided penalty that discourages predictions below the clipping threshold without penalizing predictions above it. This treatment matters because the brightest pixels are precisely those that observe the emitters. Fitting them as equalities would pull the radiances down towards the sensor ceiling, and discarding them would lose the information that the emitters are at least that bright. With the one-sided term, the clipped pixels only bound the solution from below, and its magnitude is set by the unsaturated walls, floor and furniture, whose brightness depends on each emitter through the basis images.

    The problem contains J unknowns per channel, typically fewer than twenty, but can involve tens of millions of residuals across all fitting views. We evaluate residuals and Jacobians on the GPU and solve the resulting J×J normal equations using Levenberg–Marquardt. In linear space, the objective reduces to non-negative least squares; the nonlinear camera response makes the optimization nonlinear while keeping its dimensionality low. In our experiments, the solution is insensitive to initialization.

    Suppressing spurious emitter candidates.

    Pixels directly observing a window or lamp may be saturated and therefore provide only lower-bound constraints on the predicted sensor response. Such observations alone cannot reliably distinguish an emitter from a bright reflector. Instead, the estimated radiances are constrained primarily by how well each candidate explains the illumination of unsaturated regions in the room. Consequently, a candidate that contributes little to the observed room illumination can receive near-zero radiance even if it was included in the initial user annotations.

    3.6 Differential Compositing

    Replacing the original 3DGS rendering with a path-traced image can discard view-dependent appearance and reconstruction details. We therefore transfer the lighting changes induced by the inserted object while retaining the original scene appearance. We trace the scene from the same camera with and without the inserted objects, obtaining I_with and I_without in linear radiance. Given the object mask M and the original 3DGS rendering I_3dgs, we compute

    Iₒᵤₜ=M k I_with(8)
    +(1-M) I_3dgs⊙clip((I_with)/(I_without),0,c),

    where ⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication, c=3 limits the ratio, and k is the median of I_3dgs/I_without over background pixels to compensate for exposure differences.

    The ratio captures the relative radiance change induced by the inserted object: values below one correspond to attenuation, such as cast shadows, while values above one capture increased illumination, including indirect bounce light. The original 3DGS rendering retains appearance details that the path tracer does not model explicitly, and the ratio modulates these details to incorporate the estimated lighting changes. All compositing operations are performed in linear radiance before applying the fitted camera response. Optionally, we attenuate chromatic changes in the ratio using

    r↦r̄((r)/(r̄))^η,

    where r̄ is the channel mean and η controls the strength of the transferred bounce-light colour.

    4 Experiments

item.title: 生成的多视图别直接糊上模型：Texture Consolidation 用深度拉普拉斯做置信度，再归一化亮度与饱和度 ｜ Texture Consolidation of Generated Multi-View Renderings
item.description:
一句话：反投影要靠置信度加权：轮廓附近与遮挡纹素置零，逐图先做颜色归一化再合并。

要点：

  • 问题是把多张「生成出来的」视图反投影回纹理时，各图之间存在亮度与饱和度差异，直接合并会出现明显色块与接缝
  • 置信度设计很具体：先渲染深度图、取拉普拉斯并阈值化，把深度不连续处（轮廓附近）的纹素置信度置零、周边衰减；被遮挡的纹素同样置零
  • 合并前对每张反投影结果做颜色归一化，缩小图与图之间的亮度/饱和度差异——这是「生成视图 → 可用纹理」这条管线里最少被写下来的一步

为什么值得看：现在很多管线是「多视图生成 + 反投影贴图」，但生成模型不保证跨视图颜色一致，直接合并就废。这条给的是低成本、可实现的补丁：置信度 + 归一化，任何做 AI 贴图/资产重建的团队都会用到。

中文摘要：这篇处理的是生成式管线里的收尾问题：把多张生成出来的视图反投影回同一张纹理时，各图之间的亮度与饱和度并不一致，直接合并会出现色块与接缝。作者的做法是两条：一是给反投影结果算置信度——先渲染深度图、对深度取拉普拉斯并阈值化，在深度不连续处（物体轮廓附近）把纹素置信度置零、周边衰减，被遮挡的纹素也置零；二是在合并前对每张反投影图做颜色归一化，压缩图与图之间的亮度与饱和度差异。文中给出归一化前后的对比图，显示原本的亮度/饱和度方差被明显拉平。这属于「生成视图 → 可用纹理资产」管线里最少被写下来的工程细节。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心渲染（English）

原文发布：2026-10-28

本期推送：2026-10-29

Texture Consolidation of Generated Multi-View Renderings

Abstract

We present a system for consolidating a sparse set of multi-view renderings into a single coherent texture image, providing a framework for integrating generative models for image generation within the geometry-processing pipeline. Given a texture-atlased triangle mesh and a set of renderings with associated camera parameters, we generate the texture image by: (1) back-projecting the renderings onto the mesh to obtain texture images with normalized colors and confidences; (2) solving for flow-fields on the mesh that align the colors to each other, taking into account the associated confidences; and (3) fusing the registered colors into a single texture image using gradient-domain stitching, again incorporating confidences. Our approach complements existing techniques for multi-view image generation, leveraging mesh-based optical flow and texture-space stitching. In doing so it addresses the challenge that while modern image generation pipelines generate highly convincing renderings, they struggle to produce renderings that are consistent across views. Code is available at https://github.com/hliuw/TextureConsolidation.

1 Introduction

The generation of 3D assets from generated multi-view renderings has advanced considerably in recent years [PJBM23, RMA∗23, GLAK25]. Leveraging powerful diffusion-based models, these methods generate high-quality multi-view images for diverse 3D content. However, the renderings often exhibit inconsistencies when mapped onto 3D geometry, making it difficult to integrate them into a single, view-independent, model.

Motivated by this challenge, we consider the following problem: Given a set of multi-view renderings and a texture-atlased mesh, how do we construct a globally consistent texture image?

This question has been explored for real-world RGB-D datasets, where approaches typically address the problem through view selection, pose optimization, registration, and blending. However, generated renderings differ from real-world captures in that they lack a coherent, view-independent model from which the renderings are generated, often resulting in geometric and photometric inconsistencies between renderings. As a result, while generating new views is computationally cheap, additional renderings have the down-side of introducing further inconsistency. This makes view augmentation a trade-off, in contrast to real-world captures where more data is preferred. In particular, this motivates the need for robust image registration and fusion – supporting the generation of higher-quality textures from a small number of renderings.

While many multi-view texture registration methods exist, they are predominantly designed for dense RGB-D captures, relying on view selection to discard low-quality frames affected by motion blur, and having lighting and shading artifacts. generated multi-view renderings that sparsely sample the view sphere present a different set of challenges: each point is visible in only a few views; and generated views are not geometrically consistent, so that back-projection produces misaligned textures.

We address these challenges by designing a confidence-aware pipeline for multi-view texture consolidation that back-projects the renderings to texture images and then registration and stitching in the surface domain. We extend existing optical flow [PKC∗16] and gradient-domain stitching [PGB03, LZPW04, PKCH18] techniques, adapting them to support per-texel confidences. This is achieved via quadrature-based finite-elements integration supporting sub-triangle evaluation of functions, thereby bridging texel-resolution and mesh-resolution discretizations.

Our method is agnostic to the rendering pipeline, serving as a general post-processing module that complements prior multi-view generation methods. Empirically, we show that existing registration methods for RGB-D captures degrade on generated inputs that sparsely sample the view sphere, while our framework produces high-quality texture images in this challenging setting.

2 Related Work

Textured 3D Shape Generation

Diffusion models have achieved remarkable progress in 2D image generation [RBL∗22, YZS∗23, ZRA23]. However, generating textured 3D models continues to be a challenge. Approaches differ in their choice of geometric representations and in how they couple geometry and color generation.

One common approach is to generate textured 3D shapes from user-provided text input. Approaches using Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [MST∗21] or Gaussian-Splats (GS) [KKLD23] often start by either directly optimizing the scene from text prompts, or leveraging diffusion models to first generate multi-view renderings which are then used to reconstruct the NeRF/GS model [PJBM23, WLW∗23, LGT∗23, TCC∗24, TRZ∗23, YFW∗24]. Hybrid scene representations have also been used to transition between different intermediate representations during optimization before extracting the textured mesh [CCJJ23]. Additionally, some NeRF/GS methods enable mesh extraction as a final step [LGT∗23, TRZ∗23, WZB∗25].

Another approach takes an input 3D geometry and generates color textures by back-projecting multi-view renderings [RMA∗23, CSL∗23, ZCQ∗24, GLAK25, CMZ∗24, ZSG∗24]. These methods first generate multi-view rendering from pretrained 2D diffusion models, often using depth maps as guidance. The composite color texture is then produced through aggregation of multi-view renderings and progressive inpainting of untextured regions. Our work focuses on this setting and addresses the challenge of registering and compositing such multi-view renderings.

Texture Registration and Blending

A challenge in back-projecting multi-view renderings is the lack of consistency across different views – a long-standing challenge in 3D reconstruction from photographs. Such inconsistencies typically arise from variations in lighting, occlusions, and geometric distortions. generated textures can exacerbate the problem by independently introducing different details for different renderings.

Addressing these issues typically involves some form of registration and blending. A common strategy is to align textures through warping. Eisemann et al.[EDDM∗08] and Casas et al.[CVCH14] use reprojected images to compute a correction field via optical flow. Dellepiane et al.[DMC∗12] compute optical flow between overlapping photographs to locally correct image-to-geometry misalignment. Aganj et al.[AMK09] compute the displacement using reprojected feature correspondences across interest points in different views. Inconsistency can also be mitigated by optimizing camera pose. Zhou and Koltun [ZK14] jointly optimize camera poses and non-rigid deformation per photo to maximize photometric consistency across projected color images. Huang et al.[HTD∗20] introduce adversarial texture optimization that learns tolerance to misalignments by training a discriminator on view projections, later extended by Zhao et al.[ZZS22] using Markov Random Field view initialization and FFT alignment. Fu et al.[FYL∗21] incorporate a texture detail layer to select the best-fit texture for each triangle face. Camera pose is then optimized to align these renderings, and they are regenerated at the texture charts’ boundaries to remove seams. Wang et al.[WGZF24] propose a similar method by detecting and excluding misaligned regions, optimizing camera positions, and filling in holes. Kim et al. [KYL∗26] refine an initial texture by jointly optimizing uncertainty maps and deformation grids to handle inconsistent AI-generated targets within non-differentiable production engines.

Other methods focus on view blending. This is often done as a combination of view selection and stitching. An early example is Gal et al.[GWO∗10], which assigns each face both a source image and a local image-space translation compensating for misalignment. Waechter et al.[WMG14] texture meshes from photos by filtering occluders via photo-consistency checks, selecting views based on gradient magnitude, and performing color adjustment using gradient-domain stitching [PGB03]. Pagés et al.[PBMG15] blend the contributions of all cameras across the whole mesh, using smoothly interpolated per-vertex camera ratings to suppress seams while limiting blur. Du et al.[DCC∗18] instead focus on texture blending, identifying seams using rendered depth maps and modulating them using geodesic fields. These methods are also applicable to generated multi-view renderings. Zhao et al.[ZSG∗24] select a subset of generated renderings to minimize inconsistency via combinatorial optimization and warp them using SIFT flow [LYT11]. The resulting textures are stitched by assigning each face an optimal projected texture, formulated as a joint labeling problem. Im2SurfTex [GLAK25] introduces a neural back-projection module that integrates textures by encoding geodesic-aware features and fusing neighboring pixels through cross-attention.

In our approach we use optical flow to register the textures and gradient-domain stitching to composite them, performing both over the surface. This complements earlier methods that perform view-dependent processing and rely on a final blending step to consolidate results. We provide a brief review of these techniques.

Optical Flow

Optical flow techniques were originally developed to identify the motion of objects in consecutive image frames by estimating a vector-field under the assumption of luminance constancy [HS81, FBK15, AMPA24]. They have also been used to register textures from multi-view renderings by computing an aligning flow-field and advecting the pixels [EDDM∗08, DMC∗12, CVCH14]. Traditionally, though, these methods work in the (flat) 2D image domain.

Extending optical flow to the (curved) surface domain requires evaluating the smoothness of tangent vector-fields [DGDT16, Lee18]. This is achieved by defining a Dirichlet energy for tangent vector-fields [SSC19, SWJG20, BSEH17]. With this energy, the optical flow-field can be computed using a variational formulation [LB08, PKC∗16]. Signals are then advected along the flow-field to align details and reduce the ghosting artifacts that occur with naive blending.

Gradient-domain Stitching

A popular method for seamless stitching fuses together signals by compositing their gradients, rather than colors. The approach was initially formulated for 2D images [LZPW04, PGB03] but has since been applied to the stitching of signals over a triangulated surface [DSWH14, CRK16]. More recently, the approach has been extended to operate within the texture domain, handling cross-chart discontinuities and non-uniform distortion in the texture-mapping [PKCH18].

3 Overview

table[h] Notation

The input to our method is a texture-atlased manifold triangle mesh M⊂ℝ³ and a sparse set of multi-view renderings with corresponding camera parameters, {{Yᵢ,Cᵢ}}ᵢ₌₁^K. Our goal is to produce a globally consistent texture image, I^*. This is achieved through the pipeline described below and visualized in Fig. 1.

Preprocessing. We generate texture color and confidence images for each input rendering – back-projecting each rendering onto the surface, defining per-texel confidence from visibility, depth, and viewing angle, and normalizing the colors.

Registration. We align colors in the surface domain – computing an optical flow-field for each color and confidence image, and advecting texel values along the fields.

Stitching. We fuse the optical-flow aligned texture color and confidence images – performing confidence-aware stitching in the gradient-domain.

Fig. 2 motivates the need for both registration and stitching. Just blending the back-projections using confidences creates a texture with ghosting, due to the misalignment of color features (left). Optical flow addresses the ghosting issue by aligning the back-projections to each other, but still exhibits discontinuities due to color variations across the input renderings (center). Stitching produces a seamless and ghost-free color texture (right).

4 Preliminaries

We review gradient-domain processing and optical flow computation, for signals defined over a mesh M⊂ℝ³. In what follows, we refer to functions and vector-fields as queryable if they are bounded and can be evaluated almost anywhere on the mesh. That is, if they can be integrated over the mesh.

4.1 Gradient-Domain Processing

The goal of classical gradient-domain processing is to solve for a signal f that simultaneously fits target values h and gradients v⃗:

E_gd(f,h,v⃗,α_gf)=∫_M(f-h)²+α_gf∥∇f-v⃗∥²

(1)

with α_gf the gradient-fitting weight.

Two standard applications are smoothing and stitching. In smoothing, v⃗ is set to zero and α_gf parametrizes the “extent” of the smoothing. In stitching, v⃗ is set to the composite gradients of the input images to be stitched, and α_gf is set to a large value – focusing the optimization on fitting the gradients.

Discretization

Given a basis of scalar functions {φᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N on M, the problem reduces to the solution of a sparse symmetric positive definite system, with solution coefficients, x∈ℝ^N, satisfying:

(M+α_gf·S)·x=b

with M,S∈ℝ^N×N the mass and stiffness matrices, and b∈ℝ^N encoding the scalar and gradient constraints:

Mᵢⱼ≡∫_Mφᵢ·φⱼ, Sᵢⱼ≡∫_M⟨∇φᵢ,∇φⱼ⟩,

bᵢ≡∫_Mφᵢ·h+α_gf⟨∇φᵢ,v⃗⟩.

Essential to our approach is that, using quadrature to approximate integrals, defining the linear system only requires that the φᵢ and their derivatives, as well as the constraints h and v⃗, be queryable.

4.2 Optical Flow

Given source and target signals, fₛ,fₜ:M→ℝᵈ, the goal of optical flow is to compute a tangent vector-field describing how the source should advect along the mesh so as to align with the target.

The approach uses the fact that when a signal ψ advects along a vector-field v⃗, the advected value at a point p∈M is “brought in” from the direction opposite the flow – i.e. the direction from which the flow arrives. Formally, the time-evolving signal obtained by advecting along v⃗ satisfies the PDE [MMP∗11]:

(∂ψ)/(∂t)=-⟨v⃗,∇ψ⟩.

Thus, for small time-steps ε, the advected signal is approximately:

\hboxAdv_ε·v⃗(ψ)≈ψ-ε·⟨v⃗,∇ψ⟩.

This gives an optical flow energy measuring the difference between the (approximately) advected source and the target:

E_of(v⃗,fₛ,fₜ,β_reg)=∫_M((fₛ-⟨v⃗,∇fₛ⟩)-fₜ)²+β_reg∥∇v⃗∥².(2)

The term β_reg∥∇v⃗∥² acts as a regularizer to address the under-determinedness, encouraging smoother flow-fields [HS81].

As the solution v⃗ should itself be time-varying, the optimization is iterated – at each time-step the previously estimated flow-fields are used to advect the source and a correcting flow-field is computed to register the advected source to the target.

Implementation

We follow the implementation of Prada et al.[PKC∗16] which performs the time-stepping hierarchically – initially solving for a smooth flow-field that aligns the low-frequency components and progressively solving for higher-frequencies. This is achieved by modifying the input signals and the regularization in Eq. 2 as a function of the hierarchy level. The advected source and target are replaced by their blurred versions, with the amount of blurring reduced at later levels of the hierarchy. Similarly, the smoothness regularization weight β_reg is decreased at later levels.

In principle, the deformation should be expressed as the composition of advections along the iteratively estimated flow-fields. However, both within the algorithm and as its output, Prada et al. propose using a single flow-field that is their sum.

Discretization

Given a vector-field basis, {ν⃗ᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N, the problem reduces to the solution of a sparse symmetric positive definite system, with the coefficients of the flow-field, x∈ℝ^N, satisfying:

(M^∇fₛ+β_reg·S)·x=b

where M^∇fₛ,S∈ℝ^N×N are the ∇fₛ-weighted mass and stiffness matrices, and b∈ℝ^N encodes the difference constraints:

M^∇fₛᵢⱼ≡∫_M⟨ν⃗ᵢ,∇fₛ⟩·⟨ν⃗ⱼ,∇fₛ⟩, Sᵢⱼ≡∫_M⟨∇ν⃗ᵢ,∇ν⃗ⱼ⟩,

bᵢ≡∫_M⟨ν⃗ᵢ,∇fₛ⟩·(fₜ-fₛ).

As above, using quadrature only requires that the ν⃗ᵢ, their derivatives, the signals fₛ and fₜ, and the gradient ∇fₛ be queryable.

Signal Advection

Finally, given a signal f and a flow-field v⃗, the advected signal, \hboxAdv_v⃗(f), is obtained by stepping backwards along the vector-field, using the hinge-map [DGDT16] to flatten adjacent triangles when stepping across an edge, and sampling.

5 Quadrature-based Integration

Discretizing the computation of optical flow requires resolving two conflicting challenges. On the one hand, the flow-field is expected to be relatively low-frequency, corresponding to the fact that the underlying deformation is smooth. On the other, we would like to represent the colors and confidences at the finer resolution of texel space. Additionally, both for computing the flow-field and stitching, we need the implementations to adapt to confidence.

We resolve these challenges using quadrature-based integration, which also supports mixing different signal representations. For scalar functions, we use the mesh-resolution “hat” basis and the texel-resolution basis of Prada et al.[PKCH18]. For vector-fields we use the mesh-resolution basis functions of Liu et al.[LSV∗26].

Using quadrature makes it straight-forward to incorporate color and confidence represented at texel-resolution when discretizing the flow-field at the vertex resolution. For completeness, we step through the implementation. In particular, we describe the evaluation of integrals for a triangle τ={p₀,p₁,p₂}⊂ℝ³, with the actual computation performed over the unit right triangle:

T={(s,t)∈[0,1]²|s+t≤1}.

We assume that we are given a confidence map w:T→[0,1], we set the metric tensor to be g∈ℝ^2×2 with gᵢⱼ=⟨pᵢ-p₀,pⱼ-p₀⟩, and we denote its determinant |g|. Lightly abusing notation, for a scalar- (resp. vector-)valued function f:T→ℝ (resp. v⃗:T→ℝ²), we write “f” (resp. “v⃗”) to represent both the function on the unit right triangle T and the function on the embedded triangle τ⊂ℝ³.

5.1 Integrating Scalar Functions

Given a scalar basis function φᵢ:T→ℝ and some other function f:T→ℝ, we approximate the integral of the confidence-weighted dot-product of φᵢ and f as:

∫_τw·φᵢ·f≈√|g|·∑ⱼ₌₁^Qμⱼ·w(qⱼ)·φᵢ(qⱼ)·f(qⱼ)

(3)

with {qⱼ,μⱼ}⊂T×ℝ^≥0 the quadrature locations and weights [Cow73, Tay08]. This estimate of the integral only requires that the target and confidence functions, f and w, be queryable, which is true for texture-mapped signals. A similar approach can be used to define the confidence-weighted mass and (assuming queryable derivatives of φᵢ) stiffness matrices.

5.2 Integrating Gradients of Scalar Functions

Given a tangent vector-field basis function ν⃗ᵢ:T→ℝ² and some other function f:T→ℝ, we approximate the confidence-weighted integral of the dot-product of ν⃗ᵢ and the gradient of f as:

∫_τw·⟨ν⃗ᵢ,∇f⟩≈√|g|·∑ⱼ₌₁^Qμⱼ·w(qⱼ)·⟨ν⃗ᵢ(qⱼ),∇_gf(qⱼ)⟩_g.

(4)

We note that the inner-product is equivalent to the pairing of the tangent vector-field ν⃗ᵢ with the differential of f, which is metric-independent. As above, the incorporation of confidence only requires that the functions f, ∇f, and w be queryable. This too holds for texture-mapped signals. And again, a similar approach can be used to define the confidence-weighted mass and (assuming queryable derivatives of ν⃗ᵢ) stiffness matrices.

6 Method

We now discuss the key steps of our pipeline, summarized in Alg. 1. To facilitate the presentation, we begin by describing how we adapt the traditional energies to incorporate confidence.

Gradient-Domain

Given a set of target values, target gradients, and confidences, {hᵢ,v⃗ᵢ,wᵢ}, we define the gradient-domain energy:

E_gd(f,{hᵢ,v⃗ᵢ,wᵢ},α_gf,α_reg)
≡∑ᵢ∫_Mwᵢ·((f-hᵢ)²+α_gf∥∇f-v⃗ᵢ∥²)+α_reg∥∇f∥²(5)

The additional regularization term, α_reg∥∇f∥², is needed to make the energy non-singular in regions of zero confidence. (In general, α_reg is set to a very small value and serves solely to encourage the signal to be smooth in regions with no confidence.)

In contexts where we have multiple weight functions, we normalize and rescale the weights:

wᵢ(q)←\underbrace((wᵢ(q))/(∑ⱼwⱼ(q)))(1-∏ⱼ(1-wⱼ(q)))_\mbox\scriptsizenormalization·(1-∏ⱼ(1-wⱼ(q))) (\mbox\scriptsizescaling).

Thus, the sum of the weights is (1-∏ⱼ(1-wⱼ))∈[0,1], giving the confidence that the point is covered by some target. (When all weights are zero, the normalized and rescaled weights remain zero.)

Blurring. The energy associated with blurring a signal h is obtained by setting α_gf=0 (and is independent of target gradient):

E_blur(f,h,w,α_reg)≡∫_Mw·(f-h)²+α_reg∥∇f∥²

(6)

Stitching. In the context of stitching together individual images, most often the target signals are the images themselves and the target vector-fields are their gradients, v⃗ᵢ=∇hᵢ. This gives:

E_stitch(f,{hᵢ,wᵢ},α_gf,α_reg)≡E_gd(f,{hᵢ,∇hᵢ,wᵢ},α_gf,α_reg).

(7)

This confidence-weighted expression obviates the challenges of compositing colors/gradients into a single function/vector-field, typically required as input for stitching. The confidences wᵢ implicitly dictate which values/gradients (and to what extent) should be “active” in different parts of the domain.

Optical Flow

Given source and target signals fₛ and fₜ, and confidence w, the optical flow energy is adapted as:

E_of(v⃗,fₛ,fₜ,w,β_reg)≡∫_Mw·((fₛ-⟨v⃗,∇fₛ⟩)-fₜ))²+β_reg∥∇v⃗∥².

(8)

Optimization

For the above energies, we denote their minimizers:

Stitch({hᵢ,wᵢ},α_gf,α_reg)≡\argmin_fE_stitch(f,{hᵢ,wᵢ},α_gf,α_reg)
Blur(h,w,α_reg)≡\argmin_fE_blur(f,h,w,α_reg)
Flow(fₛ,fₜ,w,β_reg)≡\argmin_v⃗E_of(v⃗,fₛ,fₜ,w,β_reg).(9)

Given a choice of queryable scalar/vector-field basis functions, the construction of the associated linear systems directly parallels the process described in Sec. 4, with integration adapted to incorporate confidence, as in Eqs. 3 and 4.

6.1 Preprocessing

Our pre-processing consists of two stages. Back-projecting to turn the renderings into texture color and confidence images, and normalization to correct for low-frequency variation of color in the generated rendering.

Back-Projection

Given the renderings and camera parameters, {{Yᵢ,Cᵢ}}ᵢ₌₁^K, we back-project the renderings onto the mesh M to obtain color and confidence textures, {{Iᵢ,wᵢ}}ᵢ₌₁^K.

Color

Given a rendering/camera {Yᵢ,Cᵢ}, we define the color at a texel by locating the corresponding point on the mesh, back-projecting using the camera parameters, and sampling Yᵢ at the back-projected position. The surface point is computed in two steps. First, we compute the barycentric coordinates of the texel with respect to the closest texture triangle. Then, we compute the barycentrically weighted average of the triangle’s corner positions in 3D. When the texel falls inside a texture triangle, the barycentric weights are positive and the average of the corners lies on the mesh. Otherwise, we map the average to the closest point on the mesh.

Confidence

Because the generated renderings may have silhouettes that are not consistent with the input geometry, back-projection can cause colors to fall far from their desired location on the surface. We address this by defining a confidence texture that combines normal and depth information. (Fig. 3 shows an example for the Bear model, where part of the belt near the silhouette of the arm is back-projected to the wrist. Combining normal and depth information, we assign texels near silhouettes lower confidence.)

Normal Confidence. We assign normal confidences by measuring the extent to which texels are front-facing to the camera. These are computed in the standard way, using the clamped dot-product of the surface normal and the camera’s viewing direction. Though this identifies locations on the silhouette, it fails to identify front-facing background pixels that are back-projected to the foreground.

Depth Confidence. To assign lower confidence to texels back-projecting to the foreground near silhouettes, we first identify pixels where the depth-map is discontinuous. This is achieved by rendering the scene from the perspective of the camera, computing the depth-map, and thresholding its Laplacian. The confidence is set to zero where the Laplacian exceeds the threshold and is reduced nearby. The confidence of occluded texels is also set to zero.

Finally, we multiply the depth and normal confidences and quantize low-confidences to zero. (See App. B for more details.)

While we instantiate these weights using normal/view-direction alignment and depth continuity, our approach equivalently accommodates other confidence information such as rendering quality/blurriness. Since our primary focus is registration and stitching, this step serves mainly to produce meaningful texture color and confidence images suitable for down-stream processing.

Color Normalization

We adjust the input signals to eliminate low-frequency color variations before estimating the flow. This is done by normalizing with respect to local estimates of the mean and scale:

I^′ᵢ←(Iᵢ-Blur(Iᵢ,wᵢ,εₙ))/(Blur(∥Iᵢ-Blur(Iᵢ,wᵢ,εₙ)∥,wᵢ,εₙ)).

(10)

The blurring is done taking into account confidence and εₙ>0 is a parameter describing the extent of the region over which the average and scale are estimated.

figure

Two back-projected renderings before (top) and after (bottom) color normalization. The input exhibits luminance and saturation variance. Normalization reduce the color inconsistency.

Normalization is crucial for the stability of optical flow. Fig. 4 shows an example of two un-normalized back-projected renderings (top) and the corresponding renderings after normalization (bottom). Due to color variations, the region of overlap is darker for the first rendering than it is for the second, resulting in (φₜ-φₛ) being set to the wrong target difference in Eq. 8. With normalization, the colors are more consistent.

6.2 Registration

Given back-projected color and confidence textures, {{I^′ᵢ,wᵢ}}ᵢ₌₁^K, our goal is to compute the optical flow-fields {v⃗ᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^K that best align the colors. Here we focus on a single time-step of the flow computation. The complete hierarchical solve is described in Alg. 1.

Direct Approach

A direct way to do this would be to define an energy that simultaneously optimizes all the flow-fields. This could be done for a pair of textures by noting that the optimization for the source flow-field v⃗ in Eq. 8 can be adapted to simultaneously optimize for the source and target flow-fields v⃗ₛ and v⃗ₜ by replacing the integrand accounting for advection along one field:

((fₛ-⟨v⃗,∇fₛ⟩)-fₜ)²

with an integrand accounting for the advection along both:

((fₛ-⟨v⃗ₛ,∇fₛ⟩)-(fₜ-⟨v⃗ₜ,∇fₜ⟩))².

One could then obtain an energy simultaneously optimizing all the flow-fields by taking the sum of the energies over all pairs of textures. Such an energy would remain sparse and quadratic. However, the system complexity would be proportional to the mesh resolution multiplied by the number of input views, which would be too expensive to solve in practice.

direct way to do this would be to define an energy that simultaneously optimizes all the optical flow-fields. This could be done by noting that for two color signals, Iₛ and Iₜ, with associated confidences, wₛ and wₜ, one can formulate the pairwise optical flow energy is:

E_of^{wₛ,wₜ}({v⃗ₛ,v⃗ₜ} | {fₛ,fₜ},α)
≡∫_Mwₛwₜ((fₛ-⟨v⃗ₛ,∇fₛ⟩)-(fₜ-⟨v⃗ₜ,∇fₜ⟩))²
+∫_Mα(∥∇v⃗ₛ∥²+∥∇v⃗ₜ∥²),

with the joint confidence is set to the product of the confidences. Then the optical flow energy simultaneously aligning all the colors signals is simply the sum of pairwise energies:

E_of^{wᵢ}({v⃗ᵢ} | {fᵢ},α)≡∑_i,jE_of^{wᵢ,wⱼ}({v⃗ᵢ,v⃗ⱼ} | {fᵢ,fⱼ},α).

The energy is quadratic and results in a sparse symmetric positive-definite system for the coefficients of the flow-fields. However, using it requires solving a system whose complexity is proportional to the mesh resolution, multiplied by the number of color signals, which is too time-consuming in practice.

Successive Signal Registration

Instead, we propose an incremental approach. We start by selecting a target signal and successively register the remaining signals to it. The target itself is evolved by blending in the advected source colors and confidences.

Source/Target Selection. To select the initial target and successive sources, we require a measure of overlap between pairs of signals. Defining the coverage of confidence w:M→ℝ^≥0 as:

⟨w⟩≡∫_Mw

we define the overlap of confidences w and w^′ to be the coverage of their product, ⟨w·w^′⟩. We then select the initial target by finding the pair of textures maximizing overlap, and use the one with larger coverage. Similarly, we select subsequent sources by finding the one maximizing the overlap with the current target.

Source Registration. Given source and target color texture images, I^′ₛ and I^′ₜ, with confidence texture images, wₛ and wₜ, we solve for the flow-field registering the source to the target:

v⃗=Flow(I^′ₛ,I^′ₜ,wₛ·wₜ,β_reg).

We advect the source’s texture color and confidence images along v⃗ and merge them into the target. The new target color is obtained by confidence-weighted blending of the textures registered so far:

I^′ₜ←(∑_i∈ℝ\hboxAdv_v⃗ᵢ(I^′ᵢ)·\hboxAdv_v⃗ᵢ(wᵢ))/(∑_i∈ℝ\hboxAdv_v⃗ᵢ(wᵢ))

where ℝ is the set of indices of the target and the sources registered to it, and the new target confidence is obtained by summing and clamping:

wₜ←\min(1, wₜ+\hboxAdv_v⃗(wₛ)).

Though the blended value is undefined where both the source and target have zero confidence, this does not cause numerical instability because the blended confidence will be zero there as well.

We note that while the target is not advected within a single pass of optical flow registration, the choice of selected target can change across the hierarchical passes. As a result it is possible that all back-projected textures are deformed at the end of the registration.

6.3 Stitching

The final step is stitching the advected texture color and confidence images into a seamless texture color image. We do this using the adaptation of classical gradient-domain stitching that supports confidences, presented in Eq. 7.
