一句话：反投影要靠置信度加权：轮廓附近与遮挡纹素置零，逐图先做颜色归一化再合并。

要点：

  • 问题是把多张「生成出来的」视图反投影回纹理时，各图之间存在亮度与饱和度差异，直接合并会出现明显色块与接缝
  • 置信度设计很具体：先渲染深度图、取拉普拉斯并阈值化，把深度不连续处（轮廓附近）的纹素置信度置零、周边衰减；被遮挡的纹素同样置零
  • 合并前对每张反投影结果做颜色归一化，缩小图与图之间的亮度/饱和度差异——这是「生成视图 → 可用纹理」这条管线里最少被写下来的一步

为什么值得看：现在很多管线是「多视图生成 + 反投影贴图」，但生成模型不保证跨视图颜色一致，直接合并就废。这条给的是低成本、可实现的补丁：置信度 + 归一化，任何做 AI 贴图/资产重建的团队都会用到。

中文摘要：这篇处理的是生成式管线里的收尾问题：把多张生成出来的视图反投影回同一张纹理时，各图之间的亮度与饱和度并不一致，直接合并会出现色块与接缝。作者的做法是两条：一是给反投影结果算置信度——先渲染深度图、对深度取拉普拉斯并阈值化，在深度不连续处（物体轮廓附近）把纹素置信度置零、周边衰减，被遮挡的纹素也置零；二是在合并前对每张反投影图做颜色归一化，压缩图与图之间的亮度与饱和度差异。文中给出归一化前后的对比图，显示原本的亮度/饱和度方差被明显拉平。这属于「生成视图 → 可用纹理资产」管线里最少被写下来的工程细节。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心渲染（English）

原文发布：2026-10-28

本期推送：2026-10-29

Texture Consolidation of Generated Multi-View Renderings

Abstract

We present a system for consolidating a sparse set of multi-view renderings into a single coherent texture image, providing a framework for integrating generative models for image generation within the geometry-processing pipeline. Given a texture-atlased triangle mesh and a set of renderings with associated camera parameters, we generate the texture image by: (1) back-projecting the renderings onto the mesh to obtain texture images with normalized colors and confidences; (2) solving for flow-fields on the mesh that align the colors to each other, taking into account the associated confidences; and (3) fusing the registered colors into a single texture image using gradient-domain stitching, again incorporating confidences. Our approach complements existing techniques for multi-view image generation, leveraging mesh-based optical flow and texture-space stitching. In doing so it addresses the challenge that while modern image generation pipelines generate highly convincing renderings, they struggle to produce renderings that are consistent across views. Code is available at https://github.com/hliuw/TextureConsolidation.

1 Introduction

The generation of 3D assets from generated multi-view renderings has advanced considerably in recent years [PJBM23, RMA∗23, GLAK25]. Leveraging powerful diffusion-based models, these methods generate high-quality multi-view images for diverse 3D content. However, the renderings often exhibit inconsistencies when mapped onto 3D geometry, making it difficult to integrate them into a single, view-independent, model.

Motivated by this challenge, we consider the following problem: Given a set of multi-view renderings and a texture-atlased mesh, how do we construct a globally consistent texture image?

This question has been explored for real-world RGB-D datasets, where approaches typically address the problem through view selection, pose optimization, registration, and blending. However, generated renderings differ from real-world captures in that they lack a coherent, view-independent model from which the renderings are generated, often resulting in geometric and photometric inconsistencies between renderings. As a result, while generating new views is computationally cheap, additional renderings have the down-side of introducing further inconsistency. This makes view augmentation a trade-off, in contrast to real-world captures where more data is preferred. In particular, this motivates the need for robust image registration and fusion – supporting the generation of higher-quality textures from a small number of renderings.

While many multi-view texture registration methods exist, they are predominantly designed for dense RGB-D captures, relying on view selection to discard low-quality frames affected by motion blur, and having lighting and shading artifacts. generated multi-view renderings that sparsely sample the view sphere present a different set of challenges: each point is visible in only a few views; and generated views are not geometrically consistent, so that back-projection produces misaligned textures.

We address these challenges by designing a confidence-aware pipeline for multi-view texture consolidation that back-projects the renderings to texture images and then registration and stitching in the surface domain. We extend existing optical flow [PKC∗16] and gradient-domain stitching [PGB03, LZPW04, PKCH18] techniques, adapting them to support per-texel confidences. This is achieved via quadrature-based finite-elements integration supporting sub-triangle evaluation of functions, thereby bridging texel-resolution and mesh-resolution discretizations.

Our method is agnostic to the rendering pipeline, serving as a general post-processing module that complements prior multi-view generation methods. Empirically, we show that existing registration methods for RGB-D captures degrade on generated inputs that sparsely sample the view sphere, while our framework produces high-quality texture images in this challenging setting.

2 Related Work

Textured 3D Shape Generation

Diffusion models have achieved remarkable progress in 2D image generation [RBL∗22, YZS∗23, ZRA23]. However, generating textured 3D models continues to be a challenge. Approaches differ in their choice of geometric representations and in how they couple geometry and color generation.

One common approach is to generate textured 3D shapes from user-provided text input. Approaches using Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [MST∗21] or Gaussian-Splats (GS) [KKLD23] often start by either directly optimizing the scene from text prompts, or leveraging diffusion models to first generate multi-view renderings which are then used to reconstruct the NeRF/GS model [PJBM23, WLW∗23, LGT∗23, TCC∗24, TRZ∗23, YFW∗24]. Hybrid scene representations have also been used to transition between different intermediate representations during optimization before extracting the textured mesh [CCJJ23]. Additionally, some NeRF/GS methods enable mesh extraction as a final step [LGT∗23, TRZ∗23, WZB∗25].

Another approach takes an input 3D geometry and generates color textures by back-projecting multi-view renderings [RMA∗23, CSL∗23, ZCQ∗24, GLAK25, CMZ∗24, ZSG∗24]. These methods first generate multi-view rendering from pretrained 2D diffusion models, often using depth maps as guidance. The composite color texture is then produced through aggregation of multi-view renderings and progressive inpainting of untextured regions. Our work focuses on this setting and addresses the challenge of registering and compositing such multi-view renderings.

Texture Registration and Blending

A challenge in back-projecting multi-view renderings is the lack of consistency across different views – a long-standing challenge in 3D reconstruction from photographs. Such inconsistencies typically arise from variations in lighting, occlusions, and geometric distortions. generated textures can exacerbate the problem by independently introducing different details for different renderings.

Addressing these issues typically involves some form of registration and blending. A common strategy is to align textures through warping. Eisemann et al.[EDDM∗08] and Casas et al.[CVCH14] use reprojected images to compute a correction field via optical flow. Dellepiane et al.[DMC∗12] compute optical flow between overlapping photographs to locally correct image-to-geometry misalignment. Aganj et al.[AMK09] compute the displacement using reprojected feature correspondences across interest points in different views. Inconsistency can also be mitigated by optimizing camera pose. Zhou and Koltun [ZK14] jointly optimize camera poses and non-rigid deformation per photo to maximize photometric consistency across projected color images. Huang et al.[HTD∗20] introduce adversarial texture optimization that learns tolerance to misalignments by training a discriminator on view projections, later extended by Zhao et al.[ZZS22] using Markov Random Field view initialization and FFT alignment. Fu et al.[FYL∗21] incorporate a texture detail layer to select the best-fit texture for each triangle face. Camera pose is then optimized to align these renderings, and they are regenerated at the texture charts’ boundaries to remove seams. Wang et al.[WGZF24] propose a similar method by detecting and excluding misaligned regions, optimizing camera positions, and filling in holes. Kim et al. [KYL∗26] refine an initial texture by jointly optimizing uncertainty maps and deformation grids to handle inconsistent AI-generated targets within non-differentiable production engines.

Other methods focus on view blending. This is often done as a combination of view selection and stitching. An early example is Gal et al.[GWO∗10], which assigns each face both a source image and a local image-space translation compensating for misalignment. Waechter et al.[WMG14] texture meshes from photos by filtering occluders via photo-consistency checks, selecting views based on gradient magnitude, and performing color adjustment using gradient-domain stitching [PGB03]. Pagés et al.[PBMG15] blend the contributions of all cameras across the whole mesh, using smoothly interpolated per-vertex camera ratings to suppress seams while limiting blur. Du et al.[DCC∗18] instead focus on texture blending, identifying seams using rendered depth maps and modulating them using geodesic fields. These methods are also applicable to generated multi-view renderings. Zhao et al.[ZSG∗24] select a subset of generated renderings to minimize inconsistency via combinatorial optimization and warp them using SIFT flow [LYT11]. The resulting textures are stitched by assigning each face an optimal projected texture, formulated as a joint labeling problem. Im2SurfTex [GLAK25] introduces a neural back-projection module that integrates textures by encoding geodesic-aware features and fusing neighboring pixels through cross-attention.

In our approach we use optical flow to register the textures and gradient-domain stitching to composite them, performing both over the surface. This complements earlier methods that perform view-dependent processing and rely on a final blending step to consolidate results. We provide a brief review of these techniques.

Optical Flow

Optical flow techniques were originally developed to identify the motion of objects in consecutive image frames by estimating a vector-field under the assumption of luminance constancy [HS81, FBK15, AMPA24]. They have also been used to register textures from multi-view renderings by computing an aligning flow-field and advecting the pixels [EDDM∗08, DMC∗12, CVCH14]. Traditionally, though, these methods work in the (flat) 2D image domain.

Extending optical flow to the (curved) surface domain requires evaluating the smoothness of tangent vector-fields [DGDT16, Lee18]. This is achieved by defining a Dirichlet energy for tangent vector-fields [SSC19, SWJG20, BSEH17]. With this energy, the optical flow-field can be computed using a variational formulation [LB08, PKC∗16]. Signals are then advected along the flow-field to align details and reduce the ghosting artifacts that occur with naive blending.

Gradient-domain Stitching

A popular method for seamless stitching fuses together signals by compositing their gradients, rather than colors. The approach was initially formulated for 2D images [LZPW04, PGB03] but has since been applied to the stitching of signals over a triangulated surface [DSWH14, CRK16]. More recently, the approach has been extended to operate within the texture domain, handling cross-chart discontinuities and non-uniform distortion in the texture-mapping [PKCH18].

3 Overview

table[h] Notation

The input to our method is a texture-atlased manifold triangle mesh M⊂ℝ³ and a sparse set of multi-view renderings with corresponding camera parameters, {{Yᵢ,Cᵢ}}ᵢ₌₁^K. Our goal is to produce a globally consistent texture image, I^*. This is achieved through the pipeline described below and visualized in Fig. 1.

Preprocessing. We generate texture color and confidence images for each input rendering – back-projecting each rendering onto the surface, defining per-texel confidence from visibility, depth, and viewing angle, and normalizing the colors.

Registration. We align colors in the surface domain – computing an optical flow-field for each color and confidence image, and advecting texel values along the fields.

Stitching. We fuse the optical-flow aligned texture color and confidence images – performing confidence-aware stitching in the gradient-domain.

Fig. 2 motivates the need for both registration and stitching. Just blending the back-projections using confidences creates a texture with ghosting, due to the misalignment of color features (left). Optical flow addresses the ghosting issue by aligning the back-projections to each other, but still exhibits discontinuities due to color variations across the input renderings (center). Stitching produces a seamless and ghost-free color texture (right).

4 Preliminaries

We review gradient-domain processing and optical flow computation, for signals defined over a mesh M⊂ℝ³. In what follows, we refer to functions and vector-fields as queryable if they are bounded and can be evaluated almost anywhere on the mesh. That is, if they can be integrated over the mesh.

4.1 Gradient-Domain Processing

The goal of classical gradient-domain processing is to solve for a signal f that simultaneously fits target values h and gradients v⃗:

E_gd(f,h,v⃗,α_gf)=∫_M(f-h)²+α_gf∥∇f-v⃗∥²

(1)

with α_gf the gradient-fitting weight.

Two standard applications are smoothing and stitching. In smoothing, v⃗ is set to zero and α_gf parametrizes the “extent” of the smoothing. In stitching, v⃗ is set to the composite gradients of the input images to be stitched, and α_gf is set to a large value – focusing the optimization on fitting the gradients.

Discretization

Given a basis of scalar functions {φᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N on M, the problem reduces to the solution of a sparse symmetric positive definite system, with solution coefficients, x∈ℝ^N, satisfying:

(M+α_gf·S)·x=b

with M,S∈ℝ^N×N the mass and stiffness matrices, and b∈ℝ^N encoding the scalar and gradient constraints:

Mᵢⱼ≡∫_Mφᵢ·φⱼ, Sᵢⱼ≡∫_M⟨∇φᵢ,∇φⱼ⟩,

bᵢ≡∫_Mφᵢ·h+α_gf⟨∇φᵢ,v⃗⟩.

Essential to our approach is that, using quadrature to approximate integrals, defining the linear system only requires that the φᵢ and their derivatives, as well as the constraints h and v⃗, be queryable.

4.2 Optical Flow

Given source and target signals, fₛ,fₜ:M→ℝᵈ, the goal of optical flow is to compute a tangent vector-field describing how the source should advect along the mesh so as to align with the target.

The approach uses the fact that when a signal ψ advects along a vector-field v⃗, the advected value at a point p∈M is “brought in” from the direction opposite the flow – i.e. the direction from which the flow arrives. Formally, the time-evolving signal obtained by advecting along v⃗ satisfies the PDE [MMP∗11]:

(∂ψ)/(∂t)=-⟨v⃗,∇ψ⟩.

Thus, for small time-steps ε, the advected signal is approximately:

\hboxAdv_ε·v⃗(ψ)≈ψ-ε·⟨v⃗,∇ψ⟩.

This gives an optical flow energy measuring the difference between the (approximately) advected source and the target:

E_of(v⃗,fₛ,fₜ,β_reg)=∫_M((fₛ-⟨v⃗,∇fₛ⟩)-fₜ)²+β_reg∥∇v⃗∥².(2)

The term β_reg∥∇v⃗∥² acts as a regularizer to address the under-determinedness, encouraging smoother flow-fields [HS81].

As the solution v⃗ should itself be time-varying, the optimization is iterated – at each time-step the previously estimated flow-fields are used to advect the source and a correcting flow-field is computed to register the advected source to the target.

Implementation

We follow the implementation of Prada et al.[PKC∗16] which performs the time-stepping hierarchically – initially solving for a smooth flow-field that aligns the low-frequency components and progressively solving for higher-frequencies. This is achieved by modifying the input signals and the regularization in Eq. 2 as a function of the hierarchy level. The advected source and target are replaced by their blurred versions, with the amount of blurring reduced at later levels of the hierarchy. Similarly, the smoothness regularization weight β_reg is decreased at later levels.

In principle, the deformation should be expressed as the composition of advections along the iteratively estimated flow-fields. However, both within the algorithm and as its output, Prada et al. propose using a single flow-field that is their sum.

Discretization

Given a vector-field basis, {ν⃗ᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N, the problem reduces to the solution of a sparse symmetric positive definite system, with the coefficients of the flow-field, x∈ℝ^N, satisfying:

(M^∇fₛ+β_reg·S)·x=b

where M^∇fₛ,S∈ℝ^N×N are the ∇fₛ-weighted mass and stiffness matrices, and b∈ℝ^N encodes the difference constraints:

M^∇fₛᵢⱼ≡∫_M⟨ν⃗ᵢ,∇fₛ⟩·⟨ν⃗ⱼ,∇fₛ⟩, Sᵢⱼ≡∫_M⟨∇ν⃗ᵢ,∇ν⃗ⱼ⟩,

bᵢ≡∫_M⟨ν⃗ᵢ,∇fₛ⟩·(fₜ-fₛ).

As above, using quadrature only requires that the ν⃗ᵢ, their derivatives, the signals fₛ and fₜ, and the gradient ∇fₛ be queryable.

Signal Advection

Finally, given a signal f and a flow-field v⃗, the advected signal, \hboxAdv_v⃗(f), is obtained by stepping backwards along the vector-field, using the hinge-map [DGDT16] to flatten adjacent triangles when stepping across an edge, and sampling.

5 Quadrature-based Integration

Discretizing the computation of optical flow requires resolving two conflicting challenges. On the one hand, the flow-field is expected to be relatively low-frequency, corresponding to the fact that the underlying deformation is smooth. On the other, we would like to represent the colors and confidences at the finer resolution of texel space. Additionally, both for computing the flow-field and stitching, we need the implementations to adapt to confidence.

We resolve these challenges using quadrature-based integration, which also supports mixing different signal representations. For scalar functions, we use the mesh-resolution “hat” basis and the texel-resolution basis of Prada et al.[PKCH18]. For vector-fields we use the mesh-resolution basis functions of Liu et al.[LSV∗26].

Using quadrature makes it straight-forward to incorporate color and confidence represented at texel-resolution when discretizing the flow-field at the vertex resolution. For completeness, we step through the implementation. In particular, we describe the evaluation of integrals for a triangle τ={p₀,p₁,p₂}⊂ℝ³, with the actual computation performed over the unit right triangle:

T={(s,t)∈[0,1]²|s+t≤1}.

We assume that we are given a confidence map w:T→[0,1], we set the metric tensor to be g∈ℝ^2×2 with gᵢⱼ=⟨pᵢ-p₀,pⱼ-p₀⟩, and we denote its determinant |g|. Lightly abusing notation, for a scalar- (resp. vector-)valued function f:T→ℝ (resp. v⃗:T→ℝ²), we write “f” (resp. “v⃗”) to represent both the function on the unit right triangle T and the function on the embedded triangle τ⊂ℝ³.

5.1 Integrating Scalar Functions

Given a scalar basis function φᵢ:T→ℝ and some other function f:T→ℝ, we approximate the integral of the confidence-weighted dot-product of φᵢ and f as:

∫_τw·φᵢ·f≈√|g|·∑ⱼ₌₁^Qμⱼ·w(qⱼ)·φᵢ(qⱼ)·f(qⱼ)

(3)

with {qⱼ,μⱼ}⊂T×ℝ^≥0 the quadrature locations and weights [Cow73, Tay08]. This estimate of the integral only requires that the target and confidence functions, f and w, be queryable, which is true for texture-mapped signals. A similar approach can be used to define the confidence-weighted mass and (assuming queryable derivatives of φᵢ) stiffness matrices.

5.2 Integrating Gradients of Scalar Functions

Given a tangent vector-field basis function ν⃗ᵢ:T→ℝ² and some other function f:T→ℝ, we approximate the confidence-weighted integral of the dot-product of ν⃗ᵢ and the gradient of f as:

∫_τw·⟨ν⃗ᵢ,∇f⟩≈√|g|·∑ⱼ₌₁^Qμⱼ·w(qⱼ)·⟨ν⃗ᵢ(qⱼ),∇_gf(qⱼ)⟩_g.

(4)

We note that the inner-product is equivalent to the pairing of the tangent vector-field ν⃗ᵢ with the differential of f, which is metric-independent. As above, the incorporation of confidence only requires that the functions f, ∇f, and w be queryable. This too holds for texture-mapped signals. And again, a similar approach can be used to define the confidence-weighted mass and (assuming queryable derivatives of ν⃗ᵢ) stiffness matrices.

6 Method

We now discuss the key steps of our pipeline, summarized in Alg. 1. To facilitate the presentation, we begin by describing how we adapt the traditional energies to incorporate confidence.

Gradient-Domain

Given a set of target values, target gradients, and confidences, {hᵢ,v⃗ᵢ,wᵢ}, we define the gradient-domain energy:

E_gd(f,{hᵢ,v⃗ᵢ,wᵢ},α_gf,α_reg)
≡∑ᵢ∫_Mwᵢ·((f-hᵢ)²+α_gf∥∇f-v⃗ᵢ∥²)+α_reg∥∇f∥²(5)

The additional regularization term, α_reg∥∇f∥², is needed to make the energy non-singular in regions of zero confidence. (In general, α_reg is set to a very small value and serves solely to encourage the signal to be smooth in regions with no confidence.)

In contexts where we have multiple weight functions, we normalize and rescale the weights:

wᵢ(q)←\underbrace((wᵢ(q))/(∑ⱼwⱼ(q)))(1-∏ⱼ(1-wⱼ(q)))_\mbox\scriptsizenormalization·(1-∏ⱼ(1-wⱼ(q))) (\mbox\scriptsizescaling).

Thus, the sum of the weights is (1-∏ⱼ(1-wⱼ))∈[0,1], giving the confidence that the point is covered by some target. (When all weights are zero, the normalized and rescaled weights remain zero.)

Blurring. The energy associated with blurring a signal h is obtained by setting α_gf=0 (and is independent of target gradient):

E_blur(f,h,w,α_reg)≡∫_Mw·(f-h)²+α_reg∥∇f∥²

(6)

Stitching. In the context of stitching together individual images, most often the target signals are the images themselves and the target vector-fields are their gradients, v⃗ᵢ=∇hᵢ. This gives:

E_stitch(f,{hᵢ,wᵢ},α_gf,α_reg)≡E_gd(f,{hᵢ,∇hᵢ,wᵢ},α_gf,α_reg).

(7)

This confidence-weighted expression obviates the challenges of compositing colors/gradients into a single function/vector-field, typically required as input for stitching. The confidences wᵢ implicitly dictate which values/gradients (and to what extent) should be “active” in different parts of the domain.

Optical Flow

Given source and target signals fₛ and fₜ, and confidence w, the optical flow energy is adapted as:

E_of(v⃗,fₛ,fₜ,w,β_reg)≡∫_Mw·((fₛ-⟨v⃗,∇fₛ⟩)-fₜ))²+β_reg∥∇v⃗∥².

(8)

Optimization

For the above energies, we denote their minimizers:

Stitch({hᵢ,wᵢ},α_gf,α_reg)≡\argmin_fE_stitch(f,{hᵢ,wᵢ},α_gf,α_reg)
Blur(h,w,α_reg)≡\argmin_fE_blur(f,h,w,α_reg)
Flow(fₛ,fₜ,w,β_reg)≡\argmin_v⃗E_of(v⃗,fₛ,fₜ,w,β_reg).(9)

Given a choice of queryable scalar/vector-field basis functions, the construction of the associated linear systems directly parallels the process described in Sec. 4, with integration adapted to incorporate confidence, as in Eqs. 3 and 4.

6.1 Preprocessing

Our pre-processing consists of two stages. Back-projecting to turn the renderings into texture color and confidence images, and normalization to correct for low-frequency variation of color in the generated rendering.

Back-Projection

Given the renderings and camera parameters, {{Yᵢ,Cᵢ}}ᵢ₌₁^K, we back-project the renderings onto the mesh M to obtain color and confidence textures, {{Iᵢ,wᵢ}}ᵢ₌₁^K.

Color

Given a rendering/camera {Yᵢ,Cᵢ}, we define the color at a texel by locating the corresponding point on the mesh, back-projecting using the camera parameters, and sampling Yᵢ at the back-projected position. The surface point is computed in two steps. First, we compute the barycentric coordinates of the texel with respect to the closest texture triangle. Then, we compute the barycentrically weighted average of the triangle’s corner positions in 3D. When the texel falls inside a texture triangle, the barycentric weights are positive and the average of the corners lies on the mesh. Otherwise, we map the average to the closest point on the mesh.

Confidence

Because the generated renderings may have silhouettes that are not consistent with the input geometry, back-projection can cause colors to fall far from their desired location on the surface. We address this by defining a confidence texture that combines normal and depth information. (Fig. 3 shows an example for the Bear model, where part of the belt near the silhouette of the arm is back-projected to the wrist. Combining normal and depth information, we assign texels near silhouettes lower confidence.)

Normal Confidence. We assign normal confidences by measuring the extent to which texels are front-facing to the camera. These are computed in the standard way, using the clamped dot-product of the surface normal and the camera’s viewing direction. Though this identifies locations on the silhouette, it fails to identify front-facing background pixels that are back-projected to the foreground.

Depth Confidence. To assign lower confidence to texels back-projecting to the foreground near silhouettes, we first identify pixels where the depth-map is discontinuous. This is achieved by rendering the scene from the perspective of the camera, computing the depth-map, and thresholding its Laplacian. The confidence is set to zero where the Laplacian exceeds the threshold and is reduced nearby. The confidence of occluded texels is also set to zero.

Finally, we multiply the depth and normal confidences and quantize low-confidences to zero. (See App. B for more details.)

While we instantiate these weights using normal/view-direction alignment and depth continuity, our approach equivalently accommodates other confidence information such as rendering quality/blurriness. Since our primary focus is registration and stitching, this step serves mainly to produce meaningful texture color and confidence images suitable for down-stream processing.

Color Normalization

We adjust the input signals to eliminate low-frequency color variations before estimating the flow. This is done by normalizing with respect to local estimates of the mean and scale:

I^′ᵢ←(Iᵢ-Blur(Iᵢ,wᵢ,εₙ))/(Blur(∥Iᵢ-Blur(Iᵢ,wᵢ,εₙ)∥,wᵢ,εₙ)).

(10)

The blurring is done taking into account confidence and εₙ>0 is a parameter describing the extent of the region over which the average and scale are estimated.

figure

Two back-projected renderings before (top) and after (bottom) color normalization. The input exhibits luminance and saturation variance. Normalization reduce the color inconsistency.

Normalization is crucial for the stability of optical flow. Fig. 4 shows an example of two un-normalized back-projected renderings (top) and the corresponding renderings after normalization (bottom). Due to color variations, the region of overlap is darker for the first rendering than it is for the second, resulting in (φₜ-φₛ) being set to the wrong target difference in Eq. 8. With normalization, the colors are more consistent.

6.2 Registration

Given back-projected color and confidence textures, {{I^′ᵢ,wᵢ}}ᵢ₌₁^K, our goal is to compute the optical flow-fields {v⃗ᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^K that best align the colors. Here we focus on a single time-step of the flow computation. The complete hierarchical solve is described in Alg. 1.

Direct Approach

A direct way to do this would be to define an energy that simultaneously optimizes all the flow-fields. This could be done for a pair of textures by noting that the optimization for the source flow-field v⃗ in Eq. 8 can be adapted to simultaneously optimize for the source and target flow-fields v⃗ₛ and v⃗ₜ by replacing the integrand accounting for advection along one field:

((fₛ-⟨v⃗,∇fₛ⟩)-fₜ)²

with an integrand accounting for the advection along both:

((fₛ-⟨v⃗ₛ,∇fₛ⟩)-(fₜ-⟨v⃗ₜ,∇fₜ⟩))².

One could then obtain an energy simultaneously optimizing all the flow-fields by taking the sum of the energies over all pairs of textures. Such an energy would remain sparse and quadratic. However, the system complexity would be proportional to the mesh resolution multiplied by the number of input views, which would be too expensive to solve in practice.

direct way to do this would be to define an energy that simultaneously optimizes all the optical flow-fields. This could be done by noting that for two color signals, Iₛ and Iₜ, with associated confidences, wₛ and wₜ, one can formulate the pairwise optical flow energy is:

E_of^{wₛ,wₜ}({v⃗ₛ,v⃗ₜ} | {fₛ,fₜ},α)
≡∫_Mwₛwₜ((fₛ-⟨v⃗ₛ,∇fₛ⟩)-(fₜ-⟨v⃗ₜ,∇fₜ⟩))²
+∫_Mα(∥∇v⃗ₛ∥²+∥∇v⃗ₜ∥²),

with the joint confidence is set to the product of the confidences. Then the optical flow energy simultaneously aligning all the colors signals is simply the sum of pairwise energies:

E_of^{wᵢ}({v⃗ᵢ} | {fᵢ},α)≡∑_i,jE_of^{wᵢ,wⱼ}({v⃗ᵢ,v⃗ⱼ} | {fᵢ,fⱼ},α).

The energy is quadratic and results in a sparse symmetric positive-definite system for the coefficients of the flow-fields. However, using it requires solving a system whose complexity is proportional to the mesh resolution, multiplied by the number of color signals, which is too time-consuming in practice.

Successive Signal Registration

Instead, we propose an incremental approach. We start by selecting a target signal and successively register the remaining signals to it. The target itself is evolved by blending in the advected source colors and confidences.

Source/Target Selection. To select the initial target and successive sources, we require a measure of overlap between pairs of signals. Defining the coverage of confidence w:M→ℝ^≥0 as:

⟨w⟩≡∫_Mw

we define the overlap of confidences w and w^′ to be the coverage of their product, ⟨w·w^′⟩. We then select the initial target by finding the pair of textures maximizing overlap, and use the one with larger coverage. Similarly, we select subsequent sources by finding the one maximizing the overlap with the current target.

Source Registration. Given source and target color texture images, I^′ₛ and I^′ₜ, with confidence texture images, wₛ and wₜ, we solve for the flow-field registering the source to the target:

v⃗=Flow(I^′ₛ,I^′ₜ,wₛ·wₜ,β_reg).

We advect the source’s texture color and confidence images along v⃗ and merge them into the target. The new target color is obtained by confidence-weighted blending of the textures registered so far:

I^′ₜ←(∑_i∈ℝ\hboxAdv_v⃗ᵢ(I^′ᵢ)·\hboxAdv_v⃗ᵢ(wᵢ))/(∑_i∈ℝ\hboxAdv_v⃗ᵢ(wᵢ))

where ℝ is the set of indices of the target and the sources registered to it, and the new target confidence is obtained by summing and clamping:

wₜ←\min(1, wₜ+\hboxAdv_v⃗(wₛ)).

Though the blended value is undefined where both the source and target have zero confidence, this does not cause numerical instability because the blended confidence will be zero there as well.

We note that while the target is not advected within a single pass of optical flow registration, the choice of selected target can change across the hierarchical passes. As a result it is possible that all back-projected textures are deformed at the end of the registration.

6.3 Stitching

The final step is stitching the advected texture color and confidence images into a seamless texture color image. We do this using the adaptation of classical gradient-domain stitching that supports confidences, presented in Eq. 7.

item.title: DXR 自 2018 年以来最大的一次更新：三角形聚成簇、TLAS 分区，光追也能直接画光栅用的全细节几何 ｜ [PREVIEW] Raytracing: Clustered Geometry, Partitioned TLAS, Indirect Acceleration Structures
item.description:
一句话：把加速结构构建单位从 BLAS 拆成可复用的三角簇，配 GPU 驱动的统一构建/更新 API。

要点：

  • 动机：动画、流送与程序化生成的几何会反复触发整块 BLAS 重建；Clustered Geometry 把构建单位拆成小的可复用三角簇，因此更新更便宜
  • 带来的直接好处是「光追可以直接用光栅化那套全细节几何」，不必再为光追单独准备简化网格——这会改变资产管线的分工

Today we’re introducing a preview of DirectX Raytracing (DXR) Clustered Geometry and Partitioned Top-Level Acceleration Structures (PTLAS), with a unified GPU-driven API for building and updating them.

This is part of a larger AgilitySDK release described in the parent post: https://devblogs.microsoft.com/directx/agilitysdk-1-620-retail-and-1-722-preview/

For DXR this is the most significant update since its debut in 2018.

Mar 2018DXR debut
Nov 2019Tier 1.1: inline raytracing and GPU-driven ray dispatch
Apr 2021Shader Model 6.6: payload access qualifiers
Feb 2026SM 6.9 / Tier 1.2: Shader Execution Reordering (SER) and Opacity Micromaps
Oct 2026

this preview

Clustered Geometry and Partitioned TLAS: GPU-driven efficient scene updates

Here’s the motivation for Clustered Geometry and Partitioned TLAS:

At object level scope within a scene, animation, streaming, and generated geometry can repeatedly incur the cost of building large bottom-level acceleration structures (BLAS). Clustered Geometry breaks the unit of building down into small reusable clusters of triangles. One benefit of more efficient builds is it can become practical to raytrace the same full-detail geometry used for rasterization, rather than simplified proxies, so ray-traced shadows and reflections match the visible scene.

At scene wide scope, updating a top-level acceleration structure (TLAS) can be costly for large worlds even if only a few instances changed. Partitioned TLAS focuses update costs on changed scene regions while retaining acceleration-structure data elsewhere.

Applications can use Clustered Geometry and PTLAS separately or together.

These features don’t require new hardware capabilities beyond existing raytracing support. Even in normal times this would be a wonderful thing.

The breadth of support will depend on hardware vendors implementing and validating drivers for each of their hardware generations. Support for some older raytracing GPUs is to be determined: implementation work may uncover performance issues, so exposing the features may be impractical for that or other reasons. For now, see Availability and prerequisites for currently supported hardware and drivers from AMD, Intel and NVIDIA (Qualcomm in 2027).

Gears of War: E-Day is an early example of a title adopting clustered geometry through NVIDIA’s vendor-specific API, RTX Mega Geometry. Standardizing these capabilities in DirectX provides a common integration path across supporting hardware, making them accessible to a broader range of future titles.

Since this is a preview, your feedback (Discord) can help refine the design before final release, or give us confidence to go to retail as soon as possible. There are various samples as well as PIX support to go with these features, detailed later in this blog.

NVIDIA has a great post with additional samples and resources here: https://github.com/NVIDIA-RTX/Whitepapers/blob/main/dx_clusters_and_ptlas/README.md

The scenes below are from that post, describing their 

dx12_forest_ray_tracing
demo which uses all of the new features to impressive effect.  This new D3D12 version is a work in progress, available soon. The sample uses cluster templates to optimize builds of its dynamic terrain. In the background, cluster templates form square patches, which are then doubled in resolution towards the midground and then recursively subdivided into triangular patches in the foreground. This achieves a nearly uniform screen-space triangle density.

Spec and API Overview

The following is a brief walkthrough of how code drives the new features.

See the spec for full detail: Clustered Geometry and Partitioned TLAS specification.

GPU-driven Acceleration Structure Builds

The raytracing acceleration-structure (RTAS) operation API has two entry points. 

GetRTASOperationPrebuildInfo()
queries conservative result and scratch requirements. 
ExecuteIndirectRTASOperations()
executes batches whose argument arrays, and where supported their counts, reside in GPU memory.

The CPU describes each operation and its workload bounds; compute shaders can generate the arguments. Cluster operations also support size-only queries and copy/move operations.

Operations submitted in one 

ExecuteIndirectRTASOperations()
call may execute in any order and must not depend on each other. Dependent stages need separate calls with barriers between them — for example, cluster builds → Cluster BLAS builds → PTLAS builds when an application combines Clustered Geometry and PTLAS.

Clustered Geometry

Clusters as raytracing building blocks

A Cluster Level Acceleration Structure (CLAS) contains an indexed mesh of up to 256 triangles and 256 vertices. An application builds a Cluster BLAS from a list of CLAS references, then creates instances of that BLAS in a non-partitioned TLAS or a Partitioned TLAS.

The point is to reduce aggregate acceleration structure build costs across smaller chunks.

Multiple Cluster BLAS can share a CLAS; TLAS instances reference BLAS, not individual CLAS.

The vertex positions in all CLAS used by a Cluster BLAS are expressed in that Cluster BLAS’s object space. There is no per-CLAS transform during assembly.

For streaming and level of detail (LOD), applications can assemble different sets of existing CLAS rather than rebuild from triangles. Meshlet-based geometry pipelines may already provide suitable triangle groupings.

The application assigns each CLAS a 32-bit 

ClusterID
, retrieved in hit shaders with 
ClusterID()
. 
PrimitiveIndex()
is local to the hit CLAS; use the pair to look up that triangle’s normals, materials, or other application data.

Shader Model 6.10 also requires support for 

TriangleObjectPositions()
and its 
RayQuery
counterparts, 
CandidateTriangleObjectPositions()
 and 
CommittedTriangleObjectPositions()
. When data access is enabled at build time, these intrinsics retrieve a triangle’s object-space vertex positions from the acceleration structure. This is useful with clustered geometry, for example to compute geometric normals without fetching positions from a separate vertex buffer.

Changing a referenced CLAS’s contents or address invalidates the Cluster BLAS, so it would need a rebuild along with dependent top-level structures.

Vertex position formats

Cluster builds support a range of vertex formats, including floating-point and normalized integer positions. For these formats, applications can also request truncation of low mantissa bits after conversion to float32, providing another way to quantize positions.

COMPRESSED1
is a fixed-point position encoding that uses a shared anchor and power-of-two scale for each cluster. Vertices store packed integer offsets from that anchor instead of three full floating-point values, with precision and range chosen for the content.

Position encodings and precision controls in the specification

Building CLAS from triangles

The 

BUILD_CLAS_FROM_TRIANGLES
operation builds one CLAS for each argument in a GPU array. Each argument references a cluster’s vertices and triangle indices.

This example lets the implementation place the CLAS within a single application-allocated result buffer. This is implicit-destination mode: the build writes an array of GPU addresses identifying where each CLAS was placed. In explicit-destination mode, the application supplies the individual result addresses instead.

With formats and workload limits already filled in 

clusterInputs
, select implicit destinations and query the batch’s result and scratch requirements:

clusterInputs.Mode = D3D12_RTAS_OPERATION_MODE_IMPLICIT_DESTINATIONS;

D3D12_RTAS_OPERATION_INPUTS inputs = {};
inputs.Type = D3D12_RTAS_OPERATION_TYPE_BUILD_CLAS_FROM_TRIANGLES;
inputs.pClusterTrianglesDesc = &clusterInputs;

D3D12_RTAS_OPERATION_PREBUILD_INFO sizes = {};
rtasDevice->GetRTASOperationPrebuildInfo(&inputs, &sizes);

Allocate 

clasResults
and 
clasScratch
using the returned sizes, plus an output address array with one entry per cluster:

D3D12_RTAS_BATCHED_OPERATION_DATA batch = {};
batch.BatchResultData = clasResults->GetGPUVirtualAddress();
batch.BatchScratchData = clasScratch->GetGPUVirtualAddress();
batch.ResultAddressArray = {
    clasAddresses->GetGPUVirtualAddress(),
    sizeof(D3D12_GPU_VIRTUAL_ADDRESS)
};
batch.IndirectArgumentArray = { argsGpuAddress, argsStride };

D3D12_RTAS_OPERATION_DESC build = {};
build.Inputs = inputs;
build.pBatchedOperationData = &batch;

rtasCommandList->ExecuteIndirectRTASOperations(
    1, &build, D3D12_EXECUTE_INDIRECT_RTAS_OPERATIONS_FLAG_NONE);

After the build and a barrier, the address array can feed a 

BUILD_BLAS_FROM_CLAS
operation to assemble the Cluster BLAS.

The sizing query must cover the entire implicit-destination batch; adding separate query results does not guarantee sufficient space.

Cluster templates for animation and generated geometry

Clustered geometry does not support refits, intentionally. For deforming meshes, cluster templates fill that role by precomputing position-independent build work. A template stores topology and other non-positional properties, but not final vertex positions. Instantiating it with positions produces a CLAS; the template itself cannot be traced.

For an animated mesh, a typical sequence is:

  • Build templates for the mesh’s clusters, optionally supplying example vertex positions as build hints.
  • Generate the current vertex positions with a compute shader.
  • Instantiate templates into CLAS using those positions.
  • Build a Cluster BLAS from the CLAS and update its top-level instances.

    • The template’s 

    VertexInstantiationFormat
    specifies the precision and range contract adhered to by stored positions, without dictating their physical storage layout. Positions supplied at instantiation use a separately selected 
    VertexSourceFormat
    . When the formats differ, instantiation converts the input to the template’s format contract.

    Templates also suit recurring topology in generated surfaces. Selecting different templates or CLAS permits topology and LOD changes without fixing the update topology of the entire object.

    Partitioned TLAS

    Partitioned TLAS is a functional superset of non-partitioned TLAS. It adds partitioned-based management and sparse updates, supporting existing BLAS types and Cluster BLAS.

    The point is to allow the cost of TLAS build to be proportional to the amount that changed in a scene as opposed to the entire scene.

    Applications assign persistent instance records to partitions. Grouping spatially coherent instances lets PTLAS build a structure for each group and combine those structures at the top level. A group that receives no changes can retain its built structure across frames.

    Frequently moving instances can instead use a special global partition, separate from those spatial groups. For building and tracing, each instance in the global partition behaves as if it were in its own partition, avoiding repeated work in larger spatial groups. Once an instance stops changing frequently, the application can move it back to a spatially appropriate partition.

    Overlapping partition bounds can hurt traversal. Global-partition membership trades partition rebuild work against the cost of handling instances individually; the best choice depends on layout and activity.

    PTLAS operation types

  • WRITE_INSTANCE
    writes complete instance records, including transforms and partition assignments. Use it to populate a PTLAS, move instances, or reassign them to partitions. Affected partitions are rebuilt.
  • UPDATE_INSTANCE
    changes only the referenced BLAS address and hit-group-table contribution, for example when swapping LODs. It does not change the instance transform. If the instance has explicit bounds, the replacement must fit within them. Without explicit bounds, updates may expand the instance bounds and trigger a partition refit.
  • TRANSLATE_PARTITION
    sets a partition’s translation without rewriting each instance’s transform, supporting origin-relative large-world coordinates. Partition translation must be enabled; each value replaces the previous translation rather than accumulating.

    • Operation argument layouts and validity rules

    Updating a Partitioned TLAS

    Sparse transform changes require 

    WRITE_INSTANCE
    , not 
    UPDATE_INSTANCE
    . After populating the PTLAS, a compute pass generates writes for just the changed instances. Each write’s stable 
    InstanceIndex
    identifies the persistent record, not its position in that frame’s write array. Unwritten records remain unchanged.

    A 

    WRITE_INSTANCE
    operation in the GPU operation buffer references that write array:

    D3D12_RTAS_PARTITIONED_TLAS_OPERATION_DATA data = {};
data.SourceAccelerationStructureData = ptlas->GetGPUVirtualAddress();
data.DestAccelerationStructureData = ptlas->GetGPUVirtualAddress();
data.ScratchAccelerationStructureData = scratch->GetGPUVirtualAddress();
data.IndirectPartitionedTlasOpCount = operationCount->GetGPUVirtualAddress();
data.IndirectPartitionedTlasOps = operations->GetGPUVirtualAddress();

D3D12_RTAS_OPERATION_DESC update = {};
update.Inputs.Type = D3D12_RTAS_OPERATION_TYPE_PARTITIONED_TLAS;
update.Inputs.pPartitionedTLASInputsDesc = &ptlasInputs;
update.pPartitionedTlasOperationData = &data;

rtasCommandList->ExecuteIndirectRTASOperations(
    1, &update, D3D12_EXECUTE_INDIRECT_RTAS_OPERATIONS_FLAG_NONE);

    Source and destination match for an in-place update; the initial build has no source. Allocation must cover declared instance and partition capacities, not just the current write count.

    IndirectPartitionedTlasOpCount
    points to the operation count, whereas each 
    WRITE_INSTANCE
    operation’s 
    ArgCount
    counts instance writes. Here the operation count is one; compute varies 
    ArgCount
    as instances change.

    Availability and prerequisites

    Use matching Agility SDK preview headers and runtime, a supporting driver, and Windows Developer Mode for experimental feature enablement.

    Agility SDK:

  • 1.722.0-preview available here:Agility SDK downloads

    • DirectX Shader Compiler:

  • Shader Model 6.10 preview release, Patch 2 (v1.10.2605.37), also available as the Microsoft.Direct3D.DXC 1.10.2605.37-preview NuGet package.

    • Drivers and hardware:

    NVIDIANVIDIA and Microsoft have been collaborating closely to bring Clusters and Partitioned Top Level Acceleration Structures to DirectX Raytracing. These features enable unprecedented levels of animated geometric detail and unlock new algorithms including path tracing of hierarchical LOD streaming solutions found in modern game engines. We are excited to fully support this update to DXR on all RTX GPUs.

    – Martin Stich, Senior Director of Engineering

    Drivers:Download the official NVIDIA drivers or use the NVIDIA App for automatic driver updates.

    Supported hardware: All RTX GPUs

    AMDClustered Geometry and Partitioned TLAS are important advancements for the DirectX Raytracing ecosystem. The ability to reuse geometry work through clusters and update only the portions of a scene that have changed can significantly improve scalability for streaming content, level-of-detail transitions, animation, and large open-world experiences.

    – Rodney Andre, Corp. VP Software Development, AMD

    Drivers:https://www.amd.com/en/resources/support-articles/release-notes/RN-RAD-MS-AGILITY-SDK-26-20-12-01.html.

    Supported hardware: AMD Radeon™ RX 9000series GPUs

    IntelThe latest agility SDK brings a major improvement in raytracing in the form of PTLAS/cluster APIs. They set the foundation for efficient updates and management of very large and complex scenes, while keeping the memory footprint low, allow developers to represent their scenes with high fidelity without excessive memory usage. We’re very happy to support this API early on to enable smooth developer adoption over the coming months!

    –Matthäus Chajdas, Senior Principal Engineer, Intel

    Drivers:https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/download/931698

    Supported hardware:

  • Intel® Arc™ B-Series Graphics
  • Intel® Core™ Ultra processor family (200V series, Series 3)
    • QualcommDirectX Clustered Geometry and Partitioned TLAS represent important advancements for next-generation gaming experiences on Snapdragon® compute platforms. Qualcomm is working closely with Microsoft to enable these features on Snapdragon X2 platforms, with driver support targeted for availability in Q1/Q2 2027.
    WARP Software Rendererhttps://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.Direct3D.WARP/1.65535.22-preview

    Before device creation, enable the preview:

    UUID features[] = {
    D3D12ExperimentalShaderModels,
    D3D12RaytracingPreview
};
ThrowIfFailed(D3D12EnableExperimentalFeatures(
    _countof(features), features, nullptr, nullptr));

    Query support through 

    ID3D12Device16
    :

    D3D12_FEATURE_DATA_D3D12_OPTIONS_RAYTRACING2 options = {};
ThrowIfFailed(device16->CheckFeatureSupport1(
    D3D12_FEATURE_D3D12_OPTIONS_RAYTRACING2,
    &options, sizeof(options), D3D12_PREVIEW_SDK_VERSION));

if (!options.ClustersAndPTLASSupported)
{
    // Fall back to traditional BLAS/TLAS path or report unsupported hardware.
}

    Clustered Geometry’s shader intrinsics use Shader Model 6.10. Raytracing pipelines that traverse Cluster BLAS opt in with 

    D3D12_RAYTRACING_PIPELINE_FLAG_ALLOW_CLUSTERED_GEOMETRY
    . Inline raytracing uses the corresponding clustered-geometry 
    RayQuery
    flag.

    Samples

    D3D12 Clustered Geometry sample

    D3D12RaytracingClusteredGeometry is a cluster sandbox for experimenting with build modes, allocation strategies, vertex formats and precision, workload size, and primary rays per pixel. Procedural objects exercise CLAS builds, while an animated sphere demonstrates template instantiation.

    The scene is programmer art, with the goal to help you build intuition for how clusters behave as you change the settings.

    You can switch between building BLAS from triangles and assembling Cluster BLAS for the same scene, with allocation sizes and GPU build timings shown in the overlay.

    In the pair of images below running on an AMD RX 9070, the first shows traditional BLAS mode, and the second Clustered Geometry mode.  Since the stats are hard to read with jpg compression, the table below highlights the differences.  This is just one configuration, so keep in mind conclusions might vary depending on settings / load / GPU.

    MetricTraditional BLAS rebuildClustered geometryCluster vs Traditional
    Frame rate1.2 FPS79 FPS~66x higher
    Per-frame GPU AS preparation/build788 ms3.11 ms~254x less time
    Per-frame GPU raytracing72.6 ms9.27 ms~7.8x less time
    Static AS memory723 MiB527 MiB27.0% less
    Animated AS memory6,794 MiB244 MiB96.4% less

inputs.pClusterTrianglesDesc = &clusterInputs;

D3D12_RTAS_OPERATION_PREBUILD_INFO sizes = {};
rtasDevice->GetRTASOperationPrebuildInfo(&inputs, &sizes);

Allocate 

clasResults
and 
clasScratch
using the returned sizes, plus an output address array with one entry per cluster:

D3D12_RTAS_BATCHED_OPERATION_DATA batch = {};
batch.BatchResultData = clasResults->GetGPUVirtualAddress();
batch.BatchScratchData = clasScratch->GetGPUVirtualAddress();
batch.ResultAddressArray = {
    clasAddresses->GetGPUVirtualAddress(),
    sizeof(D3D12_GPU_VIRTUAL_ADDRESS)
};
batch.IndirectArgumentArray = { argsGpuAddress, argsStride };

D3D12_RTAS_OPERATION_DESC build = {};
build.Inputs = inputs;
build.pBatchedOperationData = &batch;

rtasCommandList->ExecuteIndirectRTASOperations(
    1, &build, D3D12_EXECUTE_INDIRECT_RTAS_OPERATIONS_FLAG_NONE);

After the build and a barrier, the address array can feed a 

BUILD_BLAS_FROM_CLAS
operation to assemble the Cluster BLAS.

The sizing query must cover the entire implicit-destination batch; adding separate query results does not guarantee sufficient space.

Cluster templates for animation and generated geometry

Clustered geometry does not support refits, intentionally. For deforming meshes, cluster templates fill that role by precomputing position-independent build work. A template stores topology and other non-positional properties, but not final vertex positions. Instantiating it with positions produces a CLAS; the template itself cannot be traced.

For an animated mesh, a typical sequence is:

  • Build templates for the mesh’s clusters, optionally supplying example vertex positions as build hints.
  • Generate the current vertex positions with a compute shader.
  • Instantiate templates into CLAS using those positions.
  • Build a Cluster BLAS from the CLAS and update its top-level instances.

    • The template’s 

    VertexInstantiationFormat
    specifies the precision and range contract adhered to by stored positions, without dictating their physical storage layout. Positions supplied at instantiation use a separately selected 
    VertexSourceFormat
    . When the formats differ, instantiation converts the input to the template’s format contract.

    Templates also suit recurring topology in generated surfaces. Selecting different templates or CLAS permits topology and LOD changes without fixing the update topology of the entire object.

    Partitioned TLAS

    Partitioned TLAS is a functional superset of non-partitioned TLAS. It adds partitioned-based management and sparse updates, supporting existing BLAS types and Cluster BLAS.

    The point is to allow the cost of TLAS build to be proportional to the amount that changed in a scene as opposed to the entire scene.

    Applications assign persistent instance records to partitions. Grouping spatially coherent instances lets PTLAS build a structure for each group and combine those structures at the top level. A group that receives no changes can retain its built structure across frames.

    Frequently moving instances can instead use a special global partition, separate from those spatial groups. For building and tracing, each instance in the global partition behaves as if it were in its own partition, avoiding repeated work in larger spatial groups. Once an instance stops changing frequently, the application can move it back to a spatially appropriate partition.

    Overlapping partition bounds can hurt traversal. Global-partition membership trades partition rebuild work against the cost of handling instances individually; the best choice depends on layout and activity.

    PTLAS operation types

  • WRITE_INSTANCE
    writes complete instance records, including transforms and partition assignments. Use it to populate a PTLAS, move instances, or reassign them to partitions. Affected partitions are rebuilt.
  • UPDATE_INSTANCE
    changes only the referenced BLAS address and hit-group-table contribution, for example when swapping LODs. It does not change the instance transform. If the instance has explicit bounds, the replacement must fit within them. Without explicit bounds, updates may expand the instance bounds and trigger a partition refit.
  • TRANSLATE_PARTITION
    sets a partition’s translation without rewriting each instance’s transform, supporting origin-relative large-world coordinates. Partition translation must be enabled; each value replaces the previous translation rather than accumulating.

    • Operation argument layouts and validity rules

    Updating a Partitioned TLAS

    Sparse transform changes require 

    WRITE_INSTANCE
    , not 
    UPDATE_INSTANCE
    . After populating the PTLAS, a compute pass generates writes for just the changed instances. Each write’s stable 
    InstanceIndex
    identifies the persistent record, not its position in that frame’s write array. Unwritten records remain unchanged.

    A 

    WRITE_INSTANCE
    operation in the GPU operation buffer references that write array:

    D3D12_RTAS_PARTITIONED_TLAS_OPERATION_DATA data = {};
data.SourceAccelerationStructureData = ptlas->GetGPUVirtualAddress();
data.DestAccelerationStructureData = ptlas->GetGPUVirtualAddress();
data.ScratchAccelerationStructureData = scratch->GetGPUVirtualAddress();
data.IndirectPartitionedTlasOpCount = operationCount->GetGPUVirtualAddress();
data.IndirectPartitionedTlasOps = operations->GetGPUVirtualAddress();

D3D12_RTAS_OPERATION_DESC update = {};
update.Inputs.Type = D3D12_RTAS_OPERATION_TYPE_PARTITIONED_TLAS;
update.Inputs.pPartitionedTLASInputsDesc = &ptlasInputs;
update.pPartitionedTlasOperationData = &data;

rtasCommandList->ExecuteIndirectRTASOperations(
    1, &update, D3D12_EXECUTE_INDIRECT_RTAS_OPERATIONS_FLAG_NONE);

    Source and destination match for an in-place update; the initial build has no source. Allocation must cover declared instance and partition capacities, not just the current write count.

    IndirectPartitionedTlasOpCount
    points to the operation count, whereas each 
    WRITE_INSTANCE
    operation’s 
    ArgCount
    counts instance writes. Here the operation count is one; compute varies 
    ArgCount
    as instances change.

    Availability and prerequisites

    Use matching Agility SDK preview headers and runtime, a supporting driver, and Windows Developer Mode for experimental feature enablement.

    Agility SDK:

  • 1.722.0-preview available here:Agility SDK downloads

    • DirectX Shader Compiler:

  • Shader Model 6.10 preview release, Patch 2 (v1.10.2605.37), also available as the Microsoft.Direct3D.DXC 1.10.2605.37-preview NuGet package.

    • Drivers and hardware:

    NVIDIANVIDIA and Microsoft have been collaborating closely to bring Clusters and Partitioned Top Level Acceleration Structures to DirectX Raytracing. These features enable unprecedented levels of animated geometric detail and unlock new algorithms including path tracing of hierarchical LOD streaming solutions found in modern game engines. We are excited to fully support this update to DXR on all RTX GPUs.

    – Martin Stich, Senior Director of Engineering

    Drivers:Download the official NVIDIA drivers or use the NVIDIA App for automatic driver updates.

    Supported hardware: All RTX GPUs

    AMDClustered Geometry and Partitioned TLAS are important advancements for the DirectX Raytracing ecosystem. The ability to reuse geometry work through clusters and update only the portions of a scene that have changed can significantly improve scalability for streaming content, level-of-detail transitions, animation, and large open-world experiences.

    – Rodney Andre, Corp. VP Software Development, AMD

    Drivers:https://www.amd.com/en/resources/support-articles/release-notes/RN-RAD-MS-AGILITY-SDK-26-20-12-01.html.

    Supported hardware: AMD Radeon™ RX 9000series GPUs

    IntelThe latest agility SDK brings a major improvement in raytracing in the form of PTLAS/cluster APIs. They set the foundation for efficient updates and management of very large and complex scenes, while keeping the memory footprint low, allow developers to represent their scenes with high fidelity without excessive memory usage. We’re very happy to support this API early on to enable smooth developer adoption over the coming months!

    –Matthäus Chajdas, Senior Principal Engineer, Intel

    Drivers:https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/download/931698

    Supported hardware:

  • Intel® Arc™ B-Series Graphics
  • Intel® Core™ Ultra processor family (200V series, Series 3)
    • QualcommDirectX Clustered Geometry and Partitioned TLAS represent important advancements for next-generation gaming experiences on Snapdragon® compute platforms. Qualcomm is working closely with Microsoft to enable these features on Snapdragon X2 platforms, with driver support targeted for availability in Q1/Q2 2027.
    WARP Software Rendererhttps://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.Direct3D.WARP/1.65535.22-preview

    Before device creation, enable the preview:

    UUID features[] = {
    D3D12ExperimentalShaderModels,
    D3D12RaytracingPreview
};
ThrowIfFailed(D3D12EnableExperimentalFeatures(
    _countof(features), features, nullptr, nullptr));

    Query support through 

    ID3D12Device16
    :

    D3D12_FEATURE_DATA_D3D12_OPTIONS_RAYTRACING2 options = {};
ThrowIfFailed(device16->CheckFeatureSupport1(
    D3D12_FEATURE_D3D12_OPTIONS_RAYTRACING2,
    &options, sizeof(options), D3D12_PREVIEW_SDK_VERSION));

if (!options.ClustersAndPTLASSupported)
{
    // Fall back to traditional BLAS/TLAS path or report unsupported hardware.
}

    Clustered Geometry’s shader intrinsics use Shader Model 6.10. Raytracing pipelines that traverse Cluster BLAS opt in with 

    D3D12_RAYTRACING_PIPELINE_FLAG_ALLOW_CLUSTERED_GEOMETRY
    . Inline raytracing uses the corresponding clustered-geometry 
    RayQuery
    flag.

    Samples

    D3D12 Clustered Geometry sample

    D3D12RaytracingClusteredGeometry is a cluster sandbox for experimenting with build modes, allocation strategies, vertex formats and precision, workload size, and primary rays per pixel. Procedural objects exercise CLAS builds, while an animated sphere demonstrates template instantiation.

    The scene is programmer art, with the goal to help you build intuition for how clusters behave as you change the settings.

    You can switch between building BLAS from triangles and assembling Cluster BLAS for the same scene, with allocation sizes and GPU build timings shown in the overlay.

    In the pair of images below running on an AMD RX 9070, the first shows traditional BLAS mode, and the second Clustered Geometry mode.  Since the stats are hard to read with jpg compression, the table below highlights the differences.  This is just one configuration, so keep in mind conclusions might vary depending on settings / load / GPU.

    MetricTraditional BLAS rebuildClustered geometryCluster vs Traditional
    Frame rate1.2 FPS79 FPS~66x higher
    Per-frame GPU AS preparation/build788 ms3.11 ms~254x less time
    Per-frame GPU raytracing72.6 ms9.27 ms~7.8x less time
    Static AS memory723 MiB527 MiB27.0% less
    Animated AS memory6,794 MiB244 MiB96.4% less

item.title: GPU 崩溃能带回来看了：DirectX Dump Files 正式可用于零售游戏，四家驱动数据统一在 PIX 里查 ｜ DirectX Dump Files are now ready for your retail games
item.description:
一句话：从玩家机器抓 GPU 崩溃现场，用同一套 PIX 工作流跨 AMD/Intel/NVIDIA/Qualcomm 分析。

要点：

  • 需要 Agility SDK 1.620 与 PIX 2610.28：可以在玩家 PC 上、也可以在自己机器上捕获 GPU 崩溃，然后用同一套 PIX 工作流排查
  • 数据来自 Windows、Direct3D 与各家驱动，微软与 AMD、Intel、NVIDIA、Qualcomm 合作完成；因为各家提供的数据不同，看到的细节会随硬件与驱动版本变化
  • 今年 6 月是公共预览，现在正式可用于已发售游戏——意味着线上 GPU 崩溃终于有「带现场」的排查路径，而不是只有错误码与用户描述

为什么值得看：线上 GPU 崩溃一直是「只能猜」的问题域：日志有限、用户描述模糊、复现困难。能把 dump 带回来并在 PIX 里跨厂商打开，等于把 PC 端的调试体验往主机靠了一大步。对有小规模 QA 团队的团队，这能直接减少一轮无头排查。

中文摘要：微软宣布 DirectX Dump Files 正式可用于零售游戏（此前在 6 月开放公共预览）。从 Agility SDK 1.620 与 PIX 2610.28 起，开发者可以在玩家 PC 上、也可以在自己机器上捕获 GPU 崩溃，然后用同一套 PIX 工作流分析，跨硬件厂商保持一致。这项能力整合了 Windows、Direct3D 以及各家硬件驱动提供的数据，由微软与 AMD、Intel、NVIDIA、Qualcomm 合作完成；由于数据来源不同，可看到的细节会随厂商与驱动版本变化。官方给出 Learn 上的分步指南与 D3D12 Dump Files 规范。对线上问题排查来说，这补上了此前「只有错误码和用户描述」的空白。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：DirectX Dev Blog（English）

原文发布：2026-10-28

本期推送：2026-10-29

At GDC 2026, we shared our vision for bringing console-level GPU developer tools to Windows, and in June we released the DirectX Dump Files public preview. Thank you to everyone who tried the preview and sent us feedback.

Today, DirectX Dump Files are ready for your retail games. Starting with Agility SDK 1.620 and PIX 2610.28, you can capture GPU crashes on your players’ PCs and on your own machines, then investigate them in PIX using one consistent workflow across hardware vendors.

We couldn’t have done this alone. DirectX Dump Files bring together data from Windows, Direct3D, and each hardware vendor’s driver, and we built them in close collaboration with AMD, Intel, NVIDIA, and Qualcomm. Thank you to all of our hardware partners. Because each vendor provides its own data, what you’ll see varies by hardware vendor and driver version.

Step-by-step guides are on Microsoft Learn, and the full details are in the specification, D3D12: DirectX Dump Files. For everything else in this release, see the Agility SDK 1.620 announcement and the PIX 2610.28 release post.

What’s new since the preview

What’s newDetails
Ready for retailUse DirectX Dump Files in your shipping game with Agility SDK 1.620. Developer Mode isn’t required. Learn more
Final file formatDump files now use the 
.dxdmp
extension (the preview used 
.dxdmp_preview
). Learn more
Retail-friendly defaultsThe NO_OVERHEAD dump file driver option is on by default, with no impact on players. Dump files aren’t kept on players’ PCs unless your game retains or uploads them. Learn more
Broader hardware supportDriver-backed dump files are rolling out across our hardware partners. See Hardware support.
PIX markers in retail dump filesRetail PIX Markers put your PIX markers in dump files. Learn more
PIX 2610.28Hang bucketing in the Summary view; shaders and resources that help you find the root cause of a crash; and the PIX API, now generally available. Learn more
Guides on Microsoft LearnNew guides cover generating and retrieving and analyzing dump files.

From crash to analysis

How a DirectX Dump File gets from a GPU crash to PIX.

  • Generate. When your GPU work stops making progress, DirectX captures a dump file before Windows resets the GPU, so the dump file reflects the GPU’s state at the time of the crash. It includes Direct3D runtime state, hardware and driver data from drivers that support DirectX Dump Files, and up to 2 MB of your own data.
  • Retrieve. On your development and QA machines, keep dump files on disk. On players’ PCs, dump files aren’t kept by default, so the dump file end callback tells your game where each one is, and your crash pipeline uploads it. Today, retrieving dump files from players’ PCs is up to your pipeline; we’re working on making it easier.
  • Analyze. Open the dump file in PIX on any PC. You don’t need the GPU or driver that crashed, because PIX decodes each vendor’s data with plugins from our hardware partners. PIX also analyzes the dump file for you: it identifies what kind of hang occurred and points you to the shaders and resources involved, so you can fix it faster.

    • Three scenarios

    How much detail you get depends on where your game is running. Higher overhead options capture more data at a higher runtime cost, so you can choose the right balance for each scenario.

    Development and QA

    When it makes sense: A crash happens on your own machine, or your QA team hits crashes while testing across a range of PC hardware. You don’t need to reproduce it: you get a dump file when a crash happens. Detail matters more than runtime cost here.

    What to do: Call the 

    RetainDumpFile
    API to keep dump files on disk, ready to open in PIX or attach to a bug report. If the driver doesn’t support NO_OVERHEAD, or a NO_OVERHEAD dump file doesn’t have enough data to find the root cause, select MEDIUM_OVERHEAD or HIGH_OVERHEAD with 
    ConfigureDumpFile
    in your development and QA builds, or with D3DConfig on your own machine without changing code. Learn more

    Everyday retail play

    When it makes sense: Your game has shipped. You don’t want to affect your players’ experience, but if the GPU crashes, you want data you can act on.

    What to do: The NO_OVERHEAD dump file driver option is on by default, with no code changes and no impact on players. Drivers that don’t support it ignore it, and you still get a dump file with Direct3D runtime context and your application’s data. To make each dump file useful, add context such as your build ID or current level with 

    AddBlobToDumpFile
    , and use the dump file end callback to upload the dump file through your crash pipeline. Learn more

    Chasing a rare retail crash

    When it makes sense: A crash keeps showing up on players’ PCs, you can’t reproduce it, and the default dump files don’t tell you enough to fix it.

    What to do: On a few players’ PCs, turn on MEDIUM_OVERHEAD or HIGH_OVERHEAD with 

    ConfigureDumpFile
    , for example with a command-line argument or a setting your game checks at startup. Higher overhead can lower frame rates or use more memory, so keep it to a session or two, upload the dump files through your crash pipeline, and then turn it back off. Learn more

    Get started

    Here’s what you need and what to do at each stage. The Learn more links go to the step-by-step guides.

    StageWhat you needWhat to do
    1. Generate
    On the PC that crashes    		Windows 11, version 24H2 or 25H2, build 26100.8524 or 26200.8524 or later (KB5089573)
    Agility SDK 1.620 or later
    Any GPU driver. Supported drivers add hardware state and driver data; see Hardware support.
    Developer Mode isn’t required.    		DirectX generates a dump file when a crash happens, even if you skip these optional steps. They let you check support, choose how much data to capture, and add your own data.
    1. Check support with 
    CheckFeatureSupport
    (
    D3D12_FEATURE_DUMP_FILE
    ).
    2. Choose an overhead option with 
    ConfigureDumpFile
    .
    3. Register begin and end callbacks with 
    SetDumpFileCallbacks
    , and add your own data with 
    AddBlobToDumpFile
    .
    On your development machine, D3DConfig can override these settings without code changes.
    Learn more: D3D12: DirectX Dump Files spec · Learn guide
    2. Retrieve
    Locally or through your pipeline    		Development and QA: no extra setup
    Players’ PCs: a crash pipeline that can upload files    		Development and QA: call the 
    RetainDumpFile
    API, or use D3DConfig, to keep dump files in 
    %LOCALAPPDATA%\CrashDumps
    .
    Players’ PCs: in the dump file end callback, get the dump file’s path and upload it with your other crash data.
    Learn more: Learn guide
    3. Analyze
    On any PC    		PIX 2610.28 or later. You don’t need the GPU or driver that crashed.1. Set your shader object and PDB search paths in PIX.
    2. Open the 
    .dxdmp
    file and start with the Summary view, and inspect information populated in other views.
    3. Go further with the PIX API or AI agents.
    Learn more: Learn guide · PIX API samples

    Hardware support

    IHVSupported GPUsOverhead optionsPIX pluginPIX markers in dump files
    AMDRadeon RX 9000 Series and Radeon RX 7000 SeriesMEDIUM_OVERHEAD, HIGH_OVERHEADIncluded in PIX 2610.28Yes
    IntelComing soonComing soonComing soonComing soon
    NVIDIANVIDIA Turing and newer, with R620 or later driversNO_OVERHEAD, MEDIUM_OVERHEAD, HIGH_OVERHEADIncluded in PIX 2610.28Yes
    QualcommSnapdragon X2 platformComing soonComing soonComing soon

    Dump files from any GPU include Direct3D runtime context and your application’s data. NO_OVERHEAD is suitable for regular gameplay, with no impact on players; MEDIUM_OVERHEAD and HIGH_OVERHEAD capture more data at a higher runtime cost. Each hardware vendor shares which of its drivers support DirectX Dump Files. For more information, contact your hardware vendor’s developer relations representative.

    What you’ll see in PIX

    PIX uses the same views for dump files from every hardware vendor, but what each view can show depends on the data that vendor’s driver and PIX plugin provide. Views marked with an asterisk (*) depend on hardware vendor support. For screenshots and details of each view, see the PIX 2610.28 release post.

    ViewWhat it shows
    SummaryHang buckets, possible causes of the crash, and related information
    Events *Driver events and PIX markers, with execution status, from the plugin; otherwise DRED breadcrumbs and PIX markers
    Page Faults *Faulting GPU addresses and the resources that covered them from the plugin; otherwise the faulting address and allocations from DRED, if page fault reporting is on
    Resources *Resource details from the D3D12 runtime, plus extra properties and lifetime events from the plugin when available
    Shader Waves *Executing shader waves, with lanes, stage, exceptions, and the current instruction
    Shaders *DXIL, HLSL, and ISA support for executing shaders
    Shader Autos *Shader registers for a selected wave and lane
    D3D12 API ObjectsCommand queues, command allocators, and other runtime objects
    Application BlobsThe data your app added with 
    AddBlobToDumpFile
    File DetailsDriver, adapter, device, OS, and application details

    * Depends on hardware vendor support.

    Go further

  • Put your PIX markers in dump files. By default, PIX markers don’t reach the GPU driver, so they aren’t in dump files. Turn on Retail PIX Markers and they show up in your dump files, so you can see where the GPU was in your frame when it crashed. See D3D12: PIX Markers.
  • Automate analysis with the PIX API. The PIX API is now generally available and installs with PIX 2610.28, so you can analyze dump files at scale. See the PIX API documentation and samples.
  • Analyze with AI agents. PIX 2610.28 includes the DxDmp command-line tools and an MCP server for AI-assisted analysis. Learn more

    • Known issues

  • Data varies by hardware vendor. If the data in a dump file does not help you root cause the crash, let us know and ask your hardware vendor’s developer relations contact to add it.
  • Software device removals, as opposed to TDRs, don’t generate a dump file yet. Support is planned for a future release.

    • What’s next

  • More data from our hardware partners, added to their dump files and shown through their PIX plugins over time.
  • Easier uploads of dump files from your players’ PCs.
  • More hardware support as drivers and PIX plugins roll out. We’ll update this post as support lands.
  • DebugBreak(), which lets a shader trigger a dump file on purpose, coming with Shader Model 6.10 in a retail Agility SDK soon.

    • Tell us what you think

    Tell us what’s working, what isn’t, and what you’d like to see next in the #dxdmp channel on the DirectX Discord, with Help > Send Feedback in PIX, or at dxdmpsupport@microsoft.com.

    Resources

  • D3D12: DirectX Dump Files specification
  • DirectX Dump Files on Microsoft Learn
  • PIX 2610.28 download · PIX 2610.28 release post
  • DirectX 12 Agility SDK downloads · Agility SDK 1.620 announcement
  • DirectX Dump Files preview announcement · GDC 2026 session

    • Category

  • DirectX

    • Topics

  • DXDMP Files
  • PIX

    • Author

    Senior Product Manager for PIX

    Principal Software Engineer

    Stay informed

    Get notified when new posts are published.Follow this blog
